lessons.title: Spotting and continuing sequences
notes: A sequence is a list of numbers in order. Each number is called a term. The position tells you where a term is in the list.
Look at how much the numbers change each time. Check the rule between every pair of neighbouring terms. A short list can sometimes fit more than one rule.
note_points: A sequence is a list of numbers in order.
Each number is called a term.
The position tells you where a term is in the list.
Look at how much the numbers change each time.
Check the rule between every pair of neighbouring terms.
A short list can sometimes fit more than one rule.
lessons.worked: For 5, 9, 13, 17, add 4 each time. 17 + 4 = 21, then 21 + 4 = 25. The next two terms are 21 and 25.
worked_steps: The next two terms are 21 and 25.
lessons.question: Continue 7, 12, 17, 22. Give the next two terms and explain the rule.
scheme: Both new terms follow the same rule.
lessons.mistake: The position of a term is not the same as its value.

cards.definition: A number or item in a sequence.
The instruction used to get from one term to the next.

quiz.q: What comes next in 3, 7, 11, 15?
quiz.why: Add 4 each time: 15 + 4 = 19.

misconception.q: What comes next in 3, 7, 11, 15? Sam answers: “18.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Different types of sequence
notes: An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount each time. A geometric sequence multiplies by the same number each time. A quadratic sequence has changes that themselves change by a fixed amount.
Write the differences between neighbouring terms. If these are not equal, compare the next row of differences. Also check whether multiplying by the same number works.
note_points: An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount each time.
A geometric sequence multiplies by the same number each time.
A quadratic sequence has changes that themselves change by a fixed amount.
Write the differences between neighbouring terms.
If these are not equal, compare the next row of differences.
Also check whether multiplying by the same number works.
lessons.worked: For 1, 4, 9, 16, the differences are 3, 5, 7. These differences go up by 2, so this is a quadratic pattern. For 3, 6, 12, 24, multiply by 2 instead.
worked_steps: These differences go up by 2, so this is a quadratic pattern.
lessons.question: Continue 2, 6, 18, 54 by one term. Why is this not an arithmetic sequence?
scheme: The differences between terms are not equal.
lessons.mistake: A growing sequence does not always add the same amount each time.

cards.definition: A sequence that adds the same amount each time.
A sequence that multiplies by the same number each time.

quiz.q: Which sequence multiplies by the same number each time?
quiz.why: Each term in 2, 6, 18, 54 is three times the one before.

misconception.q: Which sequence multiplies by the same number each time? Sam answers: “2, 5, 8, 11.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Each term in 2, 6, 18, 54 is three times the one before.

lessons.title: A rule for any term
notes: An nth-term rule lets you find a term from its position. The letter n stands for the position. An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount each time.

Start with the difference multiplied by n. Compare this with the actual sequence and adjust by adding or subtracting. Check your rule for the first few positions. A term belongs to a sequence only if its position is a positive whole number.
note_points: An nth-term rule lets you find a term from its position.
The letter n stands for the position.
An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount each time.
Start with the difference multiplied by n.
Compare this with the actual sequence and adjust by adding or subtracting.
Check your rule for the first few positions.
A term belongs to a sequence only if its position is a positive whole number.
lessons.worked: For 7, 11, 15, 19, the difference is 4. 4n gives 4, 8, 12, 16, so add 3: the rule is 4n + 3. The twentieth term is 4 × 20 + 3 = 83.
worked_steps: 4n gives 4, 8, 12, 16, so add 3: the rule is 4n + 3.
lessons.question: Find the nth-term rule for 8, 13, 18, 23. Use it to find the tenth term.
lessons.mistake: “Add 5” finds the next term. “5n + 3” finds a term from its position.

cards.definition: A rule that finds a term from its position n.
Where a term appears in a sequence, starting at 1.

quiz.q: What is the fifth term of 3n + 2?
quiz.why: Put n = 5 into the rule: 3 × 5 + 2 = 17.

misconception.q: What is the fifth term of 3n + 2? Sam answers: “15.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Function machines and undoing steps
notes: A function machine follows a rule. It changes an input number into an output number. Inverse operations undo each other, such as adding and subtracting.
Work forwards in the order shown. To work backwards, undo the last step first. Then undo the earlier steps in reverse order.
note_points: A function machine follows a rule.
It changes an input number into an output number.
Inverse operations undo each other, such as adding and subtracting.
Work forwards in the order shown.
To work backwards, undo the last step first.
Then undo the earlier steps in reverse order.
lessons.worked: A machine does ×3 then +4. Input 6 gives 6 × 3 + 4 = 22. For output 31, undo +4: 31 − 4 = 27. Undo ×3: 27 ÷ 3 = 9, so the input was 9.
worked_steps: A machine does ×3 then +4. Input 6 gives 6 × 3 + 4 = 22.
lessons.question: A machine does ×4 then −7. Its output is 29. Find the input.
lessons.mistake: When working backwards, undo the last step first.

cards.definition: The starting number put into a function.
An operation that undoes another, such as dividing to undo multiplying.

quiz.q: A machine does ×2 then +5. Which step do you undo first?
quiz.why: Work backwards by undoing the last operation first.

misconception.q: A machine does ×2 then +5. Which step do you undo first? Sam answers: “Divide by 2.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Work backwards by undoing the last operation first.

lessons.title: Reading and writing algebra
notes: A letter can stand for a number. 3a means 3 × a, and a² means a × a. An expression has no equals sign; an equation says two things are equal.

Read brackets carefully. 2n + 3 means double n, then add 3. 2(n + 3) means add 3 to n, then double the whole result. An identity is true for every allowed value of its letters. A formula links named quantities, such as distance, speed and time.
note_points: A letter can stand for a number.
3a means 3 × a, and a² means a × a.
An expression has no equals sign; an equation says two things are equal.
Read brackets carefully.
2n + 3 means double n, then add 3.
2(n + 3) means add 3 to n, then double the whole result.
An identity is true for every allowed value of its letters.
A formula links named quantities, such as distance, speed and time.
lessons.worked: For a = 4, square first: 3a² = 3 × 16 = 48. With brackets, (3a)² = (3 × 4)² = 12² = 144. The brackets change what is squared.
worked_steps: The brackets change what is squared.
lessons.question: For a = 5, work out 2a². Explain how (2a)² is different.
scheme: In (2a)², the whole product is squared, giving 100 here.
lessons.mistake: 2a² and (2a)² do not usually give the same answer.

cards.definition: A mathematical statement without an equals sign, such as 3x + 2.
A statement that two expressions have equal values.

quiz.q: What does 4a mean?
quiz.why: A number written directly before a letter means multiply.

misconception.q: What does 4a mean? Sam answers: “4 + a.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: A number written directly before a letter means multiply.

lessons.title: Putting numbers into expressions
notes: Substitution means replacing a letter with its value. Replace the letter every time it appears. Put negative values in brackets.
Write the expression with the numbers inserted. Work out brackets and powers first. Then multiply or divide before adding or subtracting.
note_points: Substitution means replacing a letter with its value.
Replace the letter every time it appears.
Put negative values in brackets.
Write the expression with the numbers inserted.
Work out brackets and powers first.
Then multiply or divide before adding or subtracting.
lessons.worked: For x = −3 and y = 2, x² − 4y becomes (−3)² − 4 × 2. This is 9 − 8. The answer is 1.
worked_steps: For x = −3 and y = 2, x² − 4y becomes (−3)² − 4 × 2.
lessons.question: Work out 3x² − 2y when x = −2 and y = 5.
lessons.mistake: (−3)² is 9, but −3² means −(3²), which is −9.

cards.definition: Replacing a letter with its value.
Work out the value of an expression.

quiz.q: For x = −4, what is x²?
quiz.why: Put the negative value in brackets: (−4) × (−4) = 16.

misconception.q: For x = −4, what is x²? Sam answers: “−16.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Put the negative value in brackets: (−4) × (−4) = 16.

lessons.title: Keeping equations balanced
notes: An equals sign means both sides have the same value. An equation is like a balanced scale. Do the same operation to both sides to keep it balanced.
Find the operation being done to the unknown. Undo it on both sides. Put your answer back into the original equation to check.
note_points: An equals sign means both sides have the same value.
An equation is like a balanced scale.
Do the same operation to both sides to keep it balanced.
Find the operation being done to the unknown.
Undo it on both sides.
Put your answer back into the original equation to check.
lessons.worked: For x + 8 = 19, subtract 8 from both sides. This gives x = 11. Check: 11 + 8 = 19.
worked_steps: For x + 8 = 19, subtract 8 from both sides.
lessons.question: Solve x − 9 = 14. Check your answer.
lessons.mistake: Changing only one side of an equation usually breaks the balance.

cards.definition: Two quantities having the same value.
A value that makes an equation true.

quiz.q: Which keeps an equation balanced?
opts: Subtract 3 from only the left side.
quiz.why: The same operation on both sides keeps their values equal.

misconception.q: Which keeps an equation balanced? Sam answers: “Subtract 3 from only the left side.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The same operation on both sides keeps their values equal.

lessons.title: Collecting like terms
notes: Like terms have the same letters and powers. You can add or subtract their number parts. Terms in x and x² are not like terms.
Group matching terms together. Keep each term's plus or minus sign. Combine the plain numbers separately.
note_points: Like terms have the same letters and powers.
You can add or subtract their number parts.
Terms in x and x² are not like terms.
Group matching terms together.
Keep each term's plus or minus sign.
Combine the plain numbers separately.
lessons.worked: 5a + 3b − 2a + b has a terms and b terms. 5a − 2a = 3a, and 3b + b = 4b. The result is 3a + 4b.
worked_steps: 5a + 3b − 2a + b has a terms and b terms.
lessons.question: Simplify 7x + 3y − 4x + 2y. Why do x and y terms stay separate?
scheme: x terms and y terms have different letter parts.
lessons.mistake: 3x + 2y cannot be combined into 5xy.

cards.definition: Terms with exactly the same letters and powers.
The number multiplying a letter or a power.

quiz.q: Simplify 6x − 2x.
quiz.why: Subtract the coefficients and keep the x: (6 − 2)x = 4x.

misconception.q: Simplify 6x − 2x. Sam answers: “4.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Subtract the coefficients and keep the x: (6 − 2)x = 4x.

lessons.title: Solving two-step equations
notes: Solving an equation means finding a value that makes it true. Keep both sides equal at every step. Write one step on each line.
Undo addition or subtraction first in a two-step expression. Then undo multiplication or division. Check your answer in the original equation.
note_points: Solving an equation means finding a value that makes it true.
Keep both sides equal at every step.
Write one step on each line.
Undo addition or subtraction first in a two-step expression.
Then undo multiplication or division.
Check your answer in the original equation.
lessons.worked: For 3x + 5 = 26, subtract 5 to get 3x = 21. Divide both sides by 3 to get x = 7. Check: 3 × 7 + 5 = 26.
worked_steps: Divide both sides by 3 to get x = 7.
lessons.question: Solve 4x − 7 = 29.
lessons.mistake: Use each operation on the whole of both sides.

cards.definition: Find the value or values that make a statement true.
Put the answer into the original equation to see whether both sides match.

quiz.q: What is x if 2x + 3 = 11?
quiz.why: Subtract 3 to get 2x = 8, then divide by 2.

misconception.q: What is x if 2x + 3 = 11? Sam answers: “7.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Subtract 3 to get 2x = 8, then divide by 2.

lessons.title: Place value and ordering decimals
notes: Each place to the left is worth ten times as much. To the right of units are tenths, hundredths and thousandths. A zero can hold an empty place.
Line up decimal points when comparing numbers. Add zeros at the end if it helps. Compare digits from left to right.
note_points: Each place to the left is worth ten times as much.
To the right of units are tenths, hundredths and thousandths.
A zero can hold an empty place.
Line up decimal points when comparing numbers.
Add zeros at the end if it helps.
Compare digits from left to right.
lessons.worked: Write 0.47 as 0.470 to compare it with 0.407. Both have 4 tenths, but 0.470 has more hundredths. So 0.407 < 0.470.
worked_steps: Write 0.47 as 0.470 to compare it with 0.407.
Both have 4 tenths, but 0.470 has more hundredths.
lessons.question: Put 0.508, 0.58 and 0.058 in order, smallest first.
scheme: 0.58 is largest, so the order is 0.058, 0.508, 0.58.
lessons.mistake: More digits after the decimal point does not always mean a larger number.

cards.definition: The value a digit has because of its position in a number.
One of a thousand equal parts of a whole, written 0.001.

quiz.q: Which is larger: 0.62 or 0.602?
quiz.why: Write 0.62 as 0.620, then compare hundredths.

misconception.q: Which is larger: 0.62 or 0.602? Sam answers: “0.602.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Rounding whole numbers and decimals
notes: Rounding chooses a nearby number at the accuracy requested. For decimal places, count digits after the decimal point. A number line can show the two possible rounded values.
Find the two nearest allowed values. Locate the midpoint between them. Use the nearer value; at the midpoint, use the usual school rule to round up.
note_points: Rounding chooses a nearby number at the accuracy requested.
For decimal places, count digits after the decimal point.
A number line can show the two possible rounded values.
Find the two nearest allowed values.
Locate the midpoint between them.
Use the nearer value; at the midpoint, use the usual school rule to round up.
lessons.worked: To round 2.37 to one decimal place, compare 2.3 and 2.4. Their midpoint is 2.35. 2.37 is closer to 2.4, so it rounds to 2.4.
worked_steps: To round 2.37 to one decimal place, compare 2.3 and 2.4.
2.37 is closer to 2.4, so it rounds to 2.4.
lessons.question: Round 6.482 to two decimal places. Explain which digit decides the rounding.
scheme: The next digit is 2, so do not round up.
lessons.mistake: Counting decimal places begins after the decimal point, not at the first non-zero digit.

cards.definition: A digit position to the right of the decimal point.
Replacing a number with a nearby number at a stated accuracy.

quiz.q: What is 3.76 rounded to one decimal place?
quiz.why: The hundredths digit is 6, so the tenths round up from 7 to 8.

misconception.q: What is 3.76 rounded to one decimal place? Sam answers: “3.7.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The hundredths digit is 6, so the tenths round up from 7 to 8.

lessons.title: Standard form
notes: Standard form makes very large or small numbers easier to write. For a positive number, use A × 10ⁿ with A at least 1 but less than 10. The power n is a whole number, possibly negative.

For multiplication, multiply the first numbers and add the powers of ten. Then adjust so the first number is between 1 and 10. For addition, first use matching powers of ten. For division, divide the first numbers and subtract the powers of ten.
note_points: Standard form makes very large or small numbers easier to write.
For a positive number, use A × 10ⁿ with A at least 1 but less than 10.
The power n is a whole number, possibly negative.
For multiplication, multiply the first numbers and add the powers of ten.
Then adjust so the first number is between 1 and 10.
For addition, first use matching powers of ten.
For division, divide the first numbers and subtract the powers of ten.
lessons.worked: (3 × 10⁵) × (4 × 10³) = 12 × 10⁸. The first number, 12, is too large for standard form. Rewrite it as 1.2 × 10⁹.
worked_steps: The first number, 12, is too large for standard form.
lessons.question: Multiply (6 × 10³) by (5 × 10⁴). Give the answer in standard form.
lessons.mistake: A negative power of ten makes a small positive number, not a negative number.

cards.definition: A number written as A × 10ⁿ, with 1 ≤ A < 10 for positive numbers and integer n.
A whole number, including zero and negative whole numbers.

quiz.q: Which is in standard form?
quiz.why: The number before ×10 must be at least 1 and less than 10 for a positive value.

misconception.q: Which is in standard form? Sam answers: “42 × 10⁴.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The number before ×10 must be at least 1 and less than 10 for a positive value.

lessons.title: Rounding numbers
notes: Rounding gives a nearby, simpler number. Decimal places are counted from the decimal point. Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit.
Mark the last digit you need to keep. Look at the next digit: 5 or more means round up. Keep zeros needed to show the right place value.
note_points: Rounding gives a nearby, simpler number.
Decimal places are counted from the decimal point.
Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit.
Mark the last digit you need to keep.
Look at the next digit: 5 or more means round up.
Keep zeros needed to show the right place value.
lessons.worked: For 0.006847 to 2 significant figures, keep 6 and 8. The next digit is 4, so do not round up. The rounded number is 0.0068.
worked_steps: For 0.006847 to 2 significant figures, keep 6 and 8.
The next digit is 4, so do not round up.
lessons.question: Round 0.007864 to 2 significant figures.
scheme: Keep 7 and 8, then use the next digit, 6, to round up.
lessons.mistake: The zeros before the first non-zero digit do not count as significant figures.

cards.definition: A digit position to the right of the decimal point.
A digit counted from the first non-zero digit when rounding.

quiz.q: Round 4.768 to 2 decimal places.
quiz.why: Keep the hundredths digit. The next digit, 8, rounds it up.

misconception.q: Round 4.768 to 2 decimal places. Sam answers: “4.76.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Keep the hundredths digit. The next digit, 8, rounds it up.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting decimals
notes: Line up numbers by place value. Put decimal points directly under each other. Add zeros at the end if useful.
Work from the smallest place value. Exchange one larger unit for ten smaller units when needed. Check subtraction by adding your answer back.
note_points: Line up numbers by place value.
Put decimal points directly under each other.
Add zeros at the end if useful.
Work from the smallest place value.
Exchange one larger unit for ten smaller units when needed.
Check subtraction by adding your answer back.
lessons.worked: 13.7 − 8.46 becomes 13.70 − 8.46. Column subtraction gives 5.24. Check: 8.46 + 5.24 = 13.70.
lessons.question: Calculate 24.6 − 7.85.
lessons.mistake: Do not line up the last digits if the decimal points then sit in different columns.

cards.definition: A column for units, tenths or another fixed digit value.
A check that uses the operation that undoes the calculation.

quiz.q: Calculate 7.2 − 0.85.
quiz.why: Write 7.20 − 0.85 and line up the decimal points.

misconception.q: Calculate 7.2 − 0.85. Sam answers: “6.45.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Write 7.20 − 0.85 and line up the decimal points.

lessons.title: Multiplying decimals
notes: Multiplication can make a number larger or smaller. Multiplying a positive number by a value between 0 and 1 makes it smaller. Multiplying by 10 changes each digit's place value.
Multiply the numbers as whole numbers first. Count the decimal places in both starting numbers. Use that total to place the decimal point in the answer.
note_points: Multiplication can make a number larger or smaller.
Multiplying a positive number by a value between 0 and 1 makes it smaller.
Multiplying by 10 changes each digit's place value.
Multiply the numbers as whole numbers first.
Count the decimal places in both starting numbers.
Use that total to place the decimal point in the answer.
lessons.worked: For 2.4 × 0.35, calculate 24 × 35 = 840. There are three decimal places in total. The answer is 0.840, or 0.84.
worked_steps: There are three decimal places in total.
lessons.question: Calculate 1.6 × 0.45.
scheme: There are three decimal places in total.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying by 0.1 is dividing by 10, not multiplying by 10.

cards.definition: The result of multiplying numbers.
10 multiplied by itself a whole number of times, or its reciprocal for a negative power.

quiz.q: Calculate 0.6 × 0.4.
quiz.why: 6 × 4 = 24. The two starting decimal places give 0.24.

misconception.q: Calculate 0.6 × 0.4. Sam answers: “2.4.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: 6 × 4 = 24. The two starting decimal places give 0.24.

lessons.title: Dividing by decimals
notes: Division asks how many of one amount fit into another. You can multiply both numbers by the same non-zero amount without changing the answer. This can remove a decimal from the number you divide by.
Multiply both numbers by 10, 100 or another suitable power of ten. Do the easier division. Check by multiplying your answer by the original divisor.
note_points: Division asks how many of one amount fit into another.
You can multiply both numbers by the same non-zero amount without changing the answer.
This can remove a decimal from the number you divide by.
Multiply both numbers by 10, 100 or another suitable power of ten.
Do the easier division.
Check by multiplying your answer by the original divisor.
lessons.question: Calculate 8.4 ÷ 0.4.
lessons.mistake: Change both numbers by the same factor, not just one of them.

cards.definition: The number you divide by.
The answer to a division.

quiz.q: Calculate 4.8 ÷ 0.6.
quiz.why: Multiply both numbers by 10 to get 48 ÷ 6 = 8.

misconception.q: Calculate 4.8 ÷ 0.6. Sam answers: “0.8.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Multiply both numbers by 10 to get 48 ÷ 6 = 8.

lessons.title: The order of operations
notes: Work out brackets first. Then calculate powers and roots. Next do multiplication and division, working from left to right.
Finish with addition and subtraction, also from left to right. A fraction bar groups everything above and below it. Use brackets when entering a negative number with a power.
note_points: Work out brackets first.
Then calculate powers and roots.
Next do multiplication and division, working from left to right.
Finish with addition and subtraction, also from left to right.
A fraction bar groups everything above and below it.
Use brackets when entering a negative number with a power.
lessons.worked: 18 ÷ 3 × 2 means work from left to right. 18 ÷ 3 = 6, then 6 × 2 = 12. It does not mean 18 ÷ 6.
worked_steps: 18 ÷ 3 × 2 means work from left to right.
lessons.question: Calculate 20 − 12 ÷ 3 × 2.
lessons.mistake: Multiplication does not always come before division. Work left to right between those two operations.

cards.definition: The agreed order for working out a calculation.
Multiply a number by itself.

quiz.q: Calculate 10 + 2 × 3.
quiz.why: Multiply first: 2 × 3 = 6, then add 10.

misconception.q: Calculate 10 + 2 × 3. Sam answers: “36.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Mean, median, mode and range
notes: Mean = total of the values ÷ number of values. The median is the middle value after ordering the list. The mode is the most common value.
The range is largest minus smallest. For an even-sized list, average the two middle values to find the median. An extreme value can pull the mean away from most of the data.
note_points: Mean = total of the values ÷ number of values.
The median is the middle value after ordering the list.
The mode is the most common value.
The range is largest minus smallest.
For an even-sized list, average the two middle values to find the median.
An extreme value can pull the mean away from most of the data.
lessons.worked: For 2, 3, 3, 8, the total is 16 and the mean is 16 ÷ 4 = 4. The median and mode are both 3. The range is 8 − 2 = 6.
worked_steps: For 2, 3, 3, 8, the total is 16 and the mean is 16 ÷ 4 = 4.
The median and mode are both 3.
lessons.question: Find the mean and range of 4, 6, 6, 12.
scheme: The total is 28, so the mean is 28 ÷ 4 = 7.
The largest value is 12 and the smallest is 4.
lessons.mistake: Order the list before finding the median. Keep repeated values in the list.

cards.definition: The total of the values divided by how many values there are.
The middle value in an ordered list, or the mean of the two middle values.
The largest value minus the smallest.

quiz.q: Find the median of 7, 2, 9.
quiz.why: Put the list in order: 2, 7, 9. The middle value is 7.

misconception.q: Find the median of 7, 2, 9. Sam answers: “2.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Put the list in order: 2, 7, 9. The middle value is 7.

lessons.title: Finding a missing value from a mean
notes: The mean shares the total equally. Total = mean × number of values. A missing value is the part of that total you do not know.
Work out the required total. Add the known values. Subtract their total from the required total.
note_points: The mean shares the total equally.
Total = mean × number of values.
A missing value is the part of that total you do not know.
Work out the required total.
Add the known values.
Subtract their total from the required total.
lessons.worked: Four values have a mean of 6, so their total is 24. Three values are 3, 5 and 7: total 15. The missing value is 24 − 15 = 9.
worked_steps: Four values have a mean of 6, so their total is 24.
lessons.question: Five numbers have a mean of 8. Four are 4, 6, 9 and 11. Find the fifth.
lessons.mistake: The mean is not the total.

cards.definition: The sum of all the values.
A value that must be found using the information given.

quiz.q: Three numbers have a mean of 7. What is their total?

misconception.q: Three numbers have a mean of 7. What is their total? Sam answers: “7.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Averages from frequency tables
notes: Frequency means how often a value occurs. A frequency table saves writing a value out many times. The total frequency is the number of values altogether.
Multiply each value by its frequency. Add these products, then divide by total frequency. For grouped data, use class midpoints and call the mean an estimate.
note_points: Frequency means how often a value occurs.
A frequency table saves writing a value out many times.
The total frequency is the number of values altogether.
Multiply each value by its frequency.
Add these products, then divide by total frequency.
For grouped data, use class midpoints and call the mean an estimate.
lessons.worked: Values 1, 2, 3 have frequencies 2, 5, 3. The total is 1 × 2 + 2 × 5 + 3 × 3 = 21. There are 10 values, so the mean is 21 ÷ 10 = 2.1.
worked_steps: There are 10 values, so the mean is 21 ÷ 10 = 2.1.
lessons.question: Values 2, 4, 6 have frequencies 3, 2, 5. Find the mean.
scheme: The total is 44 and total frequency is 10.
lessons.mistake: Divide by total frequency, not by the number of rows.

cards.definition: How often a value or category occurs.
The value halfway between the two ends of a grouped-data interval.

quiz.q: A value 4 has frequency 3. How much does it contribute to the total?
quiz.why: The value appears three times: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.

misconception.q: A value 4 has frequency 3. How much does it contribute to the total? Sam answers: “7.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Rounding numbers
notes: Rounding gives a nearby, simpler number. Decimal places are counted from the decimal point. Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit.
Mark the last digit you need to keep. Look at the next digit: 5 or more means round up. Keep zeros needed to show the right place value.
note_points: Rounding gives a nearby, simpler number.
Decimal places are counted from the decimal point.
Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit.
Mark the last digit you need to keep.
Look at the next digit: 5 or more means round up.
Keep zeros needed to show the right place value.
lessons.worked: For 0.006847 to 2 significant figures, keep 6 and 8. The next digit is 4, so do not round up. The rounded number is 0.0068.
worked_steps: For 0.006847 to 2 significant figures, keep 6 and 8.
The next digit is 4, so do not round up.
lessons.question: Round 0.007864 to 2 significant figures.
scheme: Keep 7 and 8, then use the next digit, 6, to round up.
lessons.mistake: The zeros before the first non-zero digit do not count as significant figures.

cards.definition: A digit position to the right of the decimal point.
A digit counted from the first non-zero digit when rounding.

quiz.q: Round 4.768 to 2 decimal places.
quiz.why: Keep the hundredths digit. The next digit, 8, rounds it up.

misconception.q: Round 4.768 to 2 decimal places. Sam answers: “4.76.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Keep the hundredths digit. The next digit, 8, rounds it up.

lessons.title: Estimating and rounding intervals
notes: An estimate is a quick answer using rounded numbers. Use it to check whether an exact answer looks sensible. A rounded measurement can stand for a range of original values.
Round numbers to make the calculation easier. For a rounding interval, go half a rounding step below and above. Include the lower end but not the upper end for the usual school convention.
note_points: An estimate is a quick answer using rounded numbers.
Use it to check whether an exact answer looks sensible.
A rounded measurement can stand for a range of original values.
Round numbers to make the calculation easier.
For a rounding interval, go half a rounding step below and above.
Include the lower end but not the upper end for the usual school convention.
lessons.worked: 19.6 × 4.8 is close to 20 × 5 = 100. A length of 12 cm rounded to the nearest centimetre could be 11.5 cm. It must be less than 12.5 cm, because that would round up to 13 cm.
worked_steps: A length of 12 cm rounded to the nearest centimetre could be 11.5 cm.
It must be less than 12.5 cm, because that would round up to 13 cm.
lessons.question: A mass rounds to 8.4 g to the nearest 0.1 g. Give the possible range of masses.
lessons.mistake: An estimate is a check, not an exact answer.

cards.definition: A rough answer used to check the likely size of a result.
The range of original values that would round to a stated measurement.

quiz.q: Which is a sensible estimate of 29.7 × 4.1?
quiz.why: Round to nearby easy numbers, then keep the same operation.

misconception.q: Which is a sensible estimate of 29.7 × 4.1? Sam answers: “3 × 4 = 12.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Round to nearby easy numbers, then keep the same operation.

lessons.title: Reading and drawing charts
notes: A bar chart compares categories. A pictogram uses symbols and a key. A line graph can show change over time.
Label axes and give units where needed. Use evenly spaced numbers on a scale. Check whether an axis starts above zero and exaggerates a difference.
note_points: A bar chart compares categories.
A pictogram uses symbols and a key.
A line graph can show change over time.
Label axes and give units where needed.
Use evenly spaced numbers on a scale.
Check whether an axis starts above zero and exaggerates a difference.
lessons.worked: A pictogram key says one symbol means 4 pupils. Two full symbols mean 8 pupils, and half a symbol means 2. So 2½ symbols mean 10 pupils.
worked_steps: A pictogram key says one symbol means 4 pupils.
Two full symbols mean 8 pupils, and half a symbol means 2.
lessons.question: A pictogram uses one symbol for 8 books. How many books do 3½ symbols show?
lessons.mistake: Always read the key before counting pictogram symbols.

cards.definition: A chart using symbols to show amounts.
The explanation of what a symbol or label stands for.

quiz.q: One symbol represents 6 items. What do 2½ symbols represent?
quiz.why: Two symbols represent 12 and half a symbol represents 3, giving 15.

misconception.q: One symbol represents 6 items. What do 2½ symbols represent? Sam answers: “12.5.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Two symbols represent 12 and half a symbol represents 3, giving 15.

lessons.title: Bar charts and pictograms
notes: A bar chart compares categories. Dual bars compare two groups for each category. A composite bar stacks parts to show a total.
Start with a labelled scale and equal-width bars. Leave gaps between categories. For a pictogram, give a key and use part-symbols accurately.
note_points: A bar chart compares categories.
Dual bars compare two groups for each category.
A composite bar stacks parts to show a total.
Start with a labelled scale and equal-width bars.
Leave gaps between categories.
For a pictogram, give a key and use part-symbols accurately.
lessons.worked: A reading club has 6 Year 7 and 4 Year 8 pupils on Monday. Dual bars show 6 and 4 separately. A composite bar stacks 6 and 4 to a height of 10.
worked_steps: A reading club has 6 Year 7 and 4 Year 8 pupils on Monday.
A composite bar stacks 6 and 4 to a height of 10.
lessons.question: A composite bar contains 8 walkers and 5 cyclists. What is its total height? Explain how a dual bar chart would show the data.
scheme: A dual chart has two separate bars for the category.
A key identifies walkers and cyclists.
lessons.mistake: A stacked bar reaches the total, not the value of its final part.

cards.definition: Two bars for each category, comparing two groups.
A bar split into stacked parts that make a total.

quiz.q: A bar stacks 7 girls and 9 boys. What is the total?
quiz.why: The stacked parts add: 7 + 9 = 16.

misconception.q: A bar stacks 7 girls and 9 boys. What is the total? Sam answers: “9.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Plotting positive coordinates
notes: Coordinates locate a point on a grid. Write the horizontal x value first, then the vertical y value. The first quadrant contains points with positive x and positive y.
Start at the origin, where the axes cross. Move along by x, then up by y. Check the axis scale before counting squares.
note_points: Coordinates locate a point on a grid.
Write the horizontal x value first, then the vertical y value.
The first quadrant contains points with positive x and positive y.
Start at the origin, where the axes cross.
Move along by x, then up by y.
Check the axis scale before counting squares.
lessons.worked: For (3,2), start at (0,0). Move 3 units right and 2 units up. Mark a point and label it (3,2).
worked_steps: Move 3 units right and 2 units up.
Mark a point and label it (3,2).
lessons.question: Describe how to plot (4,3). Then explain how (3,4) would be different.
scheme: Move 4 units right from the origin.
(3,4) is 3 units right and 4 up, so it is a different point.
lessons.mistake: The coordinate order matters: along first, then up.

cards.definition: Two numbers written (x,y) to locate a point.
The region of a coordinate grid where x and y are both positive.

quiz.q: For (5,2), how far do you move right and up from the origin?
quiz.why: Read x first and y second: 5 along, then 2 up.

misconception.q: For (5,2), how far do you move right and up from the origin? Sam answers: “2 right, 5 up.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Read x first and y second: 5 along, then 2 up.

lessons.title: Scatter graphs and patterns
notes: A scatter graph shows two measurements for each item. Positive correlation means both tend to increase together. Negative correlation means one tends to fall as the other rises.

A line of best fit follows the main pattern. Do not join every dot in order. Predictions far outside the measured range are less reliable. Interpolation predicts inside the measured range; extrapolation predicts outside it. An outlier is a point far from the main pattern. Check it rather than removing it without a reason.
note_points: A scatter graph shows two measurements for each item.
Positive correlation means both tend to increase together.
Negative correlation means one tends to fall as the other rises.
A line of best fit follows the main pattern.
Do not join every dot in order.
Predictions far outside the measured range are less reliable.
Interpolation predicts inside the measured range; extrapolation predicts outside it.
An outlier is a point far from the main pattern. Check it rather than removing it without a reason.
lessons.worked: Ice-cream sales and sunburn can both rise in hot weather. This does not show that eating ice cream causes sunburn. Another factor, sunny weather, affects both.
worked_steps: Ice-cream sales and sunburn can both rise in hot weather.
This does not show that eating ice cream causes sunburn.
Another factor, sunny weather, affects both.
lessons.question: What is positive correlation? Why might a prediction far outside the measured range be unreliable?
scheme: Both measurements tend to increase together.
The pattern may change outside the measured range.
There is less evidence for a prediction beyond that range.
lessons.mistake: Correlation does not by itself prove that one thing causes the other.

cards.definition: A pattern showing how two measurements change together.
A line following the main pattern of points on a scatter graph.

quiz.q: What does negative correlation mean?
opts: One measurement tends to fall as the other rises.
There is no pattern at all.
quiz.why: Negative describes the downward pattern, not whether the plotted numbers are below zero.

misconception.q: What does negative correlation mean? Sam answers: “Both measurements must be negative.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: One measurement tends to fall as the other rises.
Negative describes the downward pattern, not whether the plotted numbers are below zero.

review.q: Is predicting inside the measured data range called interpolation or extrapolation?

lessons.title: Graphs showing change over time
notes: A time series records values in time order. Time goes on the horizontal axis. The vertical axis shows the measured value and its unit.
Choose even scales and plot each pair of values. Join readings in time order when this makes sense. Look for trends, repeating patterns and unusual points.
note_points: A time series records values in time order.
Time goes on the horizontal axis.
The vertical axis shows the measured value and its unit.
Choose even scales and plot each pair of values.
Join readings in time order when this makes sense.
Look for trends, repeating patterns and unusual points.
lessons.worked: A plant is 4 cm tall on day 0, 7 cm on day 2 and 10 cm on day 4. Plot (0,4), (2,7), (4,10). Its height rises by 3 cm every two days in these readings.
worked_steps: A plant is 4 cm tall on day 0, 7 cm on day 2 and 10 cm on day 4.
Its height rises by 3 cm every two days in these readings.
lessons.question: Temperatures at 09:00, 10:00 and 11:00 are 12°C, 15°C and 14°C. Describe the changes and name the horizontal axis.
scheme: The temperature rises by 3°C, then falls by 1°C.
The vertical axis shows temperature in °C.
lessons.mistake: Time order matters; do not sort the points by height.

cards.definition: Values of a quantity recorded over time.
The overall pattern in data.

quiz.q: Which belongs on the horizontal axis of a daily temperature graph?
quiz.why: A time series uses time on its horizontal axis.

misconception.q: Which belongs on the horizontal axis of a daily temperature graph? Sam answers: “Temperature in °C.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: A time series uses time on its horizontal axis.

lessons.title: Straight and curved relationships
notes: A straight-line relationship has a constant gradient. A curved relationship changes steepness. A pattern alone does not explain its cause.
Read both axis labels before describing a graph. Compare the changes over equal horizontal intervals. Say where a graph rises, falls or levels off.
note_points: A straight-line relationship has a constant gradient.
A curved relationship changes steepness.
A pattern alone does not explain its cause.
Read both axis labels before describing a graph.
Compare the changes over equal horizontal intervals.
Say where a graph rises, falls or levels off.
lessons.worked: For y = 2x, x values 0, 1, 2 give y values 0, 2, 4. For y = x² they give 0, 1, 4. The first has equal increases; the second does not.
worked_steps: For y = 2x, x values 0, 1, 2 give y values 0, 2, 4.
The first has equal increases; the second does not.
lessons.question: For x = 1, 2, 3, y values are 1, 4, 9. Are the points on one straight line? Explain.
scheme: The increases in y are 3 and 5.
The gradient changes, so the relationship is not one straight line.
lessons.mistake: An increasing graph can still be curved.

cards.definition: A relationship shown by a straight line.
A relationship whose graph is not one straight line.

quiz.q: Which set of y values has a constant increase when x rises by 1?
quiz.why: The increase is 3 each time.

misconception.q: Which set of y values has a constant increase when x rises by 1? Sam answers: “1, 4, 9, 16.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Coordinates and midpoints
notes: Coordinates are written (x, y). Read the horizontal x value first, then the vertical y value. Negative values let us use all four parts of the grid.
To find a midpoint, average the two x values. Then average the two y values. Use a table of values to plot points from a rule. For y = 2x − 1, an input x = −2 gives y = −5.
note_points: Coordinates are written (x, y).
Read the horizontal x value first, then the vertical y value.
Negative values let us use all four parts of the grid.
To find a midpoint, average the two x values.
Then average the two y values.
Use a table of values to plot points from a rule.
For y = 2x − 1, an input x = −2 gives y = −5.
lessons.worked: The midpoint of (−2, 3) and (6, 7) has x = (−2 + 6) ÷ 2 = 2. Its y value is (3 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5. So the midpoint is (2, 5).
worked_steps: The midpoint of (−2, 3) and (6, 7) has x = (−2 + 6) ÷ 2 = 2.
lessons.question: Find the midpoint of (−4, 2) and (8, 10).
lessons.mistake: Go along the grid first and up or down second.

cards.definition: Two numbers (x, y) that locate a point on a grid.
The point halfway along a line segment.

quiz.q: Which coordinate is read first in (x, y)?
quiz.why: Go along first, then up or down.

misconception.q: Which coordinate is read first in (x, y)? Sam answers: “The vertical y value.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Go along first, then up or down.

lessons.title: Fractions on number lines
notes: The denominator splits one whole into equal parts. The numerator counts those parts. A fraction greater than 1 lies beyond 1 on a number line.
Use equal spacing for equal steps. To compare fractions, use a common denominator or decimal. For example, 1/2 = 3/6, which is larger than 2/6.
note_points: The denominator splits one whole into equal parts.
The numerator counts those parts.
A fraction greater than 1 lies beyond 1 on a number line.
Use equal spacing for equal steps.
To compare fractions, use a common denominator or decimal.
For example, 1/2 = 3/6, which is larger than 2/6.
lessons.worked: Split 0 to 1 into four equal intervals. The third tick after 0 is 3/4. 1 1/4 is one more quarter beyond 1.
worked_steps: Split 0 to 1 into four equal intervals.
lessons.question: Put 2/3, 1/2 and 3/4 in order, smallest first. Show a common denominator.
lessons.mistake: More parts in a whole means each part is smaller.

cards.definition: A fraction with numerator 1.
A shared denominator used to compare or combine fractions.

quiz.q: Which is greater: 3/5 or 1/2?

misconception.q: Which is greater: 3/5 or 1/2? Sam answers: “1/2.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Fractions, decimals and percentages
notes: Fractions, decimals and percentages can describe the same amount. A fraction also means division. Percent means out of 100.
Divide the top of a fraction by the bottom to get a decimal. Multiply the decimal by 100 to get a percentage. Divide a percentage by 100 to turn it back into a decimal.
note_points: Fractions, decimals and percentages can describe the same amount.
A fraction also means division.
Percent means out of 100.
Divide the top of a fraction by the bottom to get a decimal.
Multiply the decimal by 100 to get a percentage.
Divide a percentage by 100 to turn it back into a decimal.
worked_steps: Also 1.25 = 125%, which is more than one whole.
lessons.question: Convert 7/20 into a decimal and a percentage.
lessons.mistake: One half is 0.5, not 0.05.

cards.definition: The top number of a fraction, counting the parts taken.
The bottom number, showing how many equal parts make a whole.
An amount out of 100.

quiz.q: What percentage is 0.4?
quiz.why: Multiply the decimal by 100: 0.4 × 100 = 40.

misconception.q: What percentage is 0.4? Sam answers: “4%.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Equivalent fractions and mixed numbers
notes: Equivalent fractions have the same value. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same non-zero number. A mixed number has a whole-number part and a fraction part.
To change a mixed number, multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator. To simplify, divide top and bottom by a common factor. Use matching denominators to compare fractions.
note_points: Equivalent fractions have the same value.
Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same non-zero number.
A mixed number has a whole-number part and a fraction part.
To change a mixed number, multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator.
To simplify, divide top and bottom by a common factor.
Use matching denominators to compare fractions.
lessons.worked: 2⅓ = (2 × 3 + 1)/3 = 7/3. 3/4 = 6/8, so 3/4 is greater than 5/8. 18/24 simplifies to 3/4.
lessons.question: Write 3⅖ as an improper fraction. Simplify 21/28.
lessons.mistake: Do the same thing to the top and bottom when making an equivalent fraction.

cards.definition: Different-looking fractions with the same value.
A fraction whose numerator is at least as large as its denominator.

quiz.q: Which fraction equals 2/3?
quiz.why: Multiply the numerator and denominator by 4.

misconception.q: Which fraction equals 2/3? Sam answers: “2/6.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Multiply the numerator and denominator by 4.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting negative numbers
notes: Negative numbers are less than zero. On a number line, numbers increase as you move right. Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding its opposite.
Use a number line to track the change. Keep the sign of a number separate from the operation sign. For a change, calculate final value minus starting value.
note_points: Negative numbers are less than zero.
On a number line, numbers increase as you move right.
Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding its opposite.
Use a number line to track the change.
Keep the sign of a number separate from the operation sign.
For a change, calculate final value minus starting value.
lessons.worked: −4 + 7 means start at −4 and move 7 steps right, reaching 3. 5 − (−3) becomes 5 + 3 = 8. A rise from −6°C to 2°C is a change of 8°C.
worked_steps: −4 + 7 means start at −4 and move 7 steps right, reaching 3.
A rise from −6°C to 2°C is a change of 8°C.
lessons.question: Calculate −7 − (−12).
lessons.mistake: Subtracting a negative number moves you to the right on a number line.

cards.definition: A number less than zero.
A number the same distance from zero on the other side, such as −4 and 4.

quiz.q: Calculate 3 − (−5).
quiz.why: Subtracting a negative means adding its opposite: 3 + 5 = 8.

misconception.q: Calculate 3 − (−5). Sam answers: “−2.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Subtracting a negative means adding its opposite: 3 + 5 = 8.

lessons.title: Positive and negative counters
notes: A positive counter stands for +1. A negative counter stands for −1. One of each makes zero: a zero pair.
Add counters when adding a number. Remove matching counters when subtracting. You can add a zero pair without changing the total.
note_points: A positive counter stands for +1.
A negative counter stands for −1.
One of each makes zero: a zero pair.
Add counters when adding a number.
Remove matching counters when subtracting.
You can add a zero pair without changing the total.
lessons.worked: Start with +2, shown by two positive counters. To subtract −1, add a zero pair, then remove its negative counter. Three positive counters remain: 2 − (−1) = 3.
worked_steps: Start with +2, shown by two positive counters.
To subtract −1, add a zero pair, then remove its negative counter.
lessons.question: Use zero pairs to explain why 3 − (−2) = 5.
scheme: Add two zero pairs and remove the two negative counters.
lessons.mistake: A subtraction sign means remove; it is separate from a number’s sign.

cards.definition: A positive and negative counter together, with total zero.
A number that can be positive, zero or negative.

quiz.q: What is the total of four positive and three negative counters?
quiz.why: Three zero pairs cancel, leaving one positive counter.

misconception.q: What is the total of four positive and three negative counters? Sam answers: “7.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Three zero pairs cancel, leaving one positive counter.

lessons.title: Multiplying and dividing negatives
notes: For two numbers, matching signs give a positive answer. Different signs give a negative answer. This works for multiplication and division.
Work out the size of the answer, then its sign. For several negative factors, count how many negative signs there are. An even number of negative factors gives a positive product.
note_points: For two numbers, matching signs give a positive answer.
Different signs give a negative answer.
This works for multiplication and division.
Work out the size of the answer, then its sign.
For several negative factors, count how many negative signs there are.

lessons.mistake: Multiply every term in a bracket, including any negative term.

cards.definition: Multiply out the brackets in an expression.
Write an expression as factors multiplied together.

quiz.q: Expand 3(x + 4).
quiz.why: Multiply both x and 4 by 3.

misconception.q: Expand 3(x + 4). Sam answers: “3x + 4.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Multiplying two brackets
notes: Every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second. A grid can help you find all four products. Collect like terms at the end.

For x² + bx + c, factorising means finding two suitable brackets. The two numbers must add to b and multiply to c. Check your brackets by expanding them. For x² + bx + c, the bracket numbers add to b and multiply to c. A difference of squares factorises as a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b).
note_points: Every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second.
A grid can help you find all four products.
Collect like terms at the end.
For x² + bx + c, factorising means finding two suitable brackets.
The two numbers must add to b and multiply to c.
Check your brackets by expanding them.
For x² + bx + c, the bracket numbers add to b and multiply to c.
A difference of squares factorises as a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b).
lessons.worked: For (x + 3)(x − 2), the four products are x², −2x, 3x and −6. Combine −2x + 3x = x. The answer is x² + x − 6.
worked_steps: For (x + 3)(x − 2), the four products are x², −2x, 3x and −6.
lessons.question: Expand (x + 5)(x − 2). Put the powers of x in order, highest first.
lessons.mistake: Do not multiply only the first terms and the last terms. There are four products.

cards.definition: An expression whose highest power of the unknown is 2.
An expression a² − b², which factorises to (a − b)(a + b).

quiz.q: Expand (x + 2)(x + 3).
quiz.why: The four products are x², 3x, 2x and 6. Combine 3x + 2x.

misconception.q: Expand (x + 2)(x + 3). Sam answers: “x² + 6.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The four products are x², 3x, 2x and 6. Combine 3x + 2x.

lessons.title: Coordinates and midpoints
notes: Coordinates are written (x, y). Read the horizontal x value first, then the vertical y value. Negative values let us use all four parts of the grid.
To find a midpoint, average the two x values. Then average the two y values. Use a table of values to plot points from a rule. For y = 2x − 1, an input x = −2 gives y = −5.
note_points: Coordinates are written (x, y).
Read the horizontal x value first, then the vertical y value.
Negative values let us use all four parts of the grid.
To find a midpoint, average the two x values.
Then average the two y values.
Use a table of values to plot points from a rule.
For y = 2x − 1, an input x = −2 gives y = −5.
lessons.worked: The midpoint of (−2, 3) and (6, 7) has x = (−2 + 6) ÷ 2 = 2. Its y value is (3 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5. So the midpoint is (2, 5).
worked_steps: The midpoint of (−2, 3) and (6, 7) has x = (−2 + 6) ÷ 2 = 2.
lessons.question: Find the midpoint of (−4, 2) and (8, 10).
lessons.mistake: Go along the grid first and up or down second.

cards.definition: Two numbers (x, y) that locate a point on a grid.
The point halfway along a line segment.

quiz.q: Which coordinate is read first in (x, y)?
quiz.why: Go along first, then up or down.

misconception.q: Which coordinate is read first in (x, y)? Sam answers: “The vertical y value.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Go along first, then up or down.

lessons.title: Straight-line graphs
notes: In y = mx + c, m is the gradient: the steepness. c is the y-intercept: where the line crosses the y-axis. Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x.

Find the gradient using two points. Put one point's x and y values into y = mx + c. Solve for c, then write the equation. Horizontal lines have gradient zero. Vertical lines have equations such as x = 3 and no defined gradient.
note_points: In y = mx + c, m is the gradient: the steepness.
c is the y-intercept: where the line crosses the y-axis.
Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x.
Find the gradient using two points.
Put one point's x and y values into y = mx + c.
Solve for c, then write the equation.
Horizontal lines have gradient zero.
Vertical lines have equations such as x = 3 and no defined gradient.
lessons.worked: Through (1, 5) and (3, 9), gradient = (9 − 5) ÷ (3 − 1) = 2. Use (1, 5): 5 = 2 × 1 + c, so c = 3. The equation is y = 2x + 3.
lessons.question: Find the equation of a line with gradient 3 passing through (2, 7).
lessons.mistake: The y-intercept is where x is zero, not where y is zero.

cards.definition: How steep a line is: change in y divided by change in x.
Where a graph crosses the y-axis, at x = 0.

quiz.q: What is the gradient of y = 4x − 2?
quiz.why: In y = mx + c, the coefficient of x is the gradient m.

misconception.q: What is the gradient of y = 4x − 2? Sam answers: “−2.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: In y = mx + c, the coefficient of x is the gradient m.

lessons.title: Curved graphs
notes: A quadratic graph such as y = x² is a curve called a parabola. Cubic graphs include an x³ term. For y = 1/x, x cannot be zero.

Use a table with negative and positive x values where allowed. Join plotted points with a smooth curve. The x-intercepts are where y is zero. The curve y = 1/x gets closer to the axes without meeting them. A circle centred at (0, 0) has equation x² + y² = r².
note_points: A quadratic graph such as y = x² is a curve called a parabola.
Cubic graphs include an x³ term.
For y = 1/x, x cannot be zero.
Use a table with negative and positive x values where allowed.
Join plotted points with a smooth curve.
The x-intercepts are where y is zero.
The curve y = 1/x gets closer to the axes without meeting them.
A circle centred at (0, 0) has equation x² + y² = r².
lessons.worked: For y = x² − 4, set y to zero: x² = 4. Both x = −2 and x = 2 work. At x = 0, y = −4, which is the y-intercept.
worked_steps: For y = x² − 4, set y to zero: x² = 4.
At x = 0, y = −4, which is the y-intercept.
lessons.question: Find both x-intercepts of y = x² − 9.
scheme: The two x-intercepts have x values −3 and 3.
lessons.mistake: Do not forget the negative solution when solving x² = a positive number.

cards.definition: The curved shape of a quadratic graph.
A point where a graph crosses or touches the x-axis, so y = 0.

quiz.q: Where are the x-intercepts of y = x² − 16?
quiz.why: Set y to zero: x² = 16. Both −4 and 4 square to 16.

misconception.q: Where are the x-intercepts of y = x² − 16? Sam answers: “Only x = 4.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Set y to zero: x² = 16. Both −4 and 4 square to 16.

review.q: For y = x² − 4, find y when x = 0.

lessons.title: Picturing multiplication and division of fractions
notes: Multiplying by a fraction finds part of an amount. An area grid can show a fraction of a fraction. Division can ask how many equal pieces fit.
For multiplication, split both directions into equal parts. Count the overlapping parts. For division, count groups of the divisor’s size.
note_points: Multiplying by a fraction finds part of an amount.
An area grid can show a fraction of a fraction.
Division can ask how many equal pieces fit.
For multiplication, split both directions into equal parts.
Count the overlapping parts.
For division, count groups of the divisor’s size.
lessons.worked: Half of three quarters is 3/8: shade three columns of four, then half their height. Three quarters divided by one quarter asks how many quarter-pieces fit. There are three, so 3/4 ÷ 1/4 = 3.
worked_steps: Half of three quarters is 3/8: shade three columns of four, then half their height.
Three quarters divided by one quarter asks how many quarter-pieces fit.
lessons.question: Use equal pieces to explain 2/3 ÷ 1/6. Then calculate 2/3 × 1/2.
lessons.mistake: Dividing by a small positive fraction can make the answer larger.

cards.definition: The multiplicative inverse of a non-zero number.
A rectangle split into equal parts to show a calculation.

quiz.q: How many quarters fit into 1 1/2?
quiz.why: 1 1/2 = 6/4, which contains six quarters.

misconception.q: How many quarters fit into 1 1/2? Sam answers: “3.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Multiplying and dividing fractions
notes: To multiply fractions, multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms. A reciprocal is a number turned upside down as a fraction. A number times its reciprocal is 1, except zero has no reciprocal.
Change mixed numbers to improper fractions first. To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal. Simplify by cancelling common factors before multiplying if helpful.
note_points: To multiply fractions, multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms.
A reciprocal is a number turned upside down as a fraction.
A number times its reciprocal is 1, except zero has no reciprocal.
Change mixed numbers to improper fractions first.
To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal.
Simplify by cancelling common factors before multiplying if helpful.
lessons.worked: 3/4 × 2/5 = 6/20 = 3/10. For 2/3 ÷ 4/5, turn over only the second fraction. 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12 = 5/6.
worked_steps: For 2/3 ÷ 4/5, turn over only the second fraction.
lessons.question: Calculate 3/5 ÷ 9/10.
lessons.mistake: For division, turn over the fraction you divide by, not both fractions.

cards.definition: A number that multiplies with the original number to make 1.
A fraction with numerator at least as large as its denominator.

quiz.q: What is the reciprocal of 3/7?
quiz.why: Turn the fraction over. 3/7 × 7/3 = 1.

misconception.q: What is the reciprocal of 3/7? Sam answers: “−3/7.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Fractions with letters
notes: Fractions with letters follow the same rules as number fractions. Find a common denominator before adding. Keep the whole numerator together.
Multiply top and bottom by the same amount. You can cancel common factors in a product. You cannot cancel just one term from a sum.
note_points: Fractions with letters follow the same rules as number fractions.
Find a common denominator before adding.
Keep the whole numerator together.
Multiply top and bottom by the same amount.
You can cancel common factors in a product.
You cannot cancel just one term from a sum.
lessons.worked: For x/3 + x/4, use denominator 12. Write 4x/12 + 3x/12. The result is 7x/12.
lessons.question: Simplify x/2 + x/5.
lessons.mistake: You cannot cancel the x from (x + 3)/x. It is part of a sum.

cards.definition: A fraction containing letters in its numerator or denominator.
A factor shared by two or more expressions or numbers.

quiz.q: Simplify x/3 + x/6.
quiz.why: Rewrite x/3 as 2x/6. Then 3x/6 = x/2.

misconception.q: Simplify x/3 + x/6. Sam answers: “2x/9.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Reflections and symmetry
notes: A reflection flips a shape across a mirror line. Each point stays the same right-angle distance from the mirror line. Line symmetry means a shape matches itself after that flip.

Reflect each corner, then join the new corners. Reflecting in the y-axis changes the sign of x. Rotational symmetry counts matches during a full turn. Reflection in the line y = x swaps the two coordinates.
note_points: A reflection flips a shape across a mirror line.
Each point stays the same right-angle distance from the mirror line.
Line symmetry means a shape matches itself after that flip.
Reflect each corner, then join the new corners.
Reflecting in the y-axis changes the sign of x.
Rotational symmetry counts matches during a full turn.
Reflection in the line y = x swaps the two coordinates.
lessons.worked: Reflect (2, 5) in the line x = 4. The point is 2 units left of the line, so its image is 2 units right. The reflected point is (6, 5).
worked_steps: The point is 2 units left of the line, so its image is 2 units right.
lessons.question: Reflect (−3, 4) in the y-axis. Give the new coordinates.
scheme: Change the sign of x and keep y the same.
lessons.mistake: A reflection keeps the shape's size and its distance from the mirror line.

cards.definition: A flip across a mirror line, keeping each point the same right-angle distance from the line.
A shape matching itself when reflected in a line.

quiz.q: Reflect (2, 3) in the x-axis. What is the image?
quiz.why: The x value stays the same and the y value changes sign.

misconception.q: Reflect (2, 3) in the x-axis. What is the image? Sam answers: “(−2, 3).” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The x value stays the same and the y value changes sign.

review.q: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a non-square rectangle?
ms: 2: it matches itself twice during a full turn.

lessons.title: Reflecting a whole shape
notes: Reflection flips a shape across a mirror line. Each point and its image are equally far from the line. The joining segment meets the mirror line at a right angle.
Reflect each vertex separately. Count perpendicular distances to the mirror line. Join the image vertices in the same order.
note_points: Reflection flips a shape across a mirror line.
Each point and its image are equally far from the line.
The joining segment meets the mirror line at a right angle.
Reflect each vertex separately.
Count perpendicular distances to the mirror line.
Join the image vertices in the same order.
lessons.worked: Reflect (2, 1) in the vertical line x = 4. The point is two units left of the line, so its image is two units right. The image is (6, 1).
worked_steps: Reflect (2, 1) in the vertical line x = 4.
The point is two units left of the line, so its image is two units right.
lessons.question: Reflect the triangle (1,1), (3,1), (1,2) in the y-axis. Give all three image vertices.
scheme: Keep y and reverse the sign of x.
lessons.mistake: Reflecting in y = x swaps coordinates; it does not just change a sign.

cards.definition: The line across which a shape is reflected.
The result of transforming a shape.

quiz.q: Reflect (2,5) in y = x. What is its image?
quiz.why: Reflection in y = x swaps x and y.

misconception.q: Reflect (2,5) in y = x. What is its image? Sam answers: “(−2,5).” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Reflection in y = x swaps x and y.

lessons.title: Naming shapes and solids
notes: A polygon is a flat shape with straight sides. A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles. A solid is three-dimensional.
Name triangles using their sides or angles. Count faces, edges and vertices on solids. A prism has an unchanged cross-section along its length.
note_points: A polygon is a flat shape with straight sides.
A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles.
A solid is three-dimensional.
Name triangles using their sides or angles.
Count faces, edges and vertices on solids.
A prism has an unchanged cross-section along its length.
lessons.worked: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides. A cuboid has six rectangular faces, twelve edges and eight vertices. A cylinder has a circular cross-section along its length.
worked_steps: An equilateral triangle has three equal sides.
A cuboid has six rectangular faces, twelve edges and eight vertices.
A cylinder has a circular cross-section along its length.
lessons.question: Name a triangle with two equal sides. State the numbers of faces, edges and vertices on a cube.
scheme: A cube has 6 faces and 12 edges.
lessons.mistake: A regular polygon needs equal angles as well as equal sides.

cards.definition: A corner where edges meet; the plural is vertices.
A solid with a constant cross-section along its length.

quiz.q: Which triangle has three equal sides?
quiz.why: Equilateral means all three sides have equal length.

misconception.q: Which triangle has three equal sides? Sam answers: “Scalene.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Equilateral means all three sides have equal length.

lessons.title: Finding areas
notes: Area measures how much surface a shape covers. A rectangle's area is base × height. A triangle's area is half base × perpendicular height.

Perpendicular means at right angles to the base. A parallelogram uses base × perpendicular height. For a trapezium, average the parallel sides and multiply by the height. Split a compound shape into simpler shapes, or subtract a cut-out. 1 m² = 10,000 cm² because a square metre has 100 rows of 100 square centimetres.
note_points: Area measures how much surface a shape covers.
A rectangle's area is base × height.
A triangle's area is half base × perpendicular height.
Perpendicular means at right angles to the base.
A parallelogram uses base × perpendicular height.
For a trapezium, average the parallel sides and multiply by the height.
Split a compound shape into simpler shapes, or subtract a cut-out.
1 m² = 10,000 cm² because a square metre has 100 rows of 100 square centimetres.
lessons.worked: A trapezium has parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm, with height 4 cm. Area = (6 + 10) ÷ 2 × 4. The answer is 32 cm².
worked_steps: A trapezium has parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm, with height 4 cm.
lessons.question: A triangle has base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm. Find its area.
lessons.mistake: The sloping side of a triangle is not always its perpendicular height.

worked_rows.work: Parallel sides: 6 cm, 10 cm; height: 4 cm

cards.definition: The amount of surface a shape covers, measured in square units.
The height measured at right angles to the base.

quiz.q: A triangle has base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. What is its area?
quiz.why: A triangle is half a matching rectangle: ½ × 8 × 5 = 20 cm².

misconception.q: A triangle has base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. What is its area? Sam answers: “40 cm².” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: A triangle is half a matching rectangle: ½ × 8 × 5 = 20 cm².

lessons.title: Volume, capacity and prisms
notes: Volume measures the space inside a solid. A cuboid's volume is length × width × height. A prism has the same cross-section all the way along.
Find the cross-section area, then multiply by the prism's length. Use cubic units for volume. 1 cm³ = 1 ml, and 1000 cm³ = 1 litre. 1000 litres = 1 m³.
note_points: Volume measures the space inside a solid.
A cuboid's volume is length × width × height.
A prism has the same cross-section all the way along.
Find the cross-section area, then multiply by the prism's length.
Use cubic units for volume.
1 cm³ = 1 ml, and 1000 cm³ = 1 litre.
1000 litres = 1 m³.
lessons.worked: A triangular prism has cross-section area ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 cm². Its length is 10 cm. Volume = 12 × 10 = 120 cm³.
worked_steps: A triangular prism has cross-section area ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 cm².
lessons.question: A cuboid measures 8 cm by 5 cm by 3 cm. Find its volume.
lessons.mistake: Surface area uses square units. Volume uses cubic units.

cards.definition: The space a three-dimensional shape occupies, measured in cubic units.
A solid with the same cross-section all the way along.

quiz.q: What is the volume of a 2 cm by 3 cm by 4 cm cuboid?
quiz.why: Multiply all three lengths: 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 cm³.

misconception.q: What is the volume of a 2 cm by 3 cm by 4 cm cuboid? Sam answers: “9 cm³.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Changing metric units
notes: Metric units measure length, mass and capacity. 100 cm = 1 m; 1000 m = 1 km. 1000 g = 1 kg; 1000 ml = 1 litre.
A smaller unit needs a larger number. For area, square the length conversion: 1 m² = 10 000 cm². For volume, cube it: 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³.
note_points: Metric units measure length, mass and capacity.
1000 g = 1 kg; 1000 ml = 1 litre.
A smaller unit needs a larger number.
For area, square the length conversion: 1 m² = 10 000 cm².
For volume, cube it: 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³.
lessons.question: Convert 3.6 m into centimetres. Explain why 1 m² is 10 000 cm².
scheme: A square metre is 100 cm by 100 cm.
lessons.mistake: The area conversion is not the same as the length conversion.

cards.definition: Units linked by powers of ten, such as metres and centimetres.
How much a container can hold.

quiz.q: How many centimetres are in 2.5 metres?
quiz.why: Each metre contains 100 centimetres: 2.5 × 100 = 250.

misconception.q: How many centimetres are in 2.5 metres? Sam answers: “25.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Density, mass and volume
notes: Density tells you the mass in each unit of volume. Density = mass ÷ volume. Materials with the same volume can have different masses.
Mass = density × volume. Volume = mass ÷ density. Check that the units match before calculating.
note_points: Density tells you the mass in each unit of volume.
Density = mass ÷ volume.
Materials with the same volume can have different masses.
Mass = density × volume.
Volume = mass ÷ density.
Check that the units match before calculating.
lessons.worked: An object has mass 180 g and volume 60 cm³. Density = 180 ÷ 60. Its density is 3 g/cm³.
worked_steps: An object has mass 180 g and volume 60 cm³.
lessons.question: An object has mass 540 g and volume 200 cm³. Find its density.
lessons.mistake: Density is not just mass. You need the volume too.

cards.definition: Mass per unit volume, calculated as mass divided by volume.
The amount a container can hold.

quiz.q: An object has mass 80 g and volume 20 cm³. What is its density?
quiz.why: Density = 80 ÷ 20 = 4 g/cm³.

misconception.q: An object has mass 80 g and volume 20 cm³. What is its density? Sam answers: “1600 g/cm³.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Solving two-step equations
notes: Solving an equation means finding a value that makes it true. Keep both sides equal at every step. Write one step on each line.
Undo addition or subtraction first in a two-step expression. Then undo multiplication or division. Check your answer in the original equation.
note_points: Solving an equation means finding a value that makes it true.
Keep both sides equal at every step.
Write one step on each line.
Undo addition or subtraction first in a two-step expression.
Then undo multiplication or division.
Check your answer in the original equation.
lessons.worked: For 3x + 5 = 26, subtract 5 to get 3x = 21. Divide both sides by 3 to get x = 7. Check: 3 × 7 + 5 = 26.
worked_steps: Divide both sides by 3 to get x = 7.
lessons.question: Solve 4x − 7 = 29.
lessons.mistake: Use each operation on the whole of both sides.

cards.definition: Find the value or values that make a statement true.
Put the answer into the original equation to see whether both sides match.

quiz.q: What is x if 2x + 3 = 11?
quiz.why: Subtract 3 to get 2x = 8, then divide by 2.

misconception.q: What is x if 2x + 3 = 11? Sam answers: “7.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Subtract 3 to get 2x = 8, then divide by 2.

lessons.title: Equations with brackets and fractions
notes: An equation says two expressions have equal value. Brackets and fraction bars group terms. The same operation on both sides keeps the equality.
Clear a denominator by multiplying both sides. Expand brackets carefully. Undo the remaining operations and check the answer.
note_points: An equation says two expressions have equal value.
Brackets and fraction bars group terms.
The same operation on both sides keeps the equality.
Clear a denominator by multiplying both sides.
Expand brackets carefully.
Undo the remaining operations and check the answer.
lessons.worked: (x + 4)/3 = 5. Multiply both sides by 3: x + 4 = 15. Subtract 4: x = 11.
lessons.question: Solve (2x − 1)/3 = 7 and check your answer.
lessons.mistake: A fraction bar divides the whole expression above it.

cards.definition: A value that makes an equation true.
An operation that undoes another operation.

quiz.q: Solve (x + 2)/4 = 3.
quiz.why: Multiply by 4, then subtract 2: x = 12 − 2 = 10.

misconception.q: Solve (x + 2)/4 = 3. Sam answers: “x = 1.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Equations with letters on both sides
notes: Some equations have an unknown on both sides. Bring the letter terms together on one side. Bring the plain numbers together on the other side.
Expand brackets if needed. Subtract a letter term from both sides. Finish solving, then check the original equation.
note_points: Some equations have an unknown on both sides.
Bring the letter terms together on one side.
Bring the plain numbers together on the other side.
Expand brackets if needed.
Subtract a letter term from both sides.
Finish solving, then check the original equation.
lessons.worked: For 5x + 3 = 2x + 21, subtract 2x: 3x + 3 = 21. Subtract 3, then divide by 3: x = 6. Check: both original sides equal 33.
lessons.question: Solve 3(x + 2) = 2x + 17.
lessons.mistake: When a question describes a real length, check that your answer makes sense as a length.

cards.definition: A value you need to find, often shown by a letter.
Write two equal amounts using mathematical expressions and an equals sign.

quiz.q: What is x if 5x = 2x + 12?
quiz.why: Subtract 2x to get 3x = 12, then divide by 3.

misconception.q: What is x if 5x = 2x + 12? Sam answers: “12.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Subtract 2x to get 3x = 12, then divide by 3.

lessons.title: Inequalities and number lines
notes: An inequality describes a set of possible values. < means less than, and > means greater than. ≤ and ≥ also allow equality.
Solve in a similar way to an equation. Reverse the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number. An open circle excludes the boundary; a filled circle includes it.
note_points: An inequality describes a set of possible values.
< means less than, and > means greater than.
≤ and ≥ also allow equality.
Solve in a similar way to an equation.
Reverse the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
An open circle excludes the boundary; a filled circle includes it.
lessons.worked: For −2x < 6, divide both sides by −2. Reverse < to >. The solution is x > −3.
lessons.question: Solve −3x ≥ 12.
lessons.mistake: Do not forget to reverse the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.

cards.definition: A statement that one expression is larger or smaller than another, possibly including equality.
The value at the end of a solution interval.

quiz.q: Solve −2x < 8.
quiz.why: Divide by −2 and reverse the sign because you divided by a negative number.

misconception.q: Solve −2x < 8. Sam answers: “x < −4.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Divide by −2 and reverse the sign because you divided by a negative number.

review.q: List the whole numbers that satisfy 0 ≤ x < 3.

lessons.title: Percentages of an amount
notes: A percentage is an amount out of 100. 10% is one tenth and 50% is one half. You can build a percentage from easier parts.
To use a calculator, change the percentage to a decimal. Multiply that decimal by the whole amount. Check that you have identified the correct whole.
note_points: A percentage is an amount out of 100.
10% is one tenth and 50% is one half.
You can build a percentage from easier parts.
To use a calculator, change the percentage to a decimal.
Multiply that decimal by the whole amount.
Check that you have identified the correct whole.
lessons.worked: For 15% of £80, find 10% = £8. 5% is half of that, or £4. 15% = £8 + £4 = £12.
lessons.question: Find 18% of £250.
lessons.mistake: A percentage above 100% is possible. It means more than the whole amount.

cards.definition: An amount out of 100.
A number you multiply by to make a change or find an amount.

quiz.q: What is 15% of 60?
quiz.why: 10% is 6 and 5% is 3, so 15% is 9.

misconception.q: What is 15% of 60? Sam answers: “15.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Percentage increases and decreases
notes: An increase adds a percentage of the original amount. A decrease takes a percentage away. Percentage change compares the change with the original amount.
For a 15% increase, multiply by 1.15. For a 15% decrease, multiply by 0.85. Percentage change = change ÷ original amount × 100%.
note_points: An increase adds a percentage of the original amount.
A decrease takes a percentage away.
Percentage change compares the change with the original amount.
For a 15% increase, multiply by 1.15.
For a 15% decrease, multiply by 0.85.
Percentage change = change ÷ original amount × 100%.
lessons.worked: A price rises from £50 to £65, so the change is £15. 15 ÷ 50 × 100 = 30%. A 20% rise followed by a 20% fall does not return to the start.
worked_steps: A price rises from £50 to £65, so the change is £15.
A 20% rise followed by a 20% fall does not return to the start.
lessons.question: A price rises from £80 to £92. Find the percentage increase.
lessons.mistake: Divide by the original amount when finding percentage change.

cards.definition: The change divided by the original amount, multiplied by 100%.
The amount before a change happened.

quiz.q: Which multiplier increases a price by 20%?
quiz.why: Keep the original 100% and add 20%, giving 120% = 1.2.

misconception.q: Which multiplier increases a price by 20%? Sam answers: “0.2.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Keep the original 100% and add 20%, giving 120% = 1.2.

lessons.title: Finding the original percentage amount
notes: After a percentage change, the new amount is a fraction of the original. A 20% reduction leaves 80% of the original. To find the original, divide by the multiplier.
Write new amount = original amount × multiplier. Repeated percentage changes use the new balance each time. Simple interest uses the original balance each time instead.
note_points: After a percentage change, the new amount is a fraction of the original.
