A 20% reduction leaves 80% of the original.
To find the original, divide by the multiplier.
Write new amount = original amount × multiplier.
Repeated percentage changes use the new balance each time.
Simple interest uses the original balance each time instead.
lessons.worked: After a 20% reduction, a coat costs £64. 80% = 0.8, so original price = 64 ÷ 0.8. The original price was £80.
worked_steps: After a 20% reduction, a coat costs £64.
lessons.question: After a 25% increase, a value is 90. What was the original value?
lessons.mistake: Do not subtract 25% of the new value to undo a 25% increase.

cards.definition: Finding the original amount before a percentage change.
Repeated growth where each change uses the latest amount.

quiz.q: A price after a 10% reduction is £45. Which calculation finds the original price?
quiz.why: The new price is 90% of the original, so divide by 0.9.

misconception.q: A price after a 10% reduction is £45. Which calculation finds the original price? Sam answers: “45 × 0.9.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The new price is 90% of the original, so divide by 0.9.

lessons.title: Types of data and sensible samples
notes: Categorical data are labels such as eye colour. Discrete numerical data are counted in separate values. Continuous data are measured and can take values between readings.
Choose data that answer the question. Use a sample that fairly represents the group. Check unusual results for recording errors before making a decision.
note_points: Categorical data are labels such as eye colour.
Discrete numerical data are counted in separate values.
Continuous data are measured and can take values between readings.
Choose data that answer the question.
Use a sample that fairly represents the group.
Check unusual results for recording errors before making a decision.
lessons.worked: Number of siblings is discrete: 0, 1, 2 and so on. Height is continuous, even if rounded to a centimetre. Favourite sport is categorical.
worked_steps: Number of siblings is discrete: 0, 1, 2 and so on.
Height is continuous, even if rounded to a centimetre.
lessons.question: Classify shoe colour, number of goals and journey time as categorical, discrete or continuous.
lessons.mistake: Rounded measurements do not become discrete just because whole numbers are recorded.

cards.definition: Numerical data with separate possible values, often counts.
Measurements that can take any value in a range.

quiz.q: Which is continuous data?
quiz.why: Mass is measured and can take values between whole numbers.

misconception.q: Which is continuous data? Sam answers: “Number of apples.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Mass is measured and can take values between whole numbers.

lessons.title: Mean, median, mode and range
notes: Mean = total of the values ÷ number of values. The median is the middle value after ordering the list. The mode is the most common value.
The range is largest minus smallest. For an even-sized list, average the two middle values to find the median. An extreme value can pull the mean away from most of the data.
note_points: Mean = total of the values ÷ number of values.
The median is the middle value after ordering the list.
The mode is the most common value.
The range is largest minus smallest.
For an even-sized list, average the two middle values to find the median.
An extreme value can pull the mean away from most of the data.
lessons.worked: For 2, 3, 3, 8, the total is 16 and the mean is 16 ÷ 4 = 4. The median and mode are both 3. The range is 8 − 2 = 6.
worked_steps: For 2, 3, 3, 8, the total is 16 and the mean is 16 ÷ 4 = 4.
The median and mode are both 3.
lessons.question: Find the mean and range of 4, 6, 6, 12.
scheme: The total is 28, so the mean is 28 ÷ 4 = 7.
The largest value is 12 and the smallest is 4.
lessons.mistake: Order the list before finding the median. Keep repeated values in the list.

cards.definition: The total of the values divided by how many values there are.
The middle value in an ordered list, or the mean of the two middle values.
The largest value minus the smallest.

quiz.q: Find the median of 7, 2, 9.
quiz.why: Put the list in order: 2, 7, 9. The middle value is 7.

misconception.q: Find the median of 7, 2, 9. Sam answers: “2.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Put the list in order: 2, 7, 9. The middle value is 7.

lessons.title: Scatter graphs and patterns
notes: A scatter graph shows two measurements for each item. Positive correlation means both tend to increase together. Negative correlation means one tends to fall as the other rises.

A line of best fit follows the main pattern. Do not join every dot in order. Predictions far outside the measured range are less reliable. Interpolation predicts inside the measured range; extrapolation predicts outside it. An outlier is a point far from the main pattern. Check it rather than removing it without a reason.
note_points: A scatter graph shows two measurements for each item.
Positive correlation means both tend to increase together.
Negative correlation means one tends to fall as the other rises.
A line of best fit follows the main pattern.
Do not join every dot in order.
Predictions far outside the measured range are less reliable.
Interpolation predicts inside the measured range; extrapolation predicts outside it.
An outlier is a point far from the main pattern. Check it rather than removing it without a reason.
lessons.worked: Ice-cream sales and sunburn can both rise in hot weather. This does not show that eating ice cream causes sunburn. Another factor, sunny weather, affects both.
worked_steps: Ice-cream sales and sunburn can both rise in hot weather.
This does not show that eating ice cream causes sunburn.
Another factor, sunny weather, affects both.
lessons.question: What is positive correlation? Why might a prediction far outside the measured range be unreliable?
scheme: Both measurements tend to increase together.
The pattern may change outside the measured range.
There is less evidence for a prediction beyond that range.
lessons.mistake: Correlation does not by itself prove that one thing causes the other.

cards.definition: A pattern showing how two measurements change together.
A line following the main pattern of points on a scatter graph.

quiz.q: What does negative correlation mean?
opts: There is no pattern at all.
One measurement tends to fall as the other rises.
quiz.why: Negative describes the downward pattern, not whether the plotted numbers are below zero.

misconception.q: What does negative correlation mean? Sam answers: “Both measurements must be negative.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: One measurement tends to fall as the other rises.
Negative describes the downward pattern, not whether the plotted numbers are below zero.

review.q: Is predicting inside the measured data range called interpolation or extrapolation?

lessons.title: Comparing data and choosing an average
notes: An average describes a typical value. The range describes spread. A fair comparison considers both.
Choose a mean or median that suits the data. An extreme value can affect the mean strongly. Use the mode for the most common category.
note_points: An average describes a typical value.
The range describes spread.
A fair comparison considers both.
Choose a mean or median that suits the data.
An extreme value can affect the mean strongly.
Use the mode for the most common category.
lessons.worked: Group A has median 12 and range 3; B has median 10 and range 8. A has the higher typical value. A is also less spread out, using these measures.
worked_steps: Group A has median 12 and range 3; B has median 10 and range 8.
A has the higher typical value.
A is also less spread out, using these measures.
lessons.question: Daily journeys have median 25 minutes and range 8 for route A; median 20 and range 18 for route B. Compare them.
scheme: Route B has a shorter typical journey using the median.
Route A has less variation using the range.
The full data would give more detail than these two measures.
lessons.mistake: A smaller range does not mean a smaller average.

worked_rows.note: A has a higher typical value

cards.definition: The way data values are spread.
A value far away from the main pattern of the data.

quiz.q: Which average is usually less affected by one very high salary?
quiz.why: The median uses position in the ordered list, rather than sharing the total.

misconception.q: Which average is usually less affected by one very high salary? Sam answers: “Mean.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The median uses position in the ordered list, rather than sharing the total.

lessons.title: Averages from frequency tables
notes: Frequency means how often a value occurs. A frequency table saves writing a value out many times. The total frequency is the number of values altogether.
Multiply each value by its frequency. Add these products, then divide by total frequency. For grouped data, use class midpoints and call the mean an estimate.
note_points: Frequency means how often a value occurs.
A frequency table saves writing a value out many times.
The total frequency is the number of values altogether.
Multiply each value by its frequency.
Add these products, then divide by total frequency.
For grouped data, use class midpoints and call the mean an estimate.
lessons.worked: Values 1, 2, 3 have frequencies 2, 5, 3. The total is 1 × 2 + 2 × 5 + 3 × 3 = 21. There are 10 values, so the mean is 21 ÷ 10 = 2.1.
worked_steps: There are 10 values, so the mean is 21 ÷ 10 = 2.1.
lessons.question: Values 2, 4, 6 have frequencies 3, 2, 5. Find the mean.
scheme: The total is 44 and total frequency is 10.
lessons.mistake: Divide by total frequency, not by the number of rows.

cards.definition: How often a value or category occurs.
The value halfway between the two ends of a grouped-data interval.

quiz.q: A value 4 has frequency 3. How much does it contribute to the total?
quiz.why: The value appears three times: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.

misconception.q: A value 4 has frequency 3. How much does it contribute to the total? Sam answers: “7.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Grouped data and estimates
notes: Grouping puts values into intervals. Discrete values are counted; continuous values are measured. Grouping hides the exact values inside each interval.
Use intervals that do not overlap. For an estimated mean, use each class midpoint. Multiply midpoint by frequency, add, then divide by total frequency.
note_points: Grouping puts values into intervals.
Discrete values are counted; continuous values are measured.
Grouping hides the exact values inside each interval.
Use intervals that do not overlap.
For an estimated mean, use each class midpoint.
Multiply midpoint by frequency, add, then divide by total frequency.
lessons.worked: Heights 140 ≤ h < 150 have frequency 2; 150 ≤ h < 160 have frequency 3. Midpoints are 145 and 155. Estimated mean = (145 × 2 + 155 × 3)/5 = 151 cm.
worked_steps: Heights 140 ≤ h < 150 have frequency 2; 150 ≤ h < 160 have frequency 3.
lessons.question: The intervals 0 ≤ t < 10 and 10 ≤ t < 20 have frequencies 3 and 7. Estimate the mean time.
lessons.mistake: The result is an estimate because the individual values are unknown.

cards.definition: A range used to group data.
The value halfway between a class’s boundaries.

quiz.q: What is the midpoint of 20 ≤ x < 30?
quiz.why: Average the boundaries: (20 + 30)/2 = 25.

misconception.q: What is the midpoint of 20 ≤ x < 30? Sam answers: “10.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Grouped data and histograms
notes: A histogram shows grouped data using bars. The bar area represents frequency. The bar height is frequency density, not always frequency.
Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width. Frequency = density × class width. A frequency polygon joins points plotted at class midpoints.
note_points: A histogram shows grouped data using bars.
The bar area represents frequency.
The bar height is frequency density, not always frequency.
Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.
Frequency = density × class width.
A frequency polygon joins points plotted at class midpoints.
lessons.worked: The class 10 ≤ x < 30 has width 20 and frequency 12. Its frequency density is 12 ÷ 20 = 0.6. A narrower class can have a taller bar but still contain fewer values.
worked_steps: The class 10 ≤ x < 30 has width 20 and frequency 12.
A narrower class can have a taller bar but still contain fewer values.
lessons.question: A histogram class has width 8 and frequency density 2.5. Find its frequency.
lessons.mistake: For unequal class widths, compare bar areas rather than just bar heights.

cards.definition: Frequency divided by class width, used for histogram bar height.
The difference between the upper and lower class boundaries.

quiz.q: A histogram class has frequency 18 and width 6. What is its density?
quiz.why: Density = 18 ÷ 6 = 3.

misconception.q: A histogram class has frequency 18 and width 6. What is its density? Sam answers: “108.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Angle facts
notes: Angles on a straight line add to 180°. Angles around a point add to 360°. Angles inside a triangle add to 180°.
Vertically opposite angles are equal. Angles inside a quadrilateral add to 360°. Write the angle rule as well as your calculation.
note_points: Angles on a straight line add to 180°.
Angles around a point add to 360°.
Angles inside a triangle add to 180°.
Vertically opposite angles are equal.
Angles inside a quadrilateral add to 360°.
Write the angle rule as well as your calculation.
lessons.worked: An isosceles triangle has a top angle of 38°. Its two equal base angles add to 180 − 38 = 142°. Each base angle is 142 ÷ 2 = 71°.
worked_steps: An isosceles triangle has a top angle of 38°.
Its two equal base angles add to 180 − 38 = 142°.
lessons.question: A triangle has angles 48° and 67°. Find the third angle.
lessons.mistake: Use angle facts rather than guessing from how a drawing looks.

cards.definition: An angle of 90°.
A triangle with two equal sides and two equal base angles.

quiz.q: Two angles in a triangle are 50° and 60°. What is the third?
quiz.why: Triangle angles add to 180°: 180 − 50 − 60 = 70°.

misconception.q: Two angles in a triangle are 50° and 60°. What is the third? Sam answers: “110°.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Quadrilaterals and geometric reasons
notes: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel opposite sides. A rectangle has four right angles. A rhombus has four equal sides; a square is both a rhombus and a rectangle.
Use marked facts rather than the appearance of a sketch. Opposite angles in a parallelogram are equal. Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
note_points: A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel opposite sides.
A rectangle has four right angles.
A rhombus has four equal sides; a square is both a rhombus and a rectangle.
Use marked facts rather than the appearance of a sketch.
Opposite angles in a parallelogram are equal.
Diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
lessons.worked: One angle in a parallelogram is 68°. The next angle is 180 − 68 = 112°. The opposite angles repeat 68° and 112°.
worked_steps: One angle in a parallelogram is 68°.
lessons.question: A parallelogram has an angle of 73°. Find the other three angles and explain the rule.
scheme: Adjacent angles sum to 180°, so the others are 107°.
lessons.mistake: A diagram can be out of scale; use the stated properties.

cards.definition: Divide into two equal parts.
A quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel.

quiz.q: What does it mean when diagonals bisect each other?
opts: All four sections must be equal.
Each cuts the other into equal halves.
quiz.why: Each diagonal is halved; the two diagonals need not have the same length.

misconception.q: What does it mean when diagonals bisect each other? Sam answers: “They must cross at 90°.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Each cuts the other into equal halves.
Each diagonal is halved; the two diagonals need not have the same length.

lessons.title: Parallel-line angles and polygons
notes: Parallel lines never meet. A line crossing them makes equal corresponding and alternate angles. Co-interior angles, on the same inside side, add to 180°.
A polygon is a closed shape with straight sides. An n-sided polygon has angle total (n − 2) × 180°. A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles.
note_points: Parallel lines never meet.
A line crossing them makes equal corresponding and alternate angles.
Co-interior angles, on the same inside side, add to 180°.
A polygon is a closed shape with straight sides.
An n-sided polygon has angle total (n − 2) × 180°.
A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles.
lessons.worked: A regular hexagon has 6 equal exterior angles. Each exterior angle is 360 ÷ 6 = 60°. Each interior angle is 180 − 60 = 120°.
worked_steps: A regular hexagon has 6 equal exterior angles.
lessons.question: Find each interior angle of a regular octagon, which has 8 sides.
scheme: An interior and its exterior angle add to 180°.
lessons.mistake: Use parallel-line markings before applying a parallel-line angle rule.

cards.definition: A closed straight-sided shape with equal sides and equal angles.
The angle between a side and the extension of a neighbouring side.

quiz.q: What is each exterior angle of a regular pentagon?
quiz.why: A full set of exterior angles adds to 360°: 360 ÷ 5 = 72°.

misconception.q: What is each exterior angle of a regular pentagon? Sam answers: “108°.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: A full set of exterior angles adds to 360°: 360 ÷ 5 = 72°.

lessons.title: Probability and possible outcomes
notes: Probability measures how likely something is. It runs from 0 for impossible to 1 for certain. For equally likely outcomes, divide the number you want by the total.
List outcomes so none are missed or repeated. P(not A) = 1 − P(A). The probabilities of all separate possible outcomes add to 1.
note_points: Probability measures how likely something is.
It runs from 0 for impossible to 1 for certain.
For equally likely outcomes, divide the number you want by the total.
List outcomes so none are missed or repeated.
P(not A) = 1 − P(A).
The probabilities of all separate possible outcomes add to 1.
lessons.worked: For a fair die, numbers above 4 are 5 and 6. P(above 4) = 2/6 = 1/3. P(not above 4) = 1 − 1/3 = 2/3.
worked_steps: For a fair die, numbers above 4 are 5 and 6.
lessons.question: A bag has 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green counters. Find the probability of not picking blue.
scheme: There are 3 + 2 = 5 counters that are not blue.
lessons.mistake: Count actual outcomes or objects. Do not assume colour categories are equally likely.

cards.definition: A number from 0 to 1 describing how likely an outcome is.
All outcomes where the stated event does not happen.

quiz.q: If P(rain) = 0.3, what is P(no rain)?
quiz.why: An event and its complement add to 1: 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.

misconception.q: If P(rain) = 0.3, what is P(no rain)? Sam answers: “1.3.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: An event and its complement add to 1: 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.

lessons.title: Probability experiments
notes: An experiment records what actually happens. Relative frequency = event count ÷ number of trials. It estimates a probability from results.
Keep a tally and count all trials. More trials usually make the estimate more stable. Even a fair random experiment can give uneven results.
note_points: An experiment records what actually happens.
Relative frequency = event count ÷ number of trials.
It estimates a probability from results.
Keep a tally and count all trials.
More trials usually make the estimate more stable.
Even a fair random experiment can give uneven results.
lessons.worked: A spinner lands on red 18 times in 50 spins. Relative frequency of red = 18/50 = 0.36. This does not guarantee 36 reds in the next 100 spins.
worked_steps: A spinner lands on red 18 times in 50 spins.
This does not guarantee 36 reds in the next 100 spins.
lessons.question: A drawing pin lands point-up 42 times in 120 trials. Estimate the probability of point-up.
scheme: Use event count divided by total trials.
This is an estimate based on the experiment.
lessons.mistake: A short run of results does not prove an object is fair or unfair.

cards.definition: The fraction of trials in which an event occurs.
One run of a probability experiment.

quiz.q: Red occurs 12 times in 40 trials. What is its relative frequency?

misconception.q: Red occurs 12 times in 40 trials. What is its relative frequency? Sam answers: “0.12.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Sample spaces
notes: A sample space lists every possible outcome. A table can keep two choices organised. For equally likely outcomes, probability = favourable outcomes ÷ all outcomes.
List every first choice down one side. List every second choice across the top. Fill every cell, without missing or repeating an outcome.
note_points: A sample space lists every possible outcome.
A table can keep two choices organised.
For equally likely outcomes, probability = favourable outcomes ÷ all outcomes.
List every first choice down one side.
List every second choice across the top.
Fill every cell, without missing or repeating an outcome.
lessons.worked: Toss a fair coin and roll a fair die. There are 2 × 6 = 12 equally likely pairs. Head and an even number has 3 pairs, so its probability is 3/12 = 1/4.
worked_steps: Toss a fair coin and roll a fair die.
Head and an even number has 3 pairs, so its probability is 3/12 = 1/4.
lessons.question: Roll two fair dice. How many ordered outcomes are possible? How many have a total of 7?
lessons.mistake: Totals from two dice are not all equally likely.

cards.definition: The set of every possible outcome.
Having the same chance of happening.

quiz.q: A coin has 2 outcomes and a spinner has 4. How many pairs are possible?
quiz.why: Every coin outcome pairs with each spinner outcome: 2 × 4 = 8.

misconception.q: A coin has 2 outcomes and a spinner has 4. How many pairs are possible? Sam answers: “6.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Every coin outcome pairs with each spinner outcome: 2 × 4 = 8.

lessons.title: Two-way tables and probability
notes: A two-way table sorts the same people or items in two ways. Row and column totals must agree. A frequency tree splits a count into smaller groups.
Fill missing counts using totals. Read which group a probability question chooses from. Use that group's total, not automatically the whole survey.
note_points: A two-way table sorts the same people or items in two ways.
Row and column totals must agree.
A frequency tree splits a count into smaller groups.
Fill missing counts using totals.
Read which group a probability question chooses from.
Use that group's total, not automatically the whole survey.
lessons.worked: There are 12 cyclists, including 5 who wear glasses. Among cyclists, the probability of glasses is 5/12. That is different from the probability for everyone in the survey.
worked_steps: There are 12 cyclists, including 5 who wear glasses.
Among cyclists, the probability of glasses is 5/12.
That is different from the probability for everyone in the survey.
lessons.question: Among 20 bus travellers, 8 play an instrument. Choose one bus traveller. Find the probability they do not play an instrument.
lessons.mistake: Use the group named in the question as your total.

cards.definition: A table sorting the same group by two categories.
The complete set of possible outcomes for the choice being made.

quiz.q: A question chooses from 12 cyclists in a group of 30. Which total goes in the probability denominator?
quiz.why: The choice is from the cyclists only, so the total is 12.

misconception.q: A question chooses from 12 cyclists in a group of 30. Which total goes in the probability denominator? Sam answers: “30.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The choice is from the cyclists only, so the total is 12.

lessons.title: Frequency trees
notes: A frequency tree splits a total into groups. The numbers are counts, not probabilities. Each pair of branches must add to its parent total.
Write the starting total. Split into categories, then split each category again. For a probability, use the total for the group being asked about.
note_points: A frequency tree splits a total into groups.
The numbers are counts, not probabilities.
Each pair of branches must add to its parent total.
Write the starting total.
Split into categories, then split each category again.
For a probability, use the total for the group being asked about.
lessons.worked: Of 30 pupils, 18 walk and 12 do not. Of the walkers, 10 carry a bag and 8 do not. The probability a walker carries a bag is 10/18 = 5/9.
worked_steps: Of 30 pupils, 18 walk and 12 do not.
Of the walkers, 10 carry a bag and 8 do not.
The probability a walker carries a bag is 10/18 = 5/9.
lessons.question: Of 40 pupils, 25 take a bus. Of the bus users, 9 have a pass. How many bus users have no pass? What fraction of bus users have a pass?
scheme: There are 25 bus users in the selected group.
lessons.mistake: Selecting bus users changes the denominator to the bus-user total.

cards.definition: A branching diagram showing counts in groups.
The count before a group is split into smaller groups.

quiz.q: A group of 24 splits into 9 and one other branch. What is missing?
quiz.why: Both branches must add to 24, so 24 − 9 = 15.

misconception.q: A group of 24 splits into 9 and one other branch. What is missing? Sam answers: “33.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Both branches must add to 24, so 24 − 9 = 15.

lessons.title: Listing and counting choices
notes: An organised list helps you count without missing anything. Multiply the number of choices at each stage. Check whether repeats are allowed and whether order matters.
A table works well for two sets of choices. A tree shows later choices branching from earlier ones. If repeats are banned, there are fewer choices at later stages.
note_points: An organised list helps you count without missing anything.
Multiply the number of choices at each stage.
Check whether repeats are allowed and whether order matters.
A table works well for two sets of choices.
A tree shows later choices branching from earlier ones.
If repeats are banned, there are fewer choices at later stages.
lessons.worked: There are 3 shirts and 4 pairs of trousers. Each shirt matches all 4 trousers. There are 3 × 4 = 12 outfits.
worked_steps: There are 3 shirts and 4 pairs of trousers.
lessons.question: Make a three-letter code from A, B, C, D with no repeated letter. How many codes are possible?
scheme: There are 4 choices for the first letter.
There are 3 choices left for the second and 2 for the third.
lessons.mistake: If repeats are banned, do not keep using the original number of choices at every stage.

cards.definition: Multiply the number of choices at each stage to count combinations.
A list organised so no possibilities are missed or repeated.

quiz.q: There are 4 tops and 3 pairs of trousers. How many outfits are possible?
quiz.why: Each of 4 tops can match 3 trousers: 4 × 3 = 12.

misconception.q: There are 4 tops and 3 pairs of trousers. How many outfits are possible? Sam answers: “7.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Each of 4 tops can match 3 trousers: 4 × 3 = 12.

lessons.title: Parts and measures of a circle
notes: A radius goes from the centre to the edge. A diameter crosses the circle through its centre and is twice the radius. The circumference is the distance around the circle.

Circumference = 2πr, or πd. Area = πr². Keep π in an exact answer instead of rounding it. For a sector, use the angle as a fraction of 360° to find its share of area or circumference. The perimeter of a semicircle includes the straight diameter as well as the curved edge.
note_points: A radius goes from the centre to the edge.
A diameter crosses the circle through its centre and is twice the radius.
The circumference is the distance around the circle.
Circumference = 2πr, or πd.
Area = πr².
Keep π in an exact answer instead of rounding it.
For a sector, use the angle as a fraction of 360° to find its share of area or circumference.
The perimeter of a semicircle includes the straight diameter as well as the curved edge.
lessons.worked: A circle has radius 3 cm. Circumference = 2 × π × 3 = 6π cm. Area = π × 3² = 9π cm².
lessons.question: Find the exact area of a circle with diameter 10 cm. Leave π in your answer.
lessons.mistake: Halve the diameter before using it as a radius.

cards.definition: The distance from the centre of a circle to its edge.
A straight line across a circle through the centre, equal to two radii.
The distance around a circle.

quiz.q: A circle has diameter 12 cm. What is its radius?
quiz.why: The radius is half the diameter: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.

misconception.q: A circle has diameter 12 cm. What is its radius? Sam answers: “24 cm.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The radius is half the diameter: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.

lessons.title: Parts of circles and curved boundaries
notes: A sector is a slice of a circle. Its angle gives its fraction of the full 360° turn. A curved edge is called an arc.
Multiply the full-circle area by angle/360. For a sector’s perimeter, add the arc and its two radii. For a semicircle, add the curved half-circumference and the diameter.
note_points: A sector is a slice of a circle.
Its angle gives its fraction of the full 360° turn.
A curved edge is called an arc.
Multiply the full-circle area by angle/360.
For a sector’s perimeter, add the arc and its two radii.
For a semicircle, add the curved half-circumference and the diameter.
lessons.worked: A semicircle has radius 4 cm. Its curved edge is half of 2π × 4 = 8π, so 4π cm. Its full perimeter is 4π + 8 cm.
worked_steps: Its curved edge is half of 2π × 4 = 8π, so 4π cm.
lessons.question: A quarter-circle has radius 6 cm. Give its exact area and full perimeter.
lessons.mistake: A sector’s perimeter includes its straight edges.

cards.definition: A region between two radii and an arc.
A part of a circle’s circumference.

quiz.q: What fraction of a full circle is a 60° sector?
quiz.why: 60/360 simplifies to 1/6.

misconception.q: What fraction of a full circle is a 60° sector? Sam answers: “1/3.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Cylinders and cones
notes: A cylinder has a circular cross-section. Its volume is circle area × height. A cone with the same base and height has one third of that volume.
Cylinder volume = πr²h. Cone volume = πr²h ÷ 3. Use the perpendicular height, not the sloping side.
note_points: A cylinder has a circular cross-section.
Its volume is circle area × height.
A cone with the same base and height has one third of that volume.
Cylinder volume = πr²h.
Cone volume = πr²h ÷ 3.
Use the perpendicular height, not the sloping side.
lessons.worked: With radius 3 cm and height 8 cm, base area = 9π cm². Cylinder volume = 9π × 8 = 72π cm³. The matching cone has volume 72π ÷ 3 = 24π cm³.
worked_steps: With radius 3 cm and height 8 cm, base area = 9π cm².
The matching cone has volume 72π ÷ 3 = 24π cm³.
lessons.question: Find the exact volume of a cone with radius 4 cm and perpendicular height 9 cm.
lessons.mistake: A cone's volume is one third of the matching cylinder, not one half.

cards.definition: A prism with a circular cross-section.
A solid with a circular base tapering to a point.

quiz.q: A cylinder has volume 60 cm³. What is the volume of a cone with the same base and perpendicular height?
quiz.why: The cone has one third of the matching cylinder volume.

misconception.q: A cylinder has volume 60 cm³. What is the volume of a cone with the same base and perpendicular height? Sam answers: “30 cm³.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The cone has one third of the matching cylinder volume.

lessons.title: Finding areas
notes: Area measures how much surface a shape covers. A rectangle's area is base × height. A triangle's area is half base × perpendicular height.

Perpendicular means at right angles to the base. A parallelogram uses base × perpendicular height. For a trapezium, average the parallel sides and multiply by the height. Split a compound shape into simpler shapes, or subtract a cut-out. 1 m² = 10,000 cm² because a square metre has 100 rows of 100 square centimetres.
note_points: Area measures how much surface a shape covers.
A rectangle's area is base × height.
A triangle's area is half base × perpendicular height.
Perpendicular means at right angles to the base.
A parallelogram uses base × perpendicular height.
For a trapezium, average the parallel sides and multiply by the height.
Split a compound shape into simpler shapes, or subtract a cut-out.
1 m² = 10,000 cm² because a square metre has 100 rows of 100 square centimetres.
lessons.worked: A trapezium has parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm, with height 4 cm. Area = (6 + 10) ÷ 2 × 4. The answer is 32 cm².
worked_steps: A trapezium has parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm, with height 4 cm.
lessons.question: A triangle has base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm. Find its area.
lessons.mistake: The sloping side of a triangle is not always its perpendicular height.

worked_rows.work: Parallel sides: 6 cm, 10 cm; height: 4 cm

cards.definition: The amount of surface a shape covers, measured in square units.
The height measured at right angles to the base.

quiz.q: A triangle has base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. What is its area?
quiz.why: A triangle is half a matching rectangle: ½ × 8 × 5 = 20 cm².

misconception.q: A triangle has base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. What is its area? Sam answers: “40 cm².” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: A triangle is half a matching rectangle: ½ × 8 × 5 = 20 cm².

lessons.title: Reading and drawing charts
notes: A bar chart compares categories. A pictogram uses symbols and a key. A line graph can show change over time.
Label axes and give units where needed. Use evenly spaced numbers on a scale. Check whether an axis starts above zero and exaggerates a difference.
note_points: A bar chart compares categories.
A pictogram uses symbols and a key.
A line graph can show change over time.
Label axes and give units where needed.
Use evenly spaced numbers on a scale.
Check whether an axis starts above zero and exaggerates a difference.
lessons.worked: A pictogram key says one symbol means 4 pupils. Two full symbols mean 8 pupils, and half a symbol means 2. So 2½ symbols mean 10 pupils.
worked_steps: A pictogram key says one symbol means 4 pupils.
Two full symbols mean 8 pupils, and half a symbol means 2.
lessons.question: A pictogram uses one symbol for 8 books. How many books do 3½ symbols show?
lessons.mistake: Always read the key before counting pictogram symbols.

cards.definition: A chart using symbols to show amounts.
The explanation of what a symbol or label stands for.

quiz.q: One symbol represents 6 items. What do 2½ symbols represent?
quiz.why: Two symbols represent 12 and half a symbol represents 3, giving 15.

misconception.q: One symbol represents 6 items. What do 2½ symbols represent? Sam answers: “12.5.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Two symbols represent 12 and half a symbol represents 3, giving 15.

lessons.title: Bar charts and pictograms
notes: A bar chart compares categories. Dual bars compare two groups for each category. A composite bar stacks parts to show a total.
Start with a labelled scale and equal-width bars. Leave gaps between categories. For a pictogram, give a key and use part-symbols accurately.
note_points: A bar chart compares categories.
Dual bars compare two groups for each category.
A composite bar stacks parts to show a total.
Start with a labelled scale and equal-width bars.
Leave gaps between categories.
For a pictogram, give a key and use part-symbols accurately.
lessons.worked: A reading club has 6 Year 7 and 4 Year 8 pupils on Monday. Dual bars show 6 and 4 separately. A composite bar stacks 6 and 4 to a height of 10.
worked_steps: A reading club has 6 Year 7 and 4 Year 8 pupils on Monday.
A composite bar stacks 6 and 4 to a height of 10.
lessons.question: A composite bar contains 8 walkers and 5 cyclists. What is its total height? Explain how a dual bar chart would show the data.
scheme: A dual chart has two separate bars for the category.
A key identifies walkers and cyclists.
lessons.mistake: A stacked bar reaches the total, not the value of its final part.

cards.definition: Two bars for each category, comparing two groups.
A bar split into stacked parts that make a total.

quiz.q: A bar stacks 7 girls and 9 boys. What is the total?
quiz.why: The stacked parts add: 7 + 9 = 16.

misconception.q: A bar stacks 7 girls and 9 boys. What is the total? Sam answers: “9.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Pie charts
notes: A full pie chart is a 360° turn. Each sector shows a fraction of the total. A larger frequency gives a larger sector angle.
Sector angle = frequency ÷ total × 360°. Check all angles add to 360°. Equal-sized sectors in different surveys may stand for different numbers of people.
note_points: A full pie chart is a 360° turn.
Each sector shows a fraction of the total.
A larger frequency gives a larger sector angle.
Sector angle = frequency ÷ total × 360°.
Check all angles add to 360°.
Equal-sized sectors in different surveys may stand for different numbers of people.
lessons.worked: 15 of 60 pupils walk to school. The fraction is 15/60 = 1/4. The sector angle is 1/4 × 360 = 90°.
lessons.question: A category contains 18 of 72 results. Find its pie-chart angle.
lessons.mistake: A sector is a share of that chart's total, not a fixed number of people.

cards.definition: A slice of a circle between two radii and an arc.
How often an outcome or category occurs.

quiz.q: What angle represents one quarter of a pie chart?
quiz.why: A full circle is 360°, so a quarter is 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.

misconception.q: What angle represents one quarter of a pie chart? Sam answers: “25°.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: A full circle is 360°, so a quarter is 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.

lessons.title: Graphs showing change over time
notes: A time series records values in time order. Time goes on the horizontal axis. The vertical axis shows the measured value and its unit.
Choose even scales and plot each pair of values. Join readings in time order when this makes sense. Look for trends, repeating patterns and unusual points.
note_points: A time series records values in time order.
Time goes on the horizontal axis.
The vertical axis shows the measured value and its unit.
Choose even scales and plot each pair of values.
Join readings in time order when this makes sense.
Look for trends, repeating patterns and unusual points.
lessons.worked: A plant is 4 cm tall on day 0, 7 cm on day 2 and 10 cm on day 4. Plot (0,4), (2,7), (4,10). Its height rises by 3 cm every two days in these readings.
worked_steps: A plant is 4 cm tall on day 0, 7 cm on day 2 and 10 cm on day 4.
Its height rises by 3 cm every two days in these readings.
lessons.question: Temperatures at 09:00, 10:00 and 11:00 are 12°C, 15°C and 14°C. Describe the changes and name the horizontal axis.
scheme: The temperature rises by 3°C, then falls by 1°C.
The vertical axis shows temperature in °C.
lessons.mistake: Time order matters; do not sort the points by height.

cards.definition: Values of a quantity recorded over time.
The overall pattern in data.

quiz.q: Which belongs on the horizontal axis of a daily temperature graph?
quiz.why: A time series uses time on its horizontal axis.

misconception.q: Which belongs on the horizontal axis of a daily temperature graph? Sam answers: “Temperature in °C.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: A time series uses time on its horizontal axis.

lessons.title: Stem-and-leaf diagrams
notes: A stem-and-leaf diagram keeps each original value. The key tells you what each stem and leaf mean. Put leaves in order and keep repeats.
Count values to find the median. Use the highest and lowest values to find the range. When comparing groups, discuss a typical value and the spread.
note_points: A stem-and-leaf diagram keeps each original value.
The key tells you what each stem and leaf mean.
Put leaves in order and keep repeats.
Count values to find the median.
Use the highest and lowest values to find the range.
When comparing groups, discuss a typical value and the spread.
lessons.worked: With key 2 ¦ 4 = 24, stem 2 with leaves 1, 4, 4, 8 means 21, 24, 24, 28. The middle two values are both 24, so the median is 24. The range is 28 − 21 = 7.
worked_steps: With key 2 ¦ 4 = 24, stem 2 with leaves 1, 4, 4, 8 means 21, 24, 24, 28.
The middle two values are both 24, so the median is 24.
lessons.question: A stem 3 has leaves 1, 2, 6, 9. With key 3 ¦ 1 = 31, find the median.
scheme: Their mean is 34, so the median is 34.
lessons.mistake: A key is essential. The same digits can stand for different place values.

cards.definition: A display separating each value into a stem and leaf while keeping individual data.
The explanation of how to read the place values in a diagram.

quiz.q: With key 2 ¦ 4 = 24, what does 3 ¦ 7 mean?
quiz.why: The stem is tens and the leaf is units, so the value is 37.

misconception.q: With key 2 ¦ 4 = 24, what does 3 ¦ 7 mean? Sam answers: “3.7.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The stem is tens and the leaf is units, so the value is 37.

lessons.title: Index laws with the same base
notes: An index tells you how many equal factors to multiply. For example, x³ = x × x × x. The base is the repeated number or letter.
When multiplying the same base, add the powers. When dividing the same non-zero base, subtract the powers. For a power of a power, multiply the powers.
note_points: An index tells you how many equal factors to multiply.
For example, x³ = x × x × x.
The base is the repeated number or letter.
When multiplying the same base, add the powers.
When dividing the same non-zero base, subtract the powers.
For a power of a power, multiply the powers.
lessons.worked: x³ × x² has five x factors, so it is x⁵. x⁷ ÷ x² = x⁵, for x ≠ 0. (x²)³ = x⁶.
worked_steps: x³ × x² has five x factors, so it is x⁵.
lessons.question: Simplify a⁴ × a³ ÷ a². State a restriction.
scheme: Add the powers when multiplying: a⁷.
a cannot be zero because a² is a divisor.
lessons.mistake: Adding x² + x³ does not give x⁵; these are unlike terms.

cards.definition: The repeated factor in a power.
The power indicating repeated multiplication.

quiz.q: Simplify x² × x⁴.
quiz.why: There are 2 + 4 = 6 factors of x.

misconception.q: Simplify x² × x⁴. Sam answers: “x⁸.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Powers and roots
notes: A power shows repeated multiplication. For example, 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2. A root undoes a power, such as √25 = 5.

For the same base, add powers when multiplying and subtract powers when dividing. A power of a power means multiply the powers. A non-zero number to power 0 is 1; a negative power means a reciprocal. For a positive number, a power of 1/n means take the nth root. For example, 8 to power −2/3 is 1 divided by (cube root of 8)², giving 1/4.
note_points: A power shows repeated multiplication.
For example, 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2.
A root undoes a power, such as √25 = 5.
For the same base, add powers when multiplying and subtract powers when dividing.
A power of a power means multiply the powers.
A non-zero number to power 0 is 1; a negative power means a reciprocal.
For a positive number, a power of 1/n means take the nth root.
For example, 8 to power −2/3 is 1 divided by (cube root of 8)², giving 1/4.
lessons.worked: 8 to power 2/3 means cube root first, then square. The cube root of 8 is 2. 2² = 4.
worked_steps: 8 to power 2/3 means cube root first, then square.
lessons.question: Work out 27 to the power 2/3.
lessons.mistake: √25 means the positive square root, 5. Solving x² = 25 gives both 5 and −5.

cards.definition: The power telling how many times a base is used as a factor.
A number that gives the original value when multiplied by itself.

quiz.q: Simplify 2³ × 2⁴.
quiz.why: For matching bases, add the powers when multiplying: 3 + 4 = 7.

misconception.q: Simplify 2³ × 2⁴. Sam answers: “2¹².” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: For matching bases, add the powers when multiplying: 3 + 4 = 7.

lessons.title: Positive and negative powers of ten
notes: 10³ = 1000 and 10¹ = 10. 10⁰ = 1. A negative power gives a reciprocal: 10⁻² = 1/100.

Multiplying by 10 makes every digit worth ten times as much. Dividing by 10 makes every digit worth one tenth as much. The decimal point marks the units position; it is the digits’ place values that change.
note_points: A negative power gives a reciprocal: 10⁻² = 1/100.
Multiplying by 10 makes every digit worth ten times as much.
Dividing by 10 makes every digit worth one tenth as much.
The decimal point marks the units position; it is the digits’ place values that change.
lessons.worked: 4.2 × 10³ = 4200. 4.2 × 10⁻³ = 0.0042. In each step the digits move to a different place value.
worked_steps: In each step the digits move to a different place value.
lessons.question: Write 10⁻⁴ as a decimal, then calculate 6.3 × 10⁻².
lessons.mistake: A negative power does not mean a negative answer.

cards.definition: A power representing a reciprocal.
A number such as 1000 = 10³ or 0.01 = 10⁻².

quiz.q: What is 10⁻³?

misconception.q: What is 10⁻³? Sam answers: “−1000.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Reading and writing standard form
notes: Standard form writes a number as A × 10ⁿ. For a positive number, 1 ≤ A < 10. n is an integer, which may be negative or zero.
Choose A with one non-zero digit before the decimal point. Find the power of ten that restores the original number. Check whether the result should be large or small.
note_points: Standard form writes a number as A × 10ⁿ.
For a positive number, 1 ≤ A < 10.
n is an integer, which may be negative or zero.
Choose A with one non-zero digit before the decimal point.
Find the power of ten that restores the original number.
Check whether the result should be large or small.
lessons.worked: 56 000 = 5.6 × 10⁴. 0.00056 = 5.6 × 10⁻⁴. The coefficient is the same, but the power changes the size.
worked_steps: The coefficient is the same, but the power changes the size.
lessons.question: Write 0.00072 in standard form and write 3.4 × 10⁵ as an ordinary number.
lessons.mistake: The coefficient must be less than 10, not equal to 10.

cards.definition: A × 10ⁿ, where 1 ≤ A < 10 for a positive number and n is an integer.
The numerical multiplier of a term.

quiz.q: Which is 0.0048 in standard form?
quiz.why: 4.8 divided by 1000 is 0.0048, and 4.8 is an allowed coefficient.

misconception.q: Which is 0.0048 in standard form? Sam answers: “48 × 10⁻⁴.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: 4.8 divided by 1000 is 0.0048, and 4.8 is an allowed coefficient.

lessons.title: Spotting and continuing sequences
notes: A sequence is a list of numbers in order. Each number is called a term. The position tells you where a term is in the list.
Look at how much the numbers change each time. Check the rule between every pair of neighbouring terms. A short list can sometimes fit more than one rule.
note_points: A sequence is a list of numbers in order.
Each number is called a term.
The position tells you where a term is in the list.
Look at how much the numbers change each time.
Check the rule between every pair of neighbouring terms.
A short list can sometimes fit more than one rule.
lessons.worked: For 5, 9, 13, 17, add 4 each time. 17 + 4 = 21, then 21 + 4 = 25. The next two terms are 21 and 25.
worked_steps: The next two terms are 21 and 25.
lessons.question: Continue 7, 12, 17, 22. Give the next two terms and explain the rule.
scheme: Both new terms follow the same rule.
lessons.mistake: The position of a term is not the same as its value.

cards.definition: A number or item in a sequence.
The instruction used to get from one term to the next.

quiz.q: What comes next in 3, 7, 11, 15?
quiz.why: Add 4 each time: 15 + 4 = 19.

misconception.q: What comes next in 3, 7, 11, 15? Sam answers: “18.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: A rule for any term
notes: An nth-term rule lets you find a term from its position. The letter n stands for the position. An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount each time.

Start with the difference multiplied by n. Compare this with the actual sequence and adjust by adding or subtracting. Check your rule for the first few positions. A term belongs to a sequence only if its position is a positive whole number.
note_points: An nth-term rule lets you find a term from its position.
The letter n stands for the position.
An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount each time.
Start with the difference multiplied by n.
Compare this with the actual sequence and adjust by adding or subtracting.
Check your rule for the first few positions.
A term belongs to a sequence only if its position is a positive whole number.
lessons.worked: For 7, 11, 15, 19, the difference is 4. 4n gives 4, 8, 12, 16, so add 3: the rule is 4n + 3. The twentieth term is 4 × 20 + 3 = 83.
worked_steps: 4n gives 4, 8, 12, 16, so add 3: the rule is 4n + 3.
lessons.question: Find the nth-term rule for 8, 13, 18, 23. Use it to find the tenth term.
lessons.mistake: “Add 5” finds the next term. “5n + 3” finds a term from its position.

cards.definition: A rule that finds a term from its position n.
Where a term appears in a sequence, starting at 1.

quiz.q: What is the fifth term of 3n + 2?
quiz.why: Put n = 5 into the rule: 3 × 5 + 2 = 17.

misconception.q: What is the fifth term of 3n + 2? Sam answers: “15.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Different types of sequence
notes: An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount each time. A geometric sequence multiplies by the same number each time. A quadratic sequence has changes that themselves change by a fixed amount.
Write the differences between neighbouring terms. If these are not equal, compare the next row of differences. Also check whether multiplying by the same number works.
note_points: An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount each time.
A geometric sequence multiplies by the same number each time.
A quadratic sequence has changes that themselves change by a fixed amount.
Write the differences between neighbouring terms.
If these are not equal, compare the next row of differences.
Also check whether multiplying by the same number works.
lessons.worked: For 1, 4, 9, 16, the differences are 3, 5, 7. These differences go up by 2, so this is a quadratic pattern. For 3, 6, 12, 24, multiply by 2 instead.
worked_steps: These differences go up by 2, so this is a quadratic pattern.
lessons.question: Continue 2, 6, 18, 54 by one term. Why is this not an arithmetic sequence?
scheme: The differences between terms are not equal.
lessons.mistake: A growing sequence does not always add the same amount each time.

cards.definition: A sequence that adds the same amount each time.
A sequence that multiplies by the same number each time.

quiz.q: Which sequence multiplies by the same number each time?
quiz.why: Each term in 2, 6, 18, 54 is three times the one before.

misconception.q: Which sequence multiplies by the same number each time? Sam answers: “2, 5, 8, 11.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Each term in 2, 6, 18, 54 is three times the one before.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting decimals
notes: Line up numbers by place value. Put decimal points directly under each other. Add zeros at the end if useful.
Work from the smallest place value. Exchange one larger unit for ten smaller units when needed. Check subtraction by adding your answer back.
note_points: Line up numbers by place value.
Put decimal points directly under each other.
Add zeros at the end if useful.
Work from the smallest place value.
Exchange one larger unit for ten smaller units when needed.
Check subtraction by adding your answer back.
lessons.worked: 13.7 − 8.46 becomes 13.70 − 8.46. Column subtraction gives 5.24. Check: 8.46 + 5.24 = 13.70.
lessons.question: Calculate 24.6 − 7.85.
lessons.mistake: Do not line up the last digits if the decimal points then sit in different columns.

cards.definition: A column for units, tenths or another fixed digit value.
A check that uses the operation that undoes the calculation.

quiz.q: Calculate 7.2 − 0.85.
quiz.why: Write 7.20 − 0.85 and line up the decimal points.

misconception.q: Calculate 7.2 − 0.85. Sam answers: “6.45.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Write 7.20 − 0.85 and line up the decimal points.

lessons.title: Multiplying decimals
notes: Multiplication can make a number larger or smaller. Multiplying a positive number by a value between 0 and 1 makes it smaller. Multiplying by 10 changes each digit's place value.
Multiply the numbers as whole numbers first. Count the decimal places in both starting numbers. Use that total to place the decimal point in the answer.
note_points: Multiplication can make a number larger or smaller.
Multiplying a positive number by a value between 0 and 1 makes it smaller.
Multiplying by 10 changes each digit's place value.
Multiply the numbers as whole numbers first.
Count the decimal places in both starting numbers.
Use that total to place the decimal point in the answer.
lessons.worked: For 2.4 × 0.35, calculate 24 × 35 = 840. There are three decimal places in total. The answer is 0.840, or 0.84.
worked_steps: There are three decimal places in total.
lessons.question: Calculate 1.6 × 0.45.
scheme: There are three decimal places in total.
lessons.mistake: Multiplying by 0.1 is dividing by 10, not multiplying by 10.

cards.definition: The result of multiplying numbers.
10 multiplied by itself a whole number of times, or its reciprocal for a negative power.

quiz.q: Calculate 0.6 × 0.4.
quiz.why: 6 × 4 = 24. The two starting decimal places give 0.24.

misconception.q: Calculate 0.6 × 0.4. Sam answers: “2.4.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: 6 × 4 = 24. The two starting decimal places give 0.24.

lessons.title: Dividing by decimals
notes: Division asks how many of one amount fit into another. You can multiply both numbers by the same non-zero amount without changing the answer. This can remove a decimal from the number you divide by.
Multiply both numbers by 10, 100 or another suitable power of ten. Do the easier division. Check by multiplying your answer by the original divisor.
note_points: Division asks how many of one amount fit into another.
You can multiply both numbers by the same non-zero amount without changing the answer.
This can remove a decimal from the number you divide by.
Multiply both numbers by 10, 100 or another suitable power of ten.
Do the easier division.
Check by multiplying your answer by the original divisor.
lessons.question: Calculate 8.4 ÷ 0.4.
lessons.mistake: Change both numbers by the same factor, not just one of them.

cards.definition: The number you divide by.
The answer to a division.

quiz.q: Calculate 4.8 ÷ 0.6.
quiz.why: Multiply both numbers by 10 to get 48 ÷ 6 = 8.

misconception.q: Calculate 4.8 ÷ 0.6. Sam answers: “0.8.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Multiply both numbers by 10 to get 48 ÷ 6 = 8.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting negative numbers
notes: Negative numbers are less than zero. On a number line, numbers increase as you move right. Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding its opposite.
Use a number line to track the change. Keep the sign of a number separate from the operation sign. For a change, calculate final value minus starting value.
note_points: Negative numbers are less than zero.
On a number line, numbers increase as you move right.
Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding its opposite.
Use a number line to track the change.
Keep the sign of a number separate from the operation sign.
For a change, calculate final value minus starting value.
lessons.worked: −4 + 7 means start at −4 and move 7 steps right, reaching 3. 5 − (−3) becomes 5 + 3 = 8. A rise from −6°C to 2°C is a change of 8°C.
worked_steps: −4 + 7 means start at −4 and move 7 steps right, reaching 3.
A rise from −6°C to 2°C is a change of 8°C.
lessons.question: Calculate −7 − (−12).
lessons.mistake: Subtracting a negative number moves you to the right on a number line.

cards.definition: A number less than zero.
A number the same distance from zero on the other side, such as −4 and 4.

quiz.q: Calculate 3 − (−5).
quiz.why: Subtracting a negative means adding its opposite: 3 + 5 = 8.

misconception.q: Calculate 3 − (−5). Sam answers: “−2.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Subtracting a negative means adding its opposite: 3 + 5 = 8.

lessons.title: Rounding numbers
notes: Rounding gives a nearby, simpler number. Decimal places are counted from the decimal point. Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit.
Mark the last digit you need to keep. Look at the next digit: 5 or more means round up. Keep zeros needed to show the right place value.
note_points: Rounding gives a nearby, simpler number.
Decimal places are counted from the decimal point.
Significant figures start at the first non-zero digit.
Mark the last digit you need to keep.
Look at the next digit: 5 or more means round up.
Keep zeros needed to show the right place value.
lessons.worked: For 0.006847 to 2 significant figures, keep 6 and 8. The next digit is 4, so do not round up. The rounded number is 0.0068.
worked_steps: For 0.006847 to 2 significant figures, keep 6 and 8.
The next digit is 4, so do not round up.
lessons.question: Round 0.007864 to 2 significant figures.
scheme: Keep 7 and 8, then use the next digit, 6, to round up.
lessons.mistake: The zeros before the first non-zero digit do not count as significant figures.

cards.definition: A digit position to the right of the decimal point.
A digit counted from the first non-zero digit when rounding.

quiz.q: Round 4.768 to 2 decimal places.
quiz.why: Keep the hundredths digit. The next digit, 8, rounds it up.

misconception.q: Round 4.768 to 2 decimal places. Sam answers: “4.76.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Keep the hundredths digit. The next digit, 8, rounds it up.

lessons.title: Estimating and rounding intervals
notes: An estimate is a quick answer using rounded numbers. Use it to check whether an exact answer looks sensible. A rounded measurement can stand for a range of original values.
Round numbers to make the calculation easier. For a rounding interval, go half a rounding step below and above. Include the lower end but not the upper end for the usual school convention.

lessons.worked: 19.6 × 4.8 is close to 20 × 5 = 100. A length of 12 cm rounded to the nearest centimetre could be 11.5 cm. It must be less than 12.5 cm, because that would round up to 13 cm.

lessons.mistake: An estimate is a check, not an exact answer.

The range of original values that would round to a stated measurement.

quiz.q: Which is a sensible estimate of 29.7 × 4.1?
quiz.why: Round to nearby easy numbers, then keep the same operation.

misconception.q: Which is a sensible estimate of 29.7 × 4.1? Sam answers: “3 × 4 = 12.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Round to nearby easy numbers, then keep the same operation.

lessons.title: Listing and counting choices
notes: An organised list helps you count without missing anything. Multiply the number of choices at each stage. Check whether repeats are allowed and whether order matters.
A table works well for two sets of choices. A tree shows later choices branching from earlier ones. If repeats are banned, there are fewer choices at later stages.

lessons.worked: There are 3 shirts and 4 pairs of trousers. Each shirt matches all 4 trousers. There are 3 × 4 = 12 outfits.
worked_steps: There are 3 shirts and 4 pairs of trousers.
lessons.question: Make a three-letter code from A, B, C, D with no repeated letter. How many codes are possible?
scheme: There are 4 choices for the first letter.
There are 3 choices left for the second and 2 for the third.

quiz.q: There are 4 tops and 3 pairs of trousers. How many outfits are possible?
quiz.why: Each of 4 tops can match 3 trousers: 4 × 3 = 12.

misconception.q: There are 4 tops and 3 pairs of trousers. How many outfits are possible? Sam answers: “7.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Each of 4 tops can match 3 trousers: 4 × 3 = 12.

lessons.title: Multiplying and dividing negatives
notes: For two numbers, matching signs give a positive answer. Different signs give a negative answer. This works for multiplication and division.
Work out the size of the answer, then its sign. For several negative factors, count how many negative signs there are. An even number of negative factors gives a positive product.

Different signs give a negative answer.

lessons.worked: (−6) × (−4) = 24. 24 ÷ (−4) = −6. (−3)² = 9, but −3² = −9 because the square comes first.
worked_steps: (−3)² = 9, but −3² = −9 because the square comes first.
lessons.question: Calculate (−8) × 3 ÷ (−4).
lessons.mistake: “Two negatives make a positive” applies here to multiplying or dividing, not to every calculation.

cards.definition: A number greater than zero.
A negative number being multiplied as part of a product.

quiz.q: Calculate (−4) × (−3).
quiz.why: For multiplication, two negative factors give a positive product.

misconception.q: Calculate (−4) × (−3). Sam answers: “−12.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: For multiplication, two negative factors give a positive product.

lessons.title: Powers and roots
notes: A power shows repeated multiplication. For example, 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2. A root undoes a power, such as √25 = 5.

For the same base, add powers when multiplying and subtract powers when dividing. A power of a power means multiply the powers. A non-zero number to power 0 is 1; a negative power means a reciprocal. For a positive number, a power of 1/n means take the nth root. For example, 8 to power −2/3 is 1 divided by (cube root of 8)², giving 1/4.

For example, 2³ = 2 × 2 × 2.

lessons.worked: 8 to power 2/3 means cube root first, then square. The cube root of 8 is 2. 2² = 4.

lessons.question: Work out 27 to the power 2/3.
lessons.mistake: √25 means the positive square root, 5. Solving x² = 25 gives both 5 and −5.

cards.definition: The power telling how many times a base is used as a factor.
A number that gives the original value when multiplied by itself.

quiz.q: Simplify 2³ × 2⁴.
quiz.why: For matching bases, add the powers when multiplying: 3 + 4 = 7.

misconception.q: Simplify 2³ × 2⁴. Sam answers: “2¹².” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: For matching bases, add the powers when multiplying: 3 + 4 = 7.

lessons.title: The order of operations
notes: Work out brackets first. Then calculate powers and roots. Next do multiplication and division, working from left to right.
Finish with addition and subtraction, also from left to right. A fraction bar groups everything above and below it. Use brackets when entering a negative number with a power.

Then calculate powers and roots.

lessons.worked: 18 ÷ 3 × 2 means work from left to right. 18 ÷ 3 = 6, then 6 × 2 = 12. It does not mean 18 ÷ 6.

cards.definition: The agreed order for working out a calculation.
Multiply a number by itself.

quiz.q: Calculate 10 + 2 × 3.
quiz.why: Multiply first: 2 × 3 = 6, then add 10.

misconception.q: Calculate 10 + 2 × 3. Sam answers: “36.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Factors, multiples and primes
notes: A factor divides into a whole number with no remainder. A multiple is found by multiplying a number by a whole number. A prime has exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself.
List factors in pairs so you do not miss any. The number 1 is not prime. Prime factorisation writes a number as prime numbers multiplied together.
note_points: A factor divides into a whole number with no remainder.
A multiple is found by multiplying a number by a whole number.
A prime has exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself.
List factors in pairs so you do not miss any.

lessons.worked: 18 has factors 1, 2, 3, 6, 9 and 18. 18 = 2 × 3 × 3. Using a power, this is 2 × 3².
lessons.question: Write 60 as a product of prime factors using powers.
lessons.mistake: Factors fit into a number. Multiples are in its times table.

cards.definition: A whole number that divides another whole number with no remainder.
A positive whole number with exactly two positive factors, 1 and itself.

quiz.q: Which number is prime?
quiz.why: 13 has only the factors 1 and 13. The number 1 is not prime.

misconception.q: Which number is prime? Sam answers: “1.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: 13 has only the factors 1 and 13. The number 1 is not prime.

lessons.title: Highest common factor and lowest common multiple
notes: The HCF is the largest factor shared by the numbers. The LCM is the smallest positive number in both times tables. Prime factors help find both.
For the HCF, multiply the prime factors shared by both numbers. For the LCM, include enough of each prime factor to build either number. A Venn diagram can keep track of shared factors.

The LCM is the smallest positive number in both times tables.

For the HCF, multiply the prime factors shared by both numbers.

lessons.question: Find the HCF and LCM of 18 and 30.
lessons.mistake: For the LCM, shared factors are not counted twice when using a prime-factor Venn diagram.

cards.definition: The highest common factor: the largest factor shared by the numbers.
The lowest common multiple: the smallest positive number in all the given times tables.

quiz.q: Find the HCF of 12 and 18.
quiz.why: The shared factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6. The largest is 6.

misconception.q: Find the HCF of 12 and 18. Sam answers: “36.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The shared factors are 1, 2, 3 and 6. The largest is 6.

lessons.title: Integers, rational and irrational numbers
notes: Integers are whole numbers, including negatives and zero. Rational numbers can be written as a fraction of integers with a non-zero denominator. Irrational numbers cannot be written that way.
Terminating decimals are rational. Recurring decimals are also rational. Roots of non-square positive integers are irrational.

lessons.worked: −4 is an integer and rational: −4 = −4/1. 0.125 is rational: it is 1/8. √2 is irrational, but √9 = 3 is rational.
lessons.question: Classify −6, 0.4 and √5. Which are integers and which are rational?
scheme: 0.4 = 2/5 is rational, but not an integer.
√5 is irrational and not an integer.
lessons.mistake: A root sign alone does not make a number irrational.

cards.definition: A number expressible as a fraction of integers, with a non-zero denominator.
A real number that cannot be written as such a fraction.

quiz.q: Which number is irrational?
quiz.why: 7 is not a square number, so √7 cannot be written as a fraction of integers.

misconception.q: Which number is irrational? Sam answers: “√16.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: 7 is not a square number, so √7 cannot be written as a fraction of integers.

lessons.title: Positive and negative powers of ten
notes: 10³ = 1000 and 10¹ = 10. 10⁰ = 1. A negative power gives a reciprocal: 10⁻² = 1/100.

Multiplying by 10 makes every digit worth ten times as much. Dividing by 10 makes every digit worth one tenth as much. The decimal point marks the units position; it is the digits’ place values that change.

lessons.question: Write 10⁻⁴ as a decimal, then calculate 6.3 × 10⁻².
lessons.mistake: A negative power does not mean a negative answer.

cards.definition: A power representing a reciprocal.
A number such as 1000 = 10³ or 0.01 = 10⁻².

quiz.q: What is 10⁻³?

misconception.q: What is 10⁻³? Sam answers: “−1000.” Explain why this is wrong.

notes: Standard form writes a number as A × 10ⁿ. For a positive number, 1 ≤ A < 10. n is an integer, which may be negative or zero.
Choose A with one non-zero digit before the decimal point. Find the power of ten that restores the original number. Check whether the result should be large or small.

lessons.title: Standard form
notes: Standard form makes very large or small numbers easier to write. For a positive number, use A × 10ⁿ with A at least 1 but less than 10. The power n is a whole number, possibly negative.

For multiplication, multiply the first numbers and add the powers of ten. Then adjust so the first number is between 1 and 10. For addition, first use matching powers of ten. For division, divide the first numbers and subtract the powers of ten.

notes: Standard form separates a coefficient and a power of ten. Use index laws when multiplying or dividing. For addition and subtraction, first use matching powers.

For a two-term denominator, a conjugate changes the middle sign, such as 2 + √3 to 2 − √3. Multiplying top and bottom by the conjugate can remove the root from the denominator.

lessons.title: Reading and writing algebra
notes: A letter can stand for a number. 3a means 3 × a, and a² means a × a. An expression has no equals sign; an equation says two things are equal.

Read brackets carefully. 2n + 3 means double n, then add 3. 2(n + 3) means add 3 to n, then double the whole result. An identity is true for every allowed value of its letters. A formula links named quantities, such as distance, speed and time.

misconception.q: What does 4a mean? Sam answers: “4 + a.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Collecting like terms
notes: Like terms have the same letters and powers. You can add or subtract their number parts. Terms in x and x² are not like terms.
Group matching terms together. Keep each term's plus or minus sign. Combine the plain numbers separately.

You can add or subtract their number parts.
Terms in x and x² are not like terms.
Group matching terms together.
Keep each term's plus or minus sign.
Combine the plain numbers separately.

worked_steps: 5a + 3b − 2a + b has a terms and b terms.

misconception.q: Simplify 6x − 2x. Sam answers: “4.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Expanding and factorising brackets
notes: Expanding means multiplying out a bracket. Multiply every term inside by the number outside. Factorising reverses this by taking out a common factor.

Watch signs when multiplying negative numbers.

notes: Factorising rewrites a sum as a product. It is the reverse of expanding. A common factor divides every term.

Find a shared number or letter factor.

For x² + bx + c, factorising means finding two suitable brackets. The two numbers must add to b and multiply to c. Check your brackets by expanding them. For x² + bx + c, the bracket numbers add to b and multiply to c. A difference of squares factorises as a² − b² = (a − b)(a + b).

Check your brackets by expanding them.

cards.definition: A fraction containing letters in its numerator or denominator.
A factor shared by two or more expressions or numbers.

quiz.q: Simplify x/3 + x/6.
quiz.why: Rewrite x/3 as 2x/6. Then 3x/6 = x/2.

misconception.q: Simplify x/3 + x/6. Sam answers: “2x/9.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Solving factorised quadratics
notes: A quadratic includes a squared unknown. If a product is zero, at least one factor must be zero. A quadratic can have two different solutions.
Rearrange to make one side zero. Factorise the quadratic. Set each factor equal to zero and solve.
note_points: A quadratic includes a squared unknown.
If a product is zero, at least one factor must be zero.
A quadratic can have two different solutions.
Rearrange to make one side zero.
Factorise the quadratic.
Set each factor equal to zero and solve.
lessons.worked: x² + 5x + 6 = 0 becomes (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0. So x + 2 = 0 or x + 3 = 0. The solutions are x = −2 and x = −3.
worked_steps: The solutions are x = −2 and x = −3.
lessons.question: Solve x² − x − 12 = 0 by factorising.
scheme: Find factors with product −12 and sum −1: −4 and 3.
lessons.mistake: The zero-product rule only applies when the product equals zero.

cards.definition: An equation whose highest power of the unknown is two.
A value that makes the equation true.

quiz.why: Set each factor to zero: x − 2 = 0 or x + 5 = 0.

misconception.q: Solve (x − 2)(x + 5) = 0. Sam answers: “x = −2 or x = 5.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Set each factor to zero: x − 2 = 0 or x + 5 = 0.

lessons.title: Identities and three brackets
notes: An identity is true for every allowed value. An equation may be true only for particular values. Three brackets can be expanded two at a time.
Expand the first two brackets. Multiply every resulting term by every term in the third. Collect like terms and check by substituting a value.
note_points: An identity is true for every allowed value.
An equation may be true only for particular values.
Three brackets can be expanded two at a time.
Expand the first two brackets.
Multiply every resulting term by every term in the third.
Collect like terms and check by substituting a value.
lessons.worked: (x + 1)(x + 2) = x² + 3x + 2. Multiply by (x + 3) to get x³ + 6x² + 11x + 6. At x = 1, both forms give 24.
lessons.question: Expand (x + 1)(x + 1)(x + 2).
lessons.mistake: Checking one value can find an error, but does not prove an identity for every value.

cards.definition: A statement true for every allowed value of its variables.
An expression with highest power three.

quiz.q: Which statement is an identity?
quiz.why: Expanding shows the first statement is true for every x.

misconception.q: Which statement is an identity? Sam answers: “x + 3 = 5.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Expanding shows the first statement is true for every x.

lessons.title: Solving two-step equations
notes: Solving an equation means finding a value that makes it true. Keep both sides equal at every step. Write one step on each line.
Undo addition or subtraction first in a two-step expression. Then undo multiplication or division. Check your answer in the original equation.
note_points: Solving an equation means finding a value that makes it true.
Keep both sides equal at every step.
Write one step on each line.
Undo addition or subtraction first in a two-step expression.
Then undo multiplication or division.
Check your answer in the original equation.
lessons.worked: For 3x + 5 = 26, subtract 5 to get 3x = 21. Divide both sides by 3 to get x = 7. Check: 3 × 7 + 5 = 26.
worked_steps: Divide both sides by 3 to get x = 7.
lessons.question: Solve 4x − 7 = 29.
lessons.mistake: Use each operation on the whole of both sides.

cards.definition: Find the value or values that make a statement true.
Put the answer into the original equation to see whether both sides match.

quiz.q: What is x if 2x + 3 = 11?
quiz.why: Subtract 3 to get 2x = 8, then divide by 2.

misconception.q: What is x if 2x + 3 = 11? Sam answers: “7.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Subtract 3 to get 2x = 8, then divide by 2.

lessons.title: Equations with brackets and fractions
notes: An equation says two expressions have equal value. Brackets and fraction bars group terms. The same operation on both sides keeps the equality.
Clear a denominator by multiplying both sides. Expand brackets carefully. Undo the remaining operations and check the answer.
note_points: An equation says two expressions have equal value.
Brackets and fraction bars group terms.
The same operation on both sides keeps the equality.
Clear a denominator by multiplying both sides.
Expand brackets carefully.
Undo the remaining operations and check the answer.
lessons.worked: (x + 4)/3 = 5. Multiply both sides by 3: x + 4 = 15. Subtract 4: x = 11.
lessons.question: Solve (2x − 1)/3 = 7 and check your answer.
lessons.mistake: A fraction bar divides the whole expression above it.

cards.definition: A value that makes an equation true.
An operation that undoes another operation.

quiz.q: Solve (x + 2)/4 = 3.
quiz.why: Multiply by 4, then subtract 2: x = 12 − 2 = 10.

misconception.q: Solve (x + 2)/4 = 3. Sam answers: “x = 1.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Equations with letters on both sides
notes: Some equations have an unknown on both sides. Bring the letter terms together on one side. Bring the plain numbers together on the other side.
Expand brackets if needed. Subtract a letter term from both sides. Finish solving, then check the original equation.
note_points: Some equations have an unknown on both sides.
Bring the letter terms together on one side.
Bring the plain numbers together on the other side.
Expand brackets if needed.
Subtract a letter term from both sides.
Finish solving, then check the original equation.
lessons.worked: For 5x + 3 = 2x + 21, subtract 2x: 3x + 3 = 21. Subtract 3, then divide by 3: x = 6. Check: both original sides equal 33.
lessons.question: Solve 3(x + 2) = 2x + 17.
lessons.mistake: When a question describes a real length, check that your answer makes sense as a length.

cards.definition: A value you need to find, often shown by a letter.
Write two equal amounts using mathematical expressions and an equals sign.

quiz.q: What is x if 5x = 2x + 12?
quiz.why: Subtract 2x to get 3x = 12, then divide by 3.

misconception.q: What is x if 5x = 2x + 12? Sam answers: “12.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Subtract 2x to get 3x = 12, then divide by 3.

lessons.title: Putting numbers into expressions
notes: Substitution means replacing a letter with its value. Replace the letter every time it appears. Put negative values in brackets.
Write the expression with the numbers inserted. Work out brackets and powers first. Then multiply or divide before adding or subtracting.
note_points: Substitution means replacing a letter with its value.
Replace the letter every time it appears.
Put negative values in brackets.
Write the expression with the numbers inserted.
Work out brackets and powers first.
Then multiply or divide before adding or subtracting.
lessons.worked: For x = −3 and y = 2, x² − 4y becomes (−3)² − 4 × 2. This is 9 − 8. The answer is 1.
worked_steps: For x = −3 and y = 2, x² − 4y becomes (−3)² − 4 × 2.
lessons.question: Work out 3x² − 2y when x = −2 and y = 5.
lessons.mistake: (−3)² is 9, but −3² means −(3²), which is −9.

cards.definition: Replacing a letter with its value.
Work out the value of an expression.

quiz.q: For x = −4, what is x²?
quiz.why: Put the negative value in brackets: (−4) × (−4) = 16.

misconception.q: For x = −4, what is x²? Sam answers: “−16.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Put the negative value in brackets: (−4) × (−4) = 16.

lessons.title: Rearranging formulae
notes: The subject of a formula is the letter standing alone. Rearranging makes a different letter stand alone. Keep the formula true by doing the same thing to both sides.
Undo the steps around the letter you want. Keep brackets around a whole expression when dividing it. Never divide by zero.
note_points: The subject of a formula is the letter standing alone.
Rearranging makes a different letter stand alone.
Keep the formula true by doing the same thing to both sides.
Undo the steps around the letter you want.
Keep brackets around a whole expression when dividing it.
Never divide by zero.
lessons.worked: From v = u + at, subtract u: v − u = at. Divide both sides by a: t = (v − u) ÷ a. This needs a ≠ 0, meaning a cannot be zero.
worked_steps: From v = u + at, subtract u: v − u = at.
Divide both sides by a: t = (v − u) ÷ a.
This needs a ≠ 0, meaning a cannot be zero.
lessons.question: Make x stand alone in y = 3x + 7. Find x when y = 25.
lessons.mistake: A formula must work generally. Checking one example is not a proof for every value.

cards.definition: The letter standing alone on one side of the equals sign.
A statement true for every allowed value, such as 2(x + 1) = 2x + 2.

quiz.q: Which makes x stand alone in y = 2x + 6?
quiz.why: Subtract 6 from both sides before dividing the whole remaining expression by 2.

misconception.q: Which makes x stand alone in y = 2x + 6? Sam answers: “x = y ÷ 2 + 6.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Subtract 6 from both sides before dividing the whole remaining expression by 2.

lessons.title: Inequalities and number lines
