notes: An inequality describes a set of possible values. < means less than, and > means greater than. ≤ and ≥ also allow equality.
Solve in a similar way to an equation. Reverse the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number. An open circle excludes the boundary; a filled circle includes it.
note_points: An inequality describes a set of possible values.
< means less than, and > means greater than.
≤ and ≥ also allow equality.
Solve in a similar way to an equation.
Reverse the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
An open circle excludes the boundary; a filled circle includes it.
lessons.worked: For −2x < 6, divide both sides by −2. Reverse < to >. The solution is x > −3.
lessons.question: Solve −3x ≥ 12.
lessons.mistake: Do not forget to reverse the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.

cards.definition: A statement that one expression is larger or smaller than another, possibly including equality.
The value at the end of a solution interval.

quiz.q: Solve −2x < 8.
quiz.why: Divide by −2 and reverse the sign because you divided by a negative number.

misconception.q: Solve −2x < 8. Sam answers: “x < −4.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Divide by −2 and reverse the sign because you divided by a negative number.

review.q: List the whole numbers that satisfy 0 ≤ x < 3.

lessons.title: Inequalities and number lines
notes: An inequality describes a set of possible values. < means less than, and > means greater than. ≤ and ≥ also allow equality.
Solve in a similar way to an equation. Reverse the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number. An open circle excludes the boundary; a filled circle includes it.
note_points: An inequality describes a set of possible values.
< means less than, and > means greater than.
≤ and ≥ also allow equality.
Solve in a similar way to an equation.
Reverse the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.
An open circle excludes the boundary; a filled circle includes it.
lessons.worked: For −2x < 6, divide both sides by −2. Reverse < to >. The solution is x > −3.
lessons.question: Solve −3x ≥ 12.
lessons.mistake: Do not forget to reverse the sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number.

cards.definition: A statement that one expression is larger or smaller than another, possibly including equality.
The value at the end of a solution interval.

quiz.q: Solve −2x < 8.
quiz.why: Divide by −2 and reverse the sign because you divided by a negative number.

misconception.q: Solve −2x < 8. Sam answers: “x < −4.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Divide by −2 and reverse the sign because you divided by a negative number.

review.q: List the whole numbers that satisfy 0 ≤ x < 3.

lessons.title: A rule for any term
notes: An nth-term rule lets you find a term from its position. The letter n stands for the position. An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount each time.

Start with the difference multiplied by n. Compare this with the actual sequence and adjust by adding or subtracting. Check your rule for the first few positions. A term belongs to a sequence only if its position is a positive whole number.
note_points: An nth-term rule lets you find a term from its position.
The letter n stands for the position.
An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount each time.
Start with the difference multiplied by n.
Compare this with the actual sequence and adjust by adding or subtracting.
Check your rule for the first few positions.
A term belongs to a sequence only if its position is a positive whole number.
lessons.worked: For 7, 11, 15, 19, the difference is 4. 4n gives 4, 8, 12, 16, so add 3: the rule is 4n + 3. The twentieth term is 4 × 20 + 3 = 83.
worked_steps: 4n gives 4, 8, 12, 16, so add 3: the rule is 4n + 3.
lessons.question: Find the nth-term rule for 8, 13, 18, 23. Use it to find the tenth term.
lessons.mistake: “Add 5” finds the next term. “5n + 3” finds a term from its position.

cards.definition: A rule that finds a term from its position n.
Where a term appears in a sequence, starting at 1.

quiz.q: What is the fifth term of 3n + 2?
quiz.why: Put n = 5 into the rule: 3 × 5 + 2 = 17.

misconception.q: What is the fifth term of 3n + 2? Sam answers: “15.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Finding a quadratic sequence rule
notes: A quadratic rule includes n². Its second differences are equal and not zero. Second differences are the differences between the first row of differences.
Half the second difference gives the number multiplying n². Subtract that n² pattern from the sequence. Find the rule for what is left, then combine the two rules.
note_points: A quadratic rule includes n².
Its second differences are equal and not zero.
Second differences are the differences between the first row of differences.
Half the second difference gives the number multiplying n².
Subtract that n² pattern from the sequence.
Find the rule for what is left, then combine the two rules.
lessons.worked: For 3, 8, 15, 24, the second difference is 2, so start with n². Subtract 1, 4, 9, 16 to leave 2, 4, 6, 8, which is 2n. The rule is n² + 2n.
worked_steps: For 3, 8, 15, 24, the second difference is 2, so start with n².
lessons.question: Find the nth-term rule for 2, 6, 12, 20. Find its sixth term.
scheme: The second difference is 2, so start with n².
Subtract n² to leave 1, 2, 3, 4, which is n.
The rule is n² + n, giving 42 at n = 6.
lessons.mistake: Use the second differences for a quadratic rule, not just the first difference.

cards.definition: The difference between neighbouring first differences.
A sequence with an n² rule and a constant, non-zero second difference.

quiz.q: The second difference is 6. What number multiplies n² in a quadratic rule?
quiz.why: The second difference is twice the n² coefficient, so divide 6 by 2.

misconception.q: The second difference is 6. What number multiplies n² in a quadratic rule? Sam answers: “6.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The second difference is twice the n² coefficient, so divide 6 by 2.

lessons.title: Different types of sequence
notes: An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount each time. A geometric sequence multiplies by the same number each time. A quadratic sequence has changes that themselves change by a fixed amount.
Write the differences between neighbouring terms. If these are not equal, compare the next row of differences. Also check whether multiplying by the same number works.
note_points: An arithmetic sequence adds the same amount each time.
A geometric sequence multiplies by the same number each time.
A quadratic sequence has changes that themselves change by a fixed amount.
Write the differences between neighbouring terms.
If these are not equal, compare the next row of differences.
Also check whether multiplying by the same number works.
lessons.worked: For 1, 4, 9, 16, the differences are 3, 5, 7. These differences go up by 2, so this is a quadratic pattern. For 3, 6, 12, 24, multiply by 2 instead.
worked_steps: These differences go up by 2, so this is a quadratic pattern.
lessons.question: Continue 2, 6, 18, 54 by one term. Why is this not an arithmetic sequence?
scheme: The differences between terms are not equal.
lessons.mistake: A growing sequence does not always add the same amount each time.

cards.definition: A sequence that adds the same amount each time.
A sequence that multiplies by the same number each time.

quiz.q: Which sequence multiplies by the same number each time?
quiz.why: Each term in 2, 6, 18, 54 is three times the one before.

misconception.q: Which sequence multiplies by the same number each time? Sam answers: “2, 5, 8, 11.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Each term in 2, 6, 18, 54 is three times the one before.

lessons.title: Equivalent fractions and mixed numbers
notes: Equivalent fractions have the same value. Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same non-zero number. A mixed number has a whole-number part and a fraction part.
To change a mixed number, multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator. To simplify, divide top and bottom by a common factor. Use matching denominators to compare fractions.
note_points: Equivalent fractions have the same value.
Multiply or divide top and bottom by the same non-zero number.
A mixed number has a whole-number part and a fraction part.
To change a mixed number, multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator.
To simplify, divide top and bottom by a common factor.
Use matching denominators to compare fractions.
lessons.worked: 2⅓ = (2 × 3 + 1)/3 = 7/3. 3/4 = 6/8, so 3/4 is greater than 5/8. 18/24 simplifies to 3/4.
lessons.question: Write 3⅖ as an improper fraction. Simplify 21/28.
lessons.mistake: Do the same thing to the top and bottom when making an equivalent fraction.

cards.definition: Different-looking fractions with the same value.
A fraction whose numerator is at least as large as its denominator.

quiz.q: Which fraction equals 2/3?
quiz.why: Multiply the numerator and denominator by 4.

misconception.q: Which fraction equals 2/3? Sam answers: “2/6.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Multiply the numerator and denominator by 4.

lessons.title: Adding and subtracting fractions
notes: Fractions need matching denominators before you add or subtract them. This makes the parts the same size. Then combine the numerators.
Find a common denominator. Multiply top and bottom of each fraction to match it. Add or subtract the tops, then simplify.
note_points: Fractions need matching denominators before you add or subtract them.
This makes the parts the same size.
Then combine the numerators.
Find a common denominator.
Multiply top and bottom of each fraction to match it.
Add or subtract the tops, then simplify.
lessons.worked: For 2/3 + 3/4, use denominator 12. Write 8/12 + 9/12 = 17/12. As a mixed number, this is 1 5/12.
worked_steps: As a mixed number, this is 1 5/12.
lessons.question: Calculate 5/6 − 1/4. Give the simplest fraction.
lessons.mistake: Do not add or subtract the denominators.

cards.definition: A matching denominator used to combine or compare fractions.
A fraction whose numerator and denominator have no common factor above 1.

quiz.q: Calculate 1/2 + 1/3.
quiz.why: Use sixths: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.

misconception.q: Calculate 1/2 + 1/3. Sam answers: “2/5.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Multiplying and dividing fractions
notes: To multiply fractions, multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms. A reciprocal is a number turned upside down as a fraction. A number times its reciprocal is 1, except zero has no reciprocal.
Change mixed numbers to improper fractions first. To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal. Simplify by cancelling common factors before multiplying if helpful.
note_points: To multiply fractions, multiply the tops and multiply the bottoms.
A reciprocal is a number turned upside down as a fraction.
A number times its reciprocal is 1, except zero has no reciprocal.
Change mixed numbers to improper fractions first.
To divide by a fraction, multiply by its reciprocal.
Simplify by cancelling common factors before multiplying if helpful.
lessons.worked: 3/4 × 2/5 = 6/20 = 3/10. For 2/3 ÷ 4/5, turn over only the second fraction. 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12 = 5/6.
worked_steps: For 2/3 ÷ 4/5, turn over only the second fraction.
lessons.question: Calculate 3/5 ÷ 9/10.
lessons.mistake: For division, turn over the fraction you divide by, not both fractions.

cards.definition: A number that multiplies with the original number to make 1.
A fraction with numerator at least as large as its denominator.

quiz.q: What is the reciprocal of 3/7?
quiz.why: Turn the fraction over. 3/7 × 7/3 = 1.

misconception.q: What is the reciprocal of 3/7? Sam answers: “−3/7.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Fractions of an amount
notes: To find one equal part, divide by the denominator. Then multiply by the numerator to find the required parts. A bar model can show these equal parts.
If you know several parts, divide to find one part first. Multiply by all the parts to find the whole. Keep the units in your answer.
note_points: To find one equal part, divide by the denominator.
Then multiply by the numerator to find the required parts.
A bar model can show these equal parts.
If you know several parts, divide to find one part first.
Multiply by all the parts to find the whole.
Keep the units in your answer.
lessons.worked: 3/5 of 80 means split 80 into 5 equal parts. One part is 80 ÷ 5 = 16. Three parts are 16 × 3 = 48.
worked_steps: 3/5 of 80 means split 80 into 5 equal parts.
lessons.question: Three quarters of a length is 27 cm. Find the whole length.
scheme: There are four quarters in the whole.
lessons.mistake: Read whether you are finding part of an amount or working backwards to the whole.

cards.definition: A fraction with numerator 1, such as 1/5.
The complete amount that a fraction describes a part of.

quiz.q: What is 3/4 of 20?
quiz.why: One quarter is 20 ÷ 4 = 5. Three quarters are 5 × 3 = 15.

misconception.q: What is 3/4 of 20? Sam answers: “5.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: One quarter is 20 ÷ 4 = 5. Three quarters are 5 × 3 = 15.

lessons.title: Recurring decimals and fractions
notes: A terminating decimal ends. A recurring decimal repeats a digit or block forever. A fraction can be changed into a decimal by division.

For a repeating block of two digits, multiply by 100. Subtract the original to cancel the repeating tail. Solve the equation and simplify the fraction. A simplified fraction has a terminating decimal when its denominator has only prime factors 2 and 5. If other prime factors remain, its decimal repeats.
note_points: A terminating decimal ends.
A recurring decimal repeats a digit or block forever.
A fraction can be changed into a decimal by division.
For a repeating block of two digits, multiply by 100.
Subtract the original to cancel the repeating tail.
Solve the equation and simplify the fraction.
A simplified fraction has a terminating decimal when its denominator has only prime factors 2 and 5.
If other prime factors remain, its decimal repeats.
lessons.question: Write 0.363636… as a fraction in simplest form.
scheme: Let x be the decimal: 100x − x = 36.
lessons.mistake: Use enough places for the repeating blocks to line up before subtracting.

cards.definition: A decimal whose digit or block of digits repeats forever.
A decimal that ends after a finite number of digits.

quiz.q: Which is recurring?
quiz.why: A recurring decimal repeats without ending. The other two decimals finish.

misconception.q: Which is recurring? Sam answers: “0.25.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: A recurring decimal repeats without ending. The other two decimals finish.

lessons.title: Fractions, decimals and percentages
notes: Fractions, decimals and percentages can describe the same amount. A fraction also means division. Percent means out of 100.
Divide the top of a fraction by the bottom to get a decimal. Multiply the decimal by 100 to get a percentage. Divide a percentage by 100 to turn it back into a decimal.
note_points: Fractions, decimals and percentages can describe the same amount.
A fraction also means division.
Percent means out of 100.
Divide the top of a fraction by the bottom to get a decimal.
Multiply the decimal by 100 to get a percentage.
Divide a percentage by 100 to turn it back into a decimal.
worked_steps: Also 1.25 = 125%, which is more than one whole.
lessons.question: Convert 7/20 into a decimal and a percentage.
lessons.mistake: One half is 0.5, not 0.05.

cards.definition: The top number of a fraction, counting the parts taken.
The bottom number, showing how many equal parts make a whole.
An amount out of 100.

quiz.q: What percentage is 0.4?
quiz.why: Multiply the decimal by 100: 0.4 × 100 = 40.

misconception.q: What percentage is 0.4? Sam answers: “4%.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Percentage increases and decreases
notes: An increase adds a percentage of the original amount. A decrease takes a percentage away. Percentage change compares the change with the original amount.
For a 15% increase, multiply by 1.15. For a 15% decrease, multiply by 0.85. Percentage change = change ÷ original amount × 100%.
note_points: An increase adds a percentage of the original amount.
A decrease takes a percentage away.
Percentage change compares the change with the original amount.
For a 15% increase, multiply by 1.15.
For a 15% decrease, multiply by 0.85.
Percentage change = change ÷ original amount × 100%.
lessons.worked: A price rises from £50 to £65, so the change is £15. 15 ÷ 50 × 100 = 30%. A 20% rise followed by a 20% fall does not return to the start.
worked_steps: A price rises from £50 to £65, so the change is £15.
A 20% rise followed by a 20% fall does not return to the start.
lessons.question: A price rises from £80 to £92. Find the percentage increase.
lessons.mistake: Divide by the original amount when finding percentage change.

cards.definition: The change divided by the original amount, multiplied by 100%.
The amount before a change happened.

quiz.q: Which multiplier increases a price by 20%?
quiz.why: Keep the original 100% and add 20%, giving 120% = 1.2.

misconception.q: Which multiplier increases a price by 20%? Sam answers: “0.2.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Keep the original 100% and add 20%, giving 120% = 1.2.

lessons.title: Finding the original percentage amount
notes: After a percentage change, the new amount is a fraction of the original. A 20% reduction leaves 80% of the original. To find the original, divide by the multiplier.
Write new amount = original amount × multiplier. Repeated percentage changes use the new balance each time. Simple interest uses the original balance each time instead.
note_points: After a percentage change, the new amount is a fraction of the original.
A 20% reduction leaves 80% of the original.
To find the original, divide by the multiplier.
Write new amount = original amount × multiplier.
Repeated percentage changes use the new balance each time.
Simple interest uses the original balance each time instead.
lessons.worked: After a 20% reduction, a coat costs £64. 80% = 0.8, so original price = 64 ÷ 0.8. The original price was £80.
worked_steps: After a 20% reduction, a coat costs £64.
lessons.question: After a 25% increase, a value is 90. What was the original value?
lessons.mistake: Do not subtract 25% of the new value to undo a 25% increase.

cards.definition: Finding the original amount before a percentage change.
Repeated growth where each change uses the latest amount.

quiz.q: A price after a 10% reduction is £45. Which calculation finds the original price?
quiz.why: The new price is 90% of the original, so divide by 0.9.

misconception.q: A price after a 10% reduction is £45. Which calculation finds the original price? Sam answers: “45 × 0.9.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The new price is 90% of the original, so divide by 0.9.

lessons.title: Repeated percentage changes
notes: Each percentage change acts on the current amount. An increase of 5% uses multiplier 1.05. Repeating the change means multiplying again.
Write a multiplier for each step. Multiply the starting amount by every multiplier. Round money at the end unless told otherwise.
note_points: Each percentage change acts on the current amount.
An increase of 5% uses multiplier 1.05.
Repeating the change means multiplying again.
Write a multiplier for each step.
Multiply the starting amount by every multiplier.
Round money at the end unless told otherwise.
lessons.worked: £200 grows by 10%, then another 10%. £200 × 1.1 × 1.1 = £242. The total increase is 21%, because the second rise acts on £220.
worked_steps: The total increase is 21%, because the second rise acts on £220.
lessons.question: A £500 item loses 20% of its value each year for two years. Find its value.
lessons.mistake: Two 10% increases are not one 20% increase.

cards.definition: A number you multiply by to apply a scale or percentage change.
A fall in value over time.

quiz.q: What multiplier represents two successive 20% decreases?
quiz.why: Multiply 0.8 by 0.8 to get 0.64.

misconception.q: What multiplier represents two successive 20% decreases? Sam answers: “0.60.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Simple and compound interest
notes: Interest is an amount added to savings or charged on borrowing. Simple interest uses the starting amount every time. Compound interest uses the changing balance.
For simple interest, find one period’s interest and multiply by the number of periods. For compound interest, repeat the percentage multiplier. Use the fixed example rate stated in the question.
note_points: Interest is an amount added to savings or charged on borrowing.
Simple interest uses the starting amount every time.
Compound interest uses the changing balance.
For simple interest, find one period’s interest and multiply by the number of periods.
For compound interest, repeat the percentage multiplier.
Use the fixed example rate stated in the question.
lessons.worked: £300 earns 4% simple interest per year: £12 each year. After three years the balance is £336. With annual compounding it is £300 × 1.04³ = £337.46 to the nearest penny.
worked_steps: £300 earns 4% simple interest per year: £12 each year.
After three years the balance is £336.
With annual compounding it is £300 × 1.04³ = £337.46 to the nearest penny.
lessons.question: £400 earns 5% compound interest each year for two years. Find the final balance.
lessons.mistake: Compound interest can earn interest on earlier interest.

cards.definition: The starting amount saved or borrowed.
Interest calculated on the changing balance.

quiz.q: £100 earns 10% simple interest per year. What is the balance after 2 years?
quiz.why: Simple interest adds £10 each year: £100 + £20.

misconception.q: £100 earns 10% simple interest per year. What is the balance after 2 years? Sam answers: “£121.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Ratios and fractions of a total
notes: A ratio compares amounts in a stated order. Red:blue = 2:3 means 2 equal parts red for every 3 blue. There are 5 parts altogether.
Use matching units before simplifying a ratio. Divide all parts by the same common factor. For a fraction of the total, add all the ratio parts first.
note_points: A ratio compares amounts in a stated order.
Red:blue = 2:3 means 2 equal parts red for every 3 blue.
There are 5 parts altogether.
Use matching units before simplifying a ratio.
Divide all parts by the same common factor.
For a fraction of the total, add all the ratio parts first.
lessons.worked: Red:blue = 6:9 simplifies to 2:3. There are 2 + 3 = 5 equal parts. The red fraction of the total is 2/5.
worked_steps: The red fraction of the total is 2/5.
lessons.question: Simplify 18:30. What fraction of the total is the first part?
scheme: The first part is 3 out of 8, or 3/8.
lessons.mistake: In the ratio 2:3, the first part is 2/5 of the total, not 2/3.

cards.definition: A comparison of amounts in a stated order.
One equal part used to represent a share.

quiz.q: For red:blue = 2:3, what fraction of all counters are red?
quiz.why: There are 5 equal parts altogether and 2 are red.

misconception.q: For red:blue = 2:3, what fraction of all counters are red? Sam answers: “2/3.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: There are 5 equal parts altogether and 2 are red.

lessons.title: Sharing in a ratio
notes: Ratio parts are equal-sized units. The total, one share or the difference can tell you how much a unit is worth. Read carefully which amount you know.
Draw the ratio units. Divide the known amount by the number of units it represents. Multiply to find each share and check the total.
note_points: Ratio parts are equal-sized units.
The total, one share or the difference can tell you how much a unit is worth.
Read carefully which amount you know.
Draw the ratio units.
Divide the known amount by the number of units it represents.
Multiply to find each share and check the total.
lessons.worked: Share £84 in the ratio 3:4: there are 7 units. One unit is £84 ÷ 7 = £12. The shares are £36 and £48.
worked_steps: Share £84 in the ratio 3:4: there are 7 units.
lessons.question: Share 96 in the ratio 5:3.
lessons.mistake: If you are given a difference, divide by the difference in units, not the total units.

cards.definition: The part of a total given to one person or group.
One equal part in a ratio model.

quiz.q: Share 35 in the ratio 2:5. What is the smaller share?
quiz.why: There are 7 units, so each is worth 5. The smaller share is 2 × 5 = 10.

misconception.q: Share 35 in the ratio 2:5. What is the smaller share? Sam answers: “14.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: There are 7 units, so each is worth 5. The smaller share is 2 × 5 = 10.

lessons.title: Ratio problems with a part or difference
notes: A ratio compares equal-sized parts. Sometimes a single amount is known. Sometimes the difference between amounts is known.
Draw the parts as equal boxes. Match the known amount to the right number of boxes. Find one box, then find the amounts needed.
note_points: A ratio compares equal-sized parts.
Sometimes a single amount is known.
Sometimes the difference between amounts is known.
Draw the parts as equal boxes.
Match the known amount to the right number of boxes.
Find one box, then find the amounts needed.
lessons.worked: Red:blue = 2:5 and there are 18 more blue. The difference is 5 − 2 = 3 parts, so each part is 6. There are 12 red and 30 blue.
worked_steps: Red:blue = 2:5 and there are 18 more blue.
The difference is 5 − 2 = 3 parts, so each part is 6.
lessons.question: A:B = 3:7. B is 24 greater than A. Find A and B.
scheme: The difference is 4 parts, so one part is 24 ÷ 4 = 6.
lessons.mistake: When given the difference, use the difference in parts, not the total parts.

cards.definition: Finding one part or one item first.
One of the equal-sized shares represented by the ratio numbers.

quiz.q: A:B = 2:5 and A = 14. What is B?
quiz.why: Two parts are 14, so one part is 7 and five parts are 35.

misconception.q: A:B = 2:5 and A = 14. What is B? Sam answers: “21.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Two parts are 14, so one part is 7 and five parts are 35.

lessons.title: Direct proportion
notes: In direct proportion, both quantities scale by the same multiplier. Doubling one doubles the other. The graph is a straight line through the origin.
Use a ratio table or double number line. Find the amount for one item first if useful. A fixed starting charge means the total cost is not directly proportional.
note_points: In direct proportion, both quantities scale by the same multiplier.
Doubling one doubles the other.
The graph is a straight line through the origin.
Use a ratio table or double number line.
Find the amount for one item first if useful.
A fixed starting charge means the total cost is not directly proportional.
lessons.worked: Three identical pens cost £4.50. One pen costs £1.50. Eight pens cost £12, assuming the same price for every pen.
worked_steps: Eight pens cost £12, assuming the same price for every pen.
lessons.question: Five identical books cost £12.50. Find the cost of eight books. State the assumption.
scheme: The price per book stays the same, with no extra fee.
lessons.mistake: A straight line that misses the origin does not show direct proportion.

cards.definition: A relationship in which quantities have a constant ratio.
The point (0, 0) where the axes cross.

quiz.q: Which rule shows direct proportion?
quiz.why: For y = 4x, the ratio y/x stays 4 and the graph passes through the origin.

misconception.q: Which rule shows direct proportion? Sam answers: “y = x + 4.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: For y = 4x, the ratio y/x stays 4 and the graph passes through the origin.

lessons.title: Conversion graphs and currencies
notes: A conversion graph links two units or currencies. Use the axis labels to choose a direction. A stated constant rate gives a straight line through zero.
Use a known pair to find the multiplier. Multiply in one direction and divide in the other. Use only the rate stated in the question.
note_points: A conversion graph links two units or currencies.
Use the axis labels to choose a direction.
A stated constant rate gives a straight line through zero.
Use a known pair to find the multiplier.
Multiply in one direction and divide in the other.
Use only the rate stated in the question.
lessons.worked: At a stated rate of £1 = €1.25, £20 = €25. To change €45 to pounds, divide by 1.25. €45 = £36 at this example rate.
worked_steps: To change €45 to pounds, divide by 1.25.
lessons.question: At a stated rate of £1 = €1.20, change €54 into pounds. Ignore fees.
lessons.mistake: Do not multiply in both directions.

cards.definition: A graph linking values measured in two different units.
A stated relationship between two currencies.

quiz.q: At £1 = €1.50, how many euros equal £8?
quiz.why: Multiply 8 by 1.50 to get 12.

misconception.q: At £1 = €1.50, how many euros equal £8? Sam answers: “€5.33.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Direct and inverse proportion
notes: Direct proportion means both amounts change by the same multiplier. For example, twice as many identical items cost twice as much. Inverse proportion means one doubles when the other halves for a fixed total job.

For direct proportion, find the amount for one first. Then multiply for the amount you need. Check whether a fixed fee or other condition changes the rule. Direct proportion can be written y = kx, where k is a fixed number. Its graph is a straight line through (0, 0). For inverse proportion, x × y stays fixed and y = k/x.
note_points: Direct proportion means both amounts change by the same multiplier.
For example, twice as many identical items cost twice as much.
Inverse proportion means one doubles when the other halves for a fixed total job.
For direct proportion, find the amount for one first.
Then multiply for the amount you need.
Check whether a fixed fee or other condition changes the rule.
Direct proportion can be written y = kx, where k is a fixed number.
Its graph is a straight line through (0, 0).
For inverse proportion, x × y stays fixed and y = k/x.
lessons.worked: Four notebooks cost £6, so one costs £6 ÷ 4 = £1.50. Ten notebooks cost 10 × £1.50 = £15. This assumes every notebook has the same price.
worked_steps: Four notebooks cost £6, so one costs £6 ÷ 4 = £1.50.
This assumes every notebook has the same price.
lessons.question: Five identical items cost £12.50. How much do eight cost at the same price per item?
lessons.mistake: A fixed starting charge means the total cost is not directly proportional to the number of items.

cards.definition: Two quantities changing by the same multiplier, with a fixed ratio.
Two quantities with a fixed product, so multiplying one divides the other by the same factor.

quiz.q: Three identical pens cost £4.50. How much do six cost?
quiz.why: Twice as many pens cost twice as much when the price per pen stays the same.

misconception.q: Three identical pens cost £4.50. How much do six cost? Sam answers: “£7.50.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Twice as many pens cost twice as much when the price per pen stays the same.

lessons.title: Scale drawings and matching shapes
notes: A scale links a drawing length to a real length. Use the same units before comparing them. Similar shapes have matching angles and the same multiplier for matching lengths.
Multiply a drawing length by the scale factor to get the real length. Recipes and exchange rates can also use the same scaling idea. If lengths scale by k, areas scale by k².
note_points: A scale links a drawing length to a real length.
Use the same units before comparing them.
Similar shapes have matching angles and the same multiplier for matching lengths.
Multiply a drawing length by the scale factor to get the real length.
Recipes and exchange rates can also use the same scaling idea.
If lengths scale by k, areas scale by k².
lessons.worked: At scale 1:200, a 3 cm drawing length represents 3 × 200 = 600 cm. 600 cm = 6 m. At a stated rate of £1 = €1.20, £35 becomes 35 × 1.20 = €42.
worked_steps: At scale 1:200, a 3 cm drawing length represents 3 × 200 = 600 cm.
At a stated rate of £1 = €1.20, £35 becomes 35 × 1.20 = €42.
lessons.question: A map scale is 1:50,000. What real distance does 6 cm represent, in kilometres?
lessons.mistake: A scale ratio compares matching length units. Convert before comparing.

cards.definition: The multiplier linking matching lengths.
Shapes with equal matching angles and one shared scale factor for matching lengths.

quiz.q: At scale 1:100, what does 4 cm on a plan represent?
quiz.why: 4 × 100 = 400 cm, which is 4 m.

misconception.q: At scale 1:100, what does 4 cm on a plan represent? Sam answers: “400 m.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Angle facts
notes: Angles on a straight line add to 180°. Angles around a point add to 360°. Angles inside a triangle add to 180°.
Vertically opposite angles are equal. Angles inside a quadrilateral add to 360°. Write the angle rule as well as your calculation.
note_points: Angles on a straight line add to 180°.
Angles around a point add to 360°.
Angles inside a triangle add to 180°.
Vertically opposite angles are equal.
Angles inside a quadrilateral add to 360°.
Write the angle rule as well as your calculation.
lessons.worked: An isosceles triangle has a top angle of 38°. Its two equal base angles add to 180 − 38 = 142°. Each base angle is 142 ÷ 2 = 71°.
worked_steps: An isosceles triangle has a top angle of 38°.
Its two equal base angles add to 180 − 38 = 142°.
lessons.question: A triangle has angles 48° and 67°. Find the third angle.
lessons.mistake: Use angle facts rather than guessing from how a drawing looks.

cards.definition: An angle of 90°.
A triangle with two equal sides and two equal base angles.

quiz.q: Two angles in a triangle are 50° and 60°. What is the third?
quiz.why: Triangle angles add to 180°: 180 − 50 − 60 = 70°.

misconception.q: Two angles in a triangle are 50° and 60°. What is the third? Sam answers: “110°.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Parallel-line angles and polygons
notes: Parallel lines never meet. A line crossing them makes equal corresponding and alternate angles. Co-interior angles, on the same inside side, add to 180°.
A polygon is a closed shape with straight sides. An n-sided polygon has angle total (n − 2) × 180°. A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles.
note_points: Parallel lines never meet.
A line crossing them makes equal corresponding and alternate angles.
Co-interior angles, on the same inside side, add to 180°.
A polygon is a closed shape with straight sides.
An n-sided polygon has angle total (n − 2) × 180°.
A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles.
lessons.worked: A regular hexagon has 6 equal exterior angles. Each exterior angle is 360 ÷ 6 = 60°. Each interior angle is 180 − 60 = 120°.
worked_steps: A regular hexagon has 6 equal exterior angles.
lessons.question: Find each interior angle of a regular octagon, which has 8 sides.
scheme: An interior and its exterior angle add to 180°.
lessons.mistake: Use parallel-line markings before applying a parallel-line angle rule.

cards.definition: A closed straight-sided shape with equal sides and equal angles.
The angle between a side and the extension of a neighbouring side.

quiz.q: What is each exterior angle of a regular pentagon?
quiz.why: A full set of exterior angles adds to 360°: 360 ÷ 5 = 72°.

misconception.q: What is each exterior angle of a regular pentagon? Sam answers: “108°.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: A full set of exterior angles adds to 360°: 360 ÷ 5 = 72°.

lessons.title: Pythagoras and right-angled triangles
notes: Pythagoras links the side lengths of a right-angled triangle. The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle. If it is labelled c, then a² + b² = c².

To find the hypotenuse, add the squares of the shorter sides. Then take the square root. To find a shorter side, subtract squares instead. For a cuboid diagonal, use a right-angled triangle on a face, then use Pythagoras again in space.
note_points: Pythagoras links the side lengths of a right-angled triangle.
The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle.
If it is labelled c, then a² + b² = c².
To find the hypotenuse, add the squares of the shorter sides.
Then take the square root.
To find a shorter side, subtract squares instead.
For a cuboid diagonal, use a right-angled triangle on a face, then use Pythagoras again in space.
lessons.worked: For shorter sides 6 cm and 8 cm, c² = 6² + 8². c² = 36 + 64 = 100. c = √100 = 10 cm.
worked_steps: For shorter sides 6 cm and 8 cm, c² = 6² + 8².
lessons.question: A right-angled triangle has shorter sides 9 cm and 12 cm. Find the hypotenuse.
lessons.mistake: Use Pythagoras only in a right-angled triangle.

cards.definition: The longest side of a right-angled triangle, opposite the right angle.
For a right-angled triangle, a² + b² = c² where c is the hypotenuse.

quiz.q: The shorter sides of a right triangle are 3 and 4. What is the hypotenuse?
quiz.why: 3² + 4² = 25, so take the square root: 5.

misconception.q: The shorter sides of a right triangle are 3 and 4. What is the hypotenuse? Sam answers: “7.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Checking right angles and coordinate distances
notes: The longest side is opposite the largest angle. If its square equals the sum of the other two squares, the triangle is right-angled. Coordinate gaps can make the two shorter sides.
Identify the longest side before checking. For a coordinate distance, find the horizontal and vertical gaps. Use Pythagoras on that right-angled triangle.
note_points: The longest side is opposite the largest angle.
If its square equals the sum of the other two squares, the triangle is right-angled.
Coordinate gaps can make the two shorter sides.
Identify the longest side before checking.
For a coordinate distance, find the horizontal and vertical gaps.
Use Pythagoras on that right-angled triangle.
lessons.worked: Sides 5, 12, 13 give 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13². So the triangle is right-angled. The distance from (1,2) to (6,14) is also 13 units.
worked_steps: The distance from (1,2) to (6,14) is also 13 units.
lessons.question: Find the distance from (−1,2) to (5,10).
scheme: The horizontal gap is 6 and vertical gap is 8.
lessons.mistake: The longest side must be the one squared on its own.

cards.definition: The side opposite the right angle in a right-angled triangle.
A statement that reverses the direction of an implication.

quiz.q: Are lengths 6, 8 and 11 a right-angled triangle?
quiz.why: 6² + 8² = 100, but 11² = 121, so the right-angle test fails.

misconception.q: Are lengths 6, 8 and 11 a right-angled triangle? Sam answers: “Yes, because 6 + 8 > 11.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: 6² + 8² = 100, but 11² = 121, so the right-angle test fails.

lessons.title: Sine, cosine and tangent
notes: Trigonometry links sides and angles in right-angled triangles. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. Opposite and adjacent are named from the angle you choose.
Sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse. Cosine = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, and tangent = opposite ÷ adjacent. Choose the ratio using the two sides you know or need, and use degree mode.
note_points: Trigonometry links sides and angles in right-angled triangles.
The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle.
Opposite and adjacent are named from the angle you choose.
Sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse.
Cosine = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, and tangent = opposite ÷ adjacent.
Choose the ratio using the two sides you know or need, and use degree mode.
lessons.worked: For a 30° angle with hypotenuse 10 cm, sin 30° = opposite ÷ 10. Multiply by 10: opposite = 10 × sin 30°. The opposite side is 5 cm.
worked_steps: For a 30° angle with hypotenuse 10 cm, sin 30° = opposite ÷ 10.
lessons.question: A right-angled triangle has a 30° angle and hypotenuse 14 cm. Find the opposite side.
lessons.mistake: Opposite and adjacent swap when you choose the other acute angle.

cards.definition: The side across from your chosen angle in a triangle.
The side next to your chosen angle, excluding the hypotenuse.

quiz.q: Which ratio is sine in a right triangle?
quiz.why: SOH reminds you: sine equals opposite over hypotenuse.

misconception.q: Which ratio is sine in a right triangle? Sam answers: “Adjacent ÷ hypotenuse.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: SOH reminds you: sine equals opposite over hypotenuse.

lessons.title: Exact trig values and looking up or down
notes: An angle of elevation is measured upwards from a horizontal line. An angle of depression is measured downwards from a horizontal line. Some special angles have exact trig values.
sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = √2/2 and sin 60° = √3/2. Cosine gives these in reverse order for 30°, 45° and 60°. tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 45° = 1 and tan 60° = √3.
note_points: An angle of elevation is measured upwards from a horizontal line.
An angle of depression is measured downwards from a horizontal line.
Some special angles have exact trig values.
Cosine gives these in reverse order for 30°, 45° and 60°.
lessons.worked: A tower is 20 m horizontally away and its top is at 45° above eye level. Height above eye level = 20 × tan 45°. Since tan 45° = 1, the height above eye level is 20 m.
worked_steps: A tower is 20 m horizontally away and its top is at 45° above eye level.
Since tan 45° = 1, the height above eye level is 20 m.
lessons.question: Find the exact value of sin 60° × cos 30°.
lessons.mistake: Keep exact roots and fractions until the end if an exact answer is requested.

cards.definition: An angle measured upwards from a horizontal line.
An angle measured downwards from a horizontal line.

quiz.q: What is the exact value of sin 30°?
quiz.why: A 30°–60°–90° triangle gives sin 30° = 1/2.

misconception.q: What is the exact value of sin 30°? Sam answers: “√3/2.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Mean, median, mode and range
notes: Mean = total of the values ÷ number of values. The median is the middle value after ordering the list. The mode is the most common value.
The range is largest minus smallest. For an even-sized list, average the two middle values to find the median. An extreme value can pull the mean away from most of the data.
note_points: Mean = total of the values ÷ number of values.
The median is the middle value after ordering the list.
The mode is the most common value.
The range is largest minus smallest.
For an even-sized list, average the two middle values to find the median.
An extreme value can pull the mean away from most of the data.
lessons.worked: For 2, 3, 3, 8, the total is 16 and the mean is 16 ÷ 4 = 4. The median and mode are both 3. The range is 8 − 2 = 6.
worked_steps: For 2, 3, 3, 8, the total is 16 and the mean is 16 ÷ 4 = 4.
The median and mode are both 3.
lessons.question: Find the mean and range of 4, 6, 6, 12.
scheme: The total is 28, so the mean is 28 ÷ 4 = 7.
The largest value is 12 and the smallest is 4.
lessons.mistake: Order the list before finding the median. Keep repeated values in the list.

cards.definition: The total of the values divided by how many values there are.
The middle value in an ordered list, or the mean of the two middle values.
The largest value minus the smallest.

quiz.q: Find the median of 7, 2, 9.
quiz.why: Put the list in order: 2, 7, 9. The middle value is 7.

misconception.q: Find the median of 7, 2, 9. Sam answers: “2.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Put the list in order: 2, 7, 9. The middle value is 7.

lessons.title: Averages from frequency tables
notes: Frequency means how often a value occurs. A frequency table saves writing a value out many times. The total frequency is the number of values altogether.
Multiply each value by its frequency. Add these products, then divide by total frequency. For grouped data, use class midpoints and call the mean an estimate.
note_points: Frequency means how often a value occurs.
A frequency table saves writing a value out many times.
The total frequency is the number of values altogether.
Multiply each value by its frequency.
Add these products, then divide by total frequency.
For grouped data, use class midpoints and call the mean an estimate.
lessons.worked: Values 1, 2, 3 have frequencies 2, 5, 3. The total is 1 × 2 + 2 × 5 + 3 × 3 = 21. There are 10 values, so the mean is 21 ÷ 10 = 2.1.
worked_steps: There are 10 values, so the mean is 21 ÷ 10 = 2.1.
lessons.question: Values 2, 4, 6 have frequencies 3, 2, 5. Find the mean.
scheme: The total is 44 and total frequency is 10.
lessons.mistake: Divide by total frequency, not by the number of rows.

cards.definition: How often a value or category occurs.
The value halfway between the two ends of a grouped-data interval.

quiz.q: A value 4 has frequency 3. How much does it contribute to the total?
quiz.why: The value appears three times: 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.

misconception.q: A value 4 has frequency 3. How much does it contribute to the total? Sam answers: “7.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Stem-and-leaf diagrams
notes: A stem-and-leaf diagram keeps each original value. The key tells you what each stem and leaf mean. Put leaves in order and keep repeats.
Count values to find the median. Use the highest and lowest values to find the range. When comparing groups, discuss a typical value and the spread.
note_points: A stem-and-leaf diagram keeps each original value.
The key tells you what each stem and leaf mean.
Put leaves in order and keep repeats.
Count values to find the median.
Use the highest and lowest values to find the range.
When comparing groups, discuss a typical value and the spread.
lessons.worked: With key 2 ¦ 4 = 24, stem 2 with leaves 1, 4, 4, 8 means 21, 24, 24, 28. The middle two values are both 24, so the median is 24. The range is 28 − 21 = 7.
worked_steps: With key 2 ¦ 4 = 24, stem 2 with leaves 1, 4, 4, 8 means 21, 24, 24, 28.
The middle two values are both 24, so the median is 24.
lessons.question: A stem 3 has leaves 1, 2, 6, 9. With key 3 ¦ 1 = 31, find the median.
scheme: Their mean is 34, so the median is 34.
lessons.mistake: A key is essential. The same digits can stand for different place values.

cards.definition: A display separating each value into a stem and leaf while keeping individual data.
The explanation of how to read the place values in a diagram.

quiz.q: With key 2 ¦ 4 = 24, what does 3 ¦ 7 mean?
quiz.why: The stem is tens and the leaf is units, so the value is 37.

misconception.q: With key 2 ¦ 4 = 24, what does 3 ¦ 7 mean? Sam answers: “3.7.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The stem is tens and the leaf is units, so the value is 37.

lessons.title: Reading and drawing charts
notes: A bar chart compares categories. A pictogram uses symbols and a key. A line graph can show change over time.
Label axes and give units where needed. Use evenly spaced numbers on a scale. Check whether an axis starts above zero and exaggerates a difference.
note_points: A bar chart compares categories.
A pictogram uses symbols and a key.
A line graph can show change over time.
Label axes and give units where needed.
Use evenly spaced numbers on a scale.
Check whether an axis starts above zero and exaggerates a difference.
lessons.worked: A pictogram key says one symbol means 4 pupils. Two full symbols mean 8 pupils, and half a symbol means 2. So 2½ symbols mean 10 pupils.
worked_steps: A pictogram key says one symbol means 4 pupils.
Two full symbols mean 8 pupils, and half a symbol means 2.
lessons.question: A pictogram uses one symbol for 8 books. How many books do 3½ symbols show?
lessons.mistake: Always read the key before counting pictogram symbols.

cards.definition: A chart using symbols to show amounts.
The explanation of what a symbol or label stands for.

quiz.q: One symbol represents 6 items. What do 2½ symbols represent?
quiz.why: Two symbols represent 12 and half a symbol represents 3, giving 15.

misconception.q: One symbol represents 6 items. What do 2½ symbols represent? Sam answers: “12.5.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Two symbols represent 12 and half a symbol represents 3, giving 15.

lessons.title: Pie charts
notes: A full pie chart is a 360° turn. Each sector shows a fraction of the total. A larger frequency gives a larger sector angle.
Sector angle = frequency ÷ total × 360°. Check all angles add to 360°. Equal-sized sectors in different surveys may stand for different numbers of people.
note_points: A full pie chart is a 360° turn.
Each sector shows a fraction of the total.
A larger frequency gives a larger sector angle.
Sector angle = frequency ÷ total × 360°.
Check all angles add to 360°.
Equal-sized sectors in different surveys may stand for different numbers of people.
lessons.worked: 15 of 60 pupils walk to school. The fraction is 15/60 = 1/4. The sector angle is 1/4 × 360 = 90°.
lessons.question: A category contains 18 of 72 results. Find its pie-chart angle.
lessons.mistake: A sector is a share of that chart's total, not a fixed number of people.

cards.definition: A slice of a circle between two radii and an arc.
How often an outcome or category occurs.

quiz.q: What angle represents one quarter of a pie chart?
quiz.why: A full circle is 360°, so a quarter is 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.

misconception.q: What angle represents one quarter of a pie chart? Sam answers: “25°.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: A full circle is 360°, so a quarter is 360 ÷ 4 = 90°.

lessons.title: Grouped data and histograms
notes: A histogram shows grouped data using bars. The bar area represents frequency. The bar height is frequency density, not always frequency.
Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width. Frequency = density × class width. A frequency polygon joins points plotted at class midpoints.
note_points: A histogram shows grouped data using bars.
The bar area represents frequency.
The bar height is frequency density, not always frequency.
Frequency density = frequency ÷ class width.
Frequency = density × class width.
A frequency polygon joins points plotted at class midpoints.
lessons.worked: The class 10 ≤ x < 30 has width 20 and frequency 12. Its frequency density is 12 ÷ 20 = 0.6. A narrower class can have a taller bar but still contain fewer values.
worked_steps: The class 10 ≤ x < 30 has width 20 and frequency 12.
A narrower class can have a taller bar but still contain fewer values.
lessons.question: A histogram class has width 8 and frequency density 2.5. Find its frequency.
lessons.mistake: For unequal class widths, compare bar areas rather than just bar heights.

cards.definition: Frequency divided by class width, used for histogram bar height.
The difference between the upper and lower class boundaries.

quiz.q: A histogram class has frequency 18 and width 6. What is its density?
quiz.why: Density = 18 ÷ 6 = 3.

misconception.q: A histogram class has frequency 18 and width 6. What is its density? Sam answers: “108.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Scatter graphs and patterns
notes: A scatter graph shows two measurements for each item. Positive correlation means both tend to increase together. Negative correlation means one tends to fall as the other rises.

A line of best fit follows the main pattern. Do not join every dot in order. Predictions far outside the measured range are less reliable. Interpolation predicts inside the measured range; extrapolation predicts outside it. An outlier is a point far from the main pattern. Check it rather than removing it without a reason.
note_points: A scatter graph shows two measurements for each item.
Positive correlation means both tend to increase together.
Negative correlation means one tends to fall as the other rises.
A line of best fit follows the main pattern.
Do not join every dot in order.
Predictions far outside the measured range are less reliable.
Interpolation predicts inside the measured range; extrapolation predicts outside it.
An outlier is a point far from the main pattern. Check it rather than removing it without a reason.
lessons.worked: Ice-cream sales and sunburn can both rise in hot weather. This does not show that eating ice cream causes sunburn. Another factor, sunny weather, affects both.
worked_steps: Ice-cream sales and sunburn can both rise in hot weather.
This does not show that eating ice cream causes sunburn.
Another factor, sunny weather, affects both.
lessons.question: What is positive correlation? Why might a prediction far outside the measured range be unreliable?
scheme: Both measurements tend to increase together.
The pattern may change outside the measured range.
There is less evidence for a prediction beyond that range.
lessons.mistake: Correlation does not by itself prove that one thing causes the other.

cards.definition: A pattern showing how two measurements change together.
A line following the main pattern of points on a scatter graph.

quiz.q: What does negative correlation mean?
opts: One measurement tends to fall as the other rises.
There is no pattern at all.
quiz.why: Negative describes the downward pattern, not whether the plotted numbers are below zero.

misconception.q: What does negative correlation mean? Sam answers: “Both measurements must be negative.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: One measurement tends to fall as the other rises.
Negative describes the downward pattern, not whether the plotted numbers are below zero.

review.q: Is predicting inside the measured data range called interpolation or extrapolation?

lessons.title: Coordinates and midpoints
notes: Coordinates are written (x, y). Read the horizontal x value first, then the vertical y value. Negative values let us use all four parts of the grid.
To find a midpoint, average the two x values. Then average the two y values. Use a table of values to plot points from a rule. For y = 2x − 1, an input x = −2 gives y = −5.
note_points: Coordinates are written (x, y).
Read the horizontal x value first, then the vertical y value.
Negative values let us use all four parts of the grid.
To find a midpoint, average the two x values.
Then average the two y values.
Use a table of values to plot points from a rule.
For y = 2x − 1, an input x = −2 gives y = −5.
lessons.worked: The midpoint of (−2, 3) and (6, 7) has x = (−2 + 6) ÷ 2 = 2. Its y value is (3 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5. So the midpoint is (2, 5).
worked_steps: The midpoint of (−2, 3) and (6, 7) has x = (−2 + 6) ÷ 2 = 2.
lessons.question: Find the midpoint of (−4, 2) and (8, 10).
lessons.mistake: Go along the grid first and up or down second.

cards.definition: Two numbers (x, y) that locate a point on a grid.
The point halfway along a line segment.

quiz.q: Which coordinate is read first in (x, y)?
quiz.why: Go along first, then up or down.

misconception.q: Which coordinate is read first in (x, y)? Sam answers: “The vertical y value.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Go along first, then up or down.

lessons.title: Speed, distance and time
notes: Average speed tells you distance travelled per unit of time. Speed = distance ÷ time. Use matching units, such as metres and seconds for m/s.
Distance = speed × time. Time = distance ÷ speed. Convert minutes to hours before finding km/h.
note_points: Average speed tells you distance travelled per unit of time.
Speed = distance ÷ time.
Use matching units, such as metres and seconds for m/s.
Distance = speed × time.
Time = distance ÷ speed.
Convert minutes to hours before finding km/h.
lessons.worked: A runner travels 150 m in 30 seconds. Speed = 150 ÷ 30. The average speed is 5 m/s.
worked_steps: A runner travels 150 m in 30 seconds.
lessons.question: A runner travels 240 m in 40 seconds. Find the average speed.
lessons.mistake: Use the total distance and total time for an average speed.

cards.definition: Total distance divided by total time.
How much one quantity changes for each unit of another.

quiz.q: A cyclist travels 100 m in 20 seconds. What is the average speed?
quiz.why: Divide distance by time: 100 ÷ 20 = 5 m/s.

misconception.q: A cyclist travels 100 m in 20 seconds. What is the average speed? Sam answers: “2000 m/s.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Distance–time graphs
notes: A distance–time graph shows distance travelled as time passes. A horizontal line means no movement. A steeper line means a greater speed.
Find the change in distance between two points. Divide by the change in time. This steepness is called the gradient.
note_points: A distance–time graph shows distance travelled as time passes.
A horizontal line means no movement.
A steeper line means a greater speed.
Find the change in distance between two points.
Divide by the change in time.
This steepness is called the gradient.
lessons.worked: From (2 s, 5 m) to (6 s, 25 m), distance changes by 20 m. Time changes by 4 seconds. Speed = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 m/s.
worked_steps: From (2 s, 5 m) to (6 s, 25 m), distance changes by 20 m.
lessons.question: A straight graph section runs from (5 s, 10 m) to (20 s, 70 m). Find the speed.
lessons.mistake: Use changes between the points, not one point's coordinates unless the line starts at zero.

cards.definition: The steepness of a line, found by dividing vertical change by horizontal change.
Not moving.

quiz.q: What does a horizontal line on a distance–time graph show?
quiz.why: Time passes but the distance does not change.

misconception.q: What does a horizontal line on a distance–time graph show? Sam answers: “The object is moving uphill.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Time passes but the distance does not change.

lessons.title: Flow rates and filling graphs
notes: A flow rate describes how much liquid moves in a unit of time. For a constant rate, volume = rate × time. A volume–time graph can show filling or draining.
Check the time and volume units. The graph’s gradient gives net flow rate. If water enters and leaves, subtract the outflow from the inflow.
note_points: A flow rate describes how much liquid moves in a unit of time.
For a constant rate, volume = rate × time.
A volume–time graph can show filling or draining.
Check the time and volume units.
The graph’s gradient gives net flow rate.
If water enters and leaves, subtract the outflow from the inflow.
lessons.worked: Water enters at 8 litres per minute and leaves at 3 litres per minute. Net filling rate is 5 litres per minute. After 6 minutes, the volume has increased by 30 litres.
worked_steps: Water enters at 8 litres per minute and leaves at 3 litres per minute.
Net filling rate is 5 litres per minute.
After 6 minutes, the volume has increased by 30 litres.
lessons.question: A tank starts with 12 litres. Water flows in at 7 litres/min and out at 2 litres/min. How much is in the tank after 4 minutes?
lessons.mistake: A starting volume changes the intercept, not the constant filling gradient.

cards.definition: The volume moving per unit time.
The overall rate after combining increases and decreases.

quiz.q: A tank gains 24 litres in 6 minutes at a constant rate. What is the rate?
quiz.why: Divide the volume change by the time: 24 ÷ 6 = 4.

misconception.q: A tank gains 24 litres in 6 minutes at a constant rate. What is the rate? Sam answers: “144 litres/min.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Divide the volume change by the time: 24 ÷ 6 = 4.

lessons.title: Converting compound units
notes: Compound units combine two kinds of measurement. Speed might be in metres per second or kilometres per hour. Convert both parts carefully.
Write the distance and time conversions. Apply them one at a time. For speed, 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h.
note_points: Compound units combine two kinds of measurement.
Speed might be in metres per second or kilometres per hour.
Convert both parts carefully.
Write the distance and time conversions.
Apply them one at a time.
For speed, 1 m/s = 3.6 km/h.
lessons.worked: 10 m/s is 10 × 3600 = 36 000 metres per hour. 36 000 m = 36 km. So 10 m/s = 36 km/h.
lessons.question: Convert 72 km/h into metres per second.
lessons.mistake: Changing kilometres to metres alone is not enough.

cards.definition: A unit combining different measurements, such as m/s.
The change in one quantity per unit change in another.

quiz.q: Convert 5 m/s into km/h.
quiz.why: Multiply by 3.6: 5 × 3.6 = 18.

misconception.q: Convert 5 m/s into km/h. Sam answers: “1.39 km/h.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Velocity–time graphs
notes: Velocity tells you speed in a stated direction. The gradient of a velocity–time graph is acceleration: change in velocity per second. The area between the line and the time axis gives displacement.
Split areas into rectangles or triangles. For motion in one direction, the area also gives distance. For total distance with reversals, add the sizes of areas without cancelling them.
note_points: Velocity tells you speed in a stated direction.
The gradient of a velocity–time graph is acceleration: change in velocity per second.
The area between the line and the time axis gives displacement.
Split areas into rectangles or triangles.
For motion in one direction, the area also gives distance.
For total distance with reversals, add the sizes of areas without cancelling them.
lessons.worked: Velocity rises from 0 to 12 m/s in 6 seconds. Acceleration = 12 ÷ 6 = 2 m/s². The triangular area is ½ × 6 × 12 = 36 m.
worked_steps: Velocity rises from 0 to 12 m/s in 6 seconds.
The triangular area is ½ × 6 × 12 = 36 m.
lessons.question: Velocity rises steadily from 0 to 8 m/s over 5 seconds. Find the distance travelled.
scheme: The graph area is a triangle.
lessons.mistake: A horizontal velocity–time line can show steady movement, not a stationary object.

cards.definition: The change in velocity each second.
Change in position, including direction, from start to finish.

quiz.q: What does the gradient of a velocity–time graph give?
quiz.why: Gradient is change in velocity divided by change in time.

misconception.q: What does the gradient of a velocity–time graph give? Sam answers: “Distance.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Gradient is change in velocity divided by change in time.

lessons.title: Straight-line graphs
notes: In y = mx + c, m is the gradient: the steepness. c is the y-intercept: where the line crosses the y-axis. Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x.

Find the gradient using two points. Put one point's x and y values into y = mx + c. Solve for c, then write the equation. Horizontal lines have gradient zero. Vertical lines have equations such as x = 3 and no defined gradient.
note_points: In y = mx + c, m is the gradient: the steepness.
c is the y-intercept: where the line crosses the y-axis.
Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x.
Find the gradient using two points.
Put one point's x and y values into y = mx + c.
Solve for c, then write the equation.
Horizontal lines have gradient zero.
Vertical lines have equations such as x = 3 and no defined gradient.
lessons.worked: Through (1, 5) and (3, 9), gradient = (9 − 5) ÷ (3 − 1) = 2. Use (1, 5): 5 = 2 × 1 + c, so c = 3. The equation is y = 2x + 3.
lessons.question: Find the equation of a line with gradient 3 passing through (2, 7).
lessons.mistake: The y-intercept is where x is zero, not where y is zero.

cards.definition: How steep a line is: change in y divided by change in x.
Where a graph crosses the y-axis, at x = 0.

quiz.q: What is the gradient of y = 4x − 2?
quiz.why: In y = mx + c, the coefficient of x is the gradient m.

misconception.q: What is the gradient of y = 4x − 2? Sam answers: “−2.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: In y = mx + c, the coefficient of x is the gradient m.

lessons.title: Finding a straight-line equation
notes: A straight line can be written y = mx + c unless it is vertical. m is the gradient. c is the y-intercept.
Read two clear points from the graph. Calculate rise divided by horizontal run. Use the intercept, or substitute a point, to find c.
note_points: A straight line can be written y = mx + c unless it is vertical.
m is the gradient.
c is the y-intercept.
Read two clear points from the graph.
Calculate rise divided by horizontal run.
Use the intercept, or substitute a point, to find c.
lessons.worked: A line passes through (0, −2) and (3, 4). Its gradient is (4 − (−2))/(3 − 0) = 2. Its equation is y = 2x − 2.
lessons.question: A line passes through (0,3) and (4,11). Find its equation.
lessons.mistake: The y-intercept is where x is zero, not where y is zero.

cards.definition: The change in y divided by the change in x.
Where a graph crosses the y-axis.

quiz.q: What is the y-intercept of y = −3x + 5?
quiz.why: Set x = 0, giving y = 5.

misconception.q: What is the y-intercept of y = −3x + 5? Sam answers: “−3.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Parallel and perpendicular graph lines
notes: Parallel lines never meet. Parallel non-vertical lines have the same gradient. Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle.
For non-vertical perpendicular lines, the gradients multiply to −1. To find the other gradient, turn the fraction over and change its sign. A horizontal and vertical line are also perpendicular.
note_points: Parallel lines never meet.
Parallel non-vertical lines have the same gradient.
Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle.
For non-vertical perpendicular lines, the gradients multiply to −1.
To find the other gradient, turn the fraction over and change its sign.
A horizontal and vertical line are also perpendicular.
lessons.worked: A line has gradient 2. A perpendicular line has gradient −1/2. Check: 2 × (−1/2) = −1.
lessons.question: Find the gradient of a line perpendicular to y = −4x + 2.
scheme: Turn it over and change the sign: 1/4.
lessons.mistake: Different y-intercepts do not stop two lines being parallel.

cards.definition: Lines in a plane that stay the same distance apart and never meet.
Lines that meet at a right angle.

quiz.q: A line has gradient 3. What is a perpendicular line gradient?
quiz.why: Perpendicular non-vertical gradients multiply to −1: 3 × (−1/3) = −1.

misconception.q: A line has gradient 3. What is a perpendicular line gradient? Sam answers: “3.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Shading a linear inequality
notes: A graph inequality describes a region of points. Its boundary is the matching equation. A solid boundary includes equality; a dashed boundary excludes it.
Draw the boundary first. Test a point away from the boundary. Shade the side whose points satisfy the inequality.
note_points: A graph inequality describes a region of points.
Its boundary is the matching equation.
A solid boundary includes equality; a dashed boundary excludes it.
Draw the boundary first.
Test a point away from the boundary.
Shade the side whose points satisfy the inequality.
lessons.worked: For y > x + 1, draw y = x + 1 dashed. (0,0) gives 0 > 1, which is false. Shade above the line, away from (0,0).
worked_steps: For y > x + 1, draw y = x + 1 dashed.
Shade above the line, away from (0,0).
lessons.question: Describe how to draw the region y ≤ 2x + 3. Is (0,0) included?
scheme: Draw y = 2x + 3 with a solid line.
Shade below the line, including the boundary.
lessons.mistake: A dashed boundary excludes every point on that line.

cards.definition: The line separating the two sides of a linear inequality.
A set of points satisfying a condition.

quiz.q: Does the boundary of y < x use a solid or dashed line?
quiz.why: The strict inequality excludes equality, so the boundary is dashed.

misconception.q: Does the boundary of y < x use a solid or dashed line? Sam answers: “Solid.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The strict inequality excludes equality, so the boundary is dashed.

lessons.title: Curved graphs
notes: A quadratic graph such as y = x² is a curve called a parabola. Cubic graphs include an x³ term. For y = 1/x, x cannot be zero.

Use a table with negative and positive x values where allowed. Join plotted points with a smooth curve. The x-intercepts are where y is zero. The curve y = 1/x gets closer to the axes without meeting them. A circle centred at (0, 0) has equation x² + y² = r².
note_points: A quadratic graph such as y = x² is a curve called a parabola.
Cubic graphs include an x³ term.
For y = 1/x, x cannot be zero.
Use a table with negative and positive x values where allowed.
Join plotted points with a smooth curve.
The x-intercepts are where y is zero.
The curve y = 1/x gets closer to the axes without meeting them.
A circle centred at (0, 0) has equation x² + y² = r².
lessons.worked: For y = x² − 4, set y to zero: x² = 4. Both x = −2 and x = 2 work. At x = 0, y = −4, which is the y-intercept.
worked_steps: For y = x² − 4, set y to zero: x² = 4.
At x = 0, y = −4, which is the y-intercept.
lessons.question: Find both x-intercepts of y = x² − 9.
scheme: The two x-intercepts have x values −3 and 3.
lessons.mistake: Do not forget the negative solution when solving x² = a positive number.

cards.definition: The curved shape of a quadratic graph.
A point where a graph crosses or touches the x-axis, so y = 0.

quiz.q: Where are the x-intercepts of y = x² − 16?
quiz.why: Set y to zero: x² = 16. Both −4 and 4 square to 16.

misconception.q: Where are the x-intercepts of y = x² − 16? Sam answers: “Only x = 4.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Set y to zero: x² = 16. Both −4 and 4 square to 16.

review.q: For y = x² − 4, find y when x = 0.

lessons.title: Reciprocal, exponential and cubic graphs
notes: A reciprocal graph such as y = 1/x has two separate branches. An exponential graph such as y = 2ˣ multiplies by the same factor for each unit rise in x. A cubic graph such as y = x³ has a different shape from a quadratic.
Build a table with suitable negative, zero and positive inputs. For 1/x, skip x = 0 and keep the branches separate. Use the graph plotter to compare the families.
note_points: A reciprocal graph such as y = 1/x has two separate branches.
An exponential graph such as y = 2ˣ multiplies by the same factor for each unit rise in x.
A cubic graph such as y = x³ has a different shape from a quadratic.
Build a table with suitable negative, zero and positive inputs.
For 1/x, skip x = 0 and keep the branches separate.
Use the graph plotter to compare the families.
lessons.question: Give the y-intercept of y = 2ˣ. Explain why y = 1/x has no y-intercept.
scheme: At x = 0, 2⁰ = 1, so the intercept is (0,1).
For 1/x, x = 0 would divide by zero.
So it has no point on the y-axis.
lessons.mistake: Do not join the two reciprocal branches across x = 0.

cards.definition: Growth by a constant multiplier over equal input steps.
A line a curve gets closer to; for 1/x these are the axes.

quiz.q: What is 2⁻¹?
quiz.why: A negative power means a reciprocal: 2⁻¹ = 1/2.

misconception.q: What is 2⁻¹? Sam answers: “−2.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: A negative power means a reciprocal: 2⁻¹ = 1/2.

lessons.title: Nets and surface area
notes: A net unfolds a solid’s outside into flat faces. Surface area is the total area of these faces. Volume measures the space inside instead.
Sketch or list every face. Find each face’s area. Add them, counting equal faces the correct number of times.
note_points: A net unfolds a solid’s outside into flat faces.
Surface area is the total area of these faces.
Volume measures the space inside instead.
Sketch or list every face.
Find each face’s area.
Add them, counting equal faces the correct number of times.
lessons.worked: A cuboid is 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. Its three face pairs have areas 12, 8 and 6 cm². Surface area = 2(12 + 8 + 6) = 52 cm².
worked_steps: A cuboid is 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm.
Its three face pairs have areas 12, 8 and 6 cm².
lessons.question: A closed cuboid is 5 cm by 4 cm by 3 cm. Find its surface area.
scheme: The face areas are 20, 15 and 12 cm².
lessons.mistake: Use square units for surface area, not cubic units.

cards.definition: A flat arrangement of faces that folds to make a solid.
The total area of a solid’s outside faces.

quiz.q: A cube has edge 3 cm. What is its surface area?
quiz.why: There are six faces, each of area 3 × 3 = 9 cm².

misconception.q: A cube has edge 3 cm. What is its surface area? Sam answers: “27 cm².” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: There are six faces, each of area 3 × 3 = 9 cm².

lessons.title: Finding areas
notes: Area measures how much surface a shape covers. A rectangle's area is base × height. A triangle's area is half base × perpendicular height.

Perpendicular means at right angles to the base. A parallelogram uses base × perpendicular height. For a trapezium, average the parallel sides and multiply by the height. Split a compound shape into simpler shapes, or subtract a cut-out. 1 m² = 10,000 cm² because a square metre has 100 rows of 100 square centimetres.
note_points: Area measures how much surface a shape covers.
A rectangle's area is base × height.
A triangle's area is half base × perpendicular height.
Perpendicular means at right angles to the base.
A parallelogram uses base × perpendicular height.
For a trapezium, average the parallel sides and multiply by the height.
Split a compound shape into simpler shapes, or subtract a cut-out.
1 m² = 10,000 cm² because a square metre has 100 rows of 100 square centimetres.
lessons.worked: A trapezium has parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm, with height 4 cm. Area = (6 + 10) ÷ 2 × 4. The answer is 32 cm².
worked_steps: A trapezium has parallel sides 6 cm and 10 cm, with height 4 cm.
lessons.question: A triangle has base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm. Find its area.
lessons.mistake: The sloping side of a triangle is not always its perpendicular height.

worked_rows.work: Parallel sides: 6 cm, 10 cm; height: 4 cm

cards.definition: The amount of surface a shape covers, measured in square units.
The height measured at right angles to the base.

quiz.q: A triangle has base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. What is its area?
quiz.why: A triangle is half a matching rectangle: ½ × 8 × 5 = 20 cm².

misconception.q: A triangle has base 8 cm and perpendicular height 5 cm. What is its area? Sam answers: “40 cm².” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: A triangle is half a matching rectangle: ½ × 8 × 5 = 20 cm².

lessons.title: Parts and measures of a circle
notes: A radius goes from the centre to the edge. A diameter crosses the circle through its centre and is twice the radius. The circumference is the distance around the circle.

Circumference = 2πr, or πd. Area = πr². Keep π in an exact answer instead of rounding it. For a sector, use the angle as a fraction of 360° to find its share of area or circumference. The perimeter of a semicircle includes the straight diameter as well as the curved edge.
note_points: A radius goes from the centre to the edge.
A diameter crosses the circle through its centre and is twice the radius.
The circumference is the distance around the circle.
Circumference = 2πr, or πd.
Area = πr².
Keep π in an exact answer instead of rounding it.
For a sector, use the angle as a fraction of 360° to find its share of area or circumference.
The perimeter of a semicircle includes the straight diameter as well as the curved edge.
lessons.worked: A circle has radius 3 cm. Circumference = 2 × π × 3 = 6π cm. Area = π × 3² = 9π cm².
lessons.question: Find the exact area of a circle with diameter 10 cm. Leave π in your answer.
lessons.mistake: Halve the diameter before using it as a radius.

cards.definition: The distance from the centre of a circle to its edge.
A straight line across a circle through the centre, equal to two radii.
The distance around a circle.

quiz.q: A circle has diameter 12 cm. What is its radius?
quiz.why: The radius is half the diameter: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.

misconception.q: A circle has diameter 12 cm. What is its radius? Sam answers: “24 cm.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The radius is half the diameter: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 cm.

lessons.title: Volume, capacity and prisms
notes: Volume measures the space inside a solid. A cuboid's volume is length × width × height. A prism has the same cross-section all the way along.
Find the cross-section area, then multiply by the prism's length. Use cubic units for volume. 1 cm³ = 1 ml, and 1000 cm³ = 1 litre. 1000 litres = 1 m³.
note_points: Volume measures the space inside a solid.
A cuboid's volume is length × width × height.
A prism has the same cross-section all the way along.
Find the cross-section area, then multiply by the prism's length.
Use cubic units for volume.
1 cm³ = 1 ml, and 1000 cm³ = 1 litre.
1000 litres = 1 m³.
lessons.worked: A triangular prism has cross-section area ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 cm². Its length is 10 cm. Volume = 12 × 10 = 120 cm³.
worked_steps: A triangular prism has cross-section area ½ × 6 × 4 = 12 cm².
lessons.question: A cuboid measures 8 cm by 5 cm by 3 cm. Find its volume.
lessons.mistake: Surface area uses square units. Volume uses cubic units.

cards.definition: The space a three-dimensional shape occupies, measured in cubic units.
A solid with the same cross-section all the way along.

quiz.q: What is the volume of a 2 cm by 3 cm by 4 cm cuboid?
quiz.why: Multiply all three lengths: 2 × 3 × 4 = 24 cm³.

misconception.q: What is the volume of a 2 cm by 3 cm by 4 cm cuboid? Sam answers: “9 cm³.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Cylinders and cones
notes: A cylinder has a circular cross-section. Its volume is circle area × height. A cone with the same base and height has one third of that volume.
Cylinder volume = πr²h. Cone volume = πr²h ÷ 3. Use the perpendicular height, not the sloping side.
note_points: A cylinder has a circular cross-section.
Its volume is circle area × height.
A cone with the same base and height has one third of that volume.
Cylinder volume = πr²h.
