misconception.q: Red occurs 12 times in 40 trials. What is its relative frequency? Sam answers: “0.12.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Expected outcomes
notes: An expected frequency is a prediction over many trials. Expected frequency = probability × number of trials. Actual results can differ because outcomes are random.
Use a probability supported by the question or experiment. Multiply by the planned number of trials. Describe the result as an expectation, not a guarantee.
note_points: An expected frequency is a prediction over many trials.
Expected frequency = probability × number of trials.
Actual results can differ because outcomes are random.
Use a probability supported by the question or experiment.
Multiply by the planned number of trials.
Describe the result as an expectation, not a guarantee.
lessons.worked: A fair die has probability 1/6 of showing 4. In 180 rolls, the expected number of 4s is 180 × 1/6 = 30. The actual number need not be exactly 30.
worked_steps: A fair die has probability 1/6 of showing 4.
In 180 rolls, the expected number of 4s is 180 × 1/6 = 30.
The actual number need not be exactly 30.
lessons.question: A spinner has probability 0.35 of red. Find the expected number of reds in 200 spins.
scheme: This is an expected count, not a promised result.
lessons.mistake: A long-term probability does not force an exact count in one experiment.

cards.definition: Probability multiplied by the number of trials.
Differences in results caused by chance.

quiz.q: A coin is fair. How many heads are expected in 80 tosses?
quiz.why: The expected count is 80 × 1/2 = 40, but the actual count can vary.

misconception.q: A coin is fair. How many heads are expected in 80 tosses? Sam answers: “80.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The expected count is 80 × 1/2 = 40, but the actual count can vary.

lessons.title: Independent and mutually exclusive events
notes: Independent events do not affect each other’s probability. Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together. These are different ideas.
For independent events, multiply probabilities to find both happening. For mutually exclusive alternatives, add probabilities to find either. Check the situation before choosing a rule.
note_points: Independent events do not affect each other’s probability.
Mutually exclusive events cannot happen together.
These are different ideas.
For independent events, multiply probabilities to find both happening.
For mutually exclusive alternatives, add probabilities to find either.
Check the situation before choosing a rule.
lessons.worked: Two fair coin tosses are independent. P(head then head) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. On one die roll, 1 and 6 are mutually exclusive, so P(1 or 6) = 2/6.
worked_steps: Two fair coin tosses are independent.
On one die roll, 1 and 6 are mutually exclusive, so P(1 or 6) = 2/6.
lessons.question: A fair coin is tossed and a fair die rolled independently. Find P(head and a 6).
lessons.mistake: Drawing without replacement can change the next probability.

worked_rows.work: P(H then H) = ½ × ½ = ¼

worked_rows.note: One die roll: cannot get both

cards.definition: Events for which one happening does not change the other’s probability.
Events that cannot happen together.

quiz.q: On a single die roll, are “a 2” and “a 5” mutually exclusive?
quiz.why: One roll cannot show both 2 and 5.

misconception.q: On a single die roll, are “a 2” and “a 5” mutually exclusive? Sam answers: “No, they are independent.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: One roll cannot show both 2 and 5.

lessons.title: Enlargement from a centre
notes: An enlargement changes distances from a chosen centre by a scale factor. Matching angles stay equal. A fractional positive factor between 0 and 1 makes the image smaller.
Draw a ray from the centre through each vertex. Multiply every centre-to-vertex distance by the factor. A negative factor puts the image on the opposite side of the centre.
note_points: An enlargement changes distances from a chosen centre by a scale factor.
Matching angles stay equal.
A fractional positive factor between 0 and 1 makes the image smaller.
Draw a ray from the centre through each vertex.
Multiply every centre-to-vertex distance by the factor.
A negative factor puts the image on the opposite side of the centre.
lessons.worked: Enlarge (2,1) from (0,0) with factor 3. Multiply both coordinates by 3. The image is (6,3).
lessons.question: Enlarge (4,6) from (0,0) by scale factor 1/2. Then describe the effect of factor −1.
scheme: Factor −1 puts each point the same distance on the opposite side of the centre.
It gives (−4,−6) for the original point.
lessons.mistake: A full description needs both centre and scale factor.

cards.definition: The fixed point from which distances are scaled.
A transformation scaling every distance from a centre by one factor.

quiz.q: Enlarge (3,2) from the origin by factor 2.
quiz.why: Both centre-to-point coordinate distances double.

misconception.q: Enlarge (3,2) from the origin by factor 2. Sam answers: “(5,4).” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Rotating about a point
notes: A rotation turns a shape around a centre. It preserves size and shape. Its description needs a centre, angle and direction.
Mark the centre and use tracing paper if useful. Turn every vertex through the same angle. Measure from the centre, not from a shape’s corner unless that is the centre.
note_points: A rotation turns a shape around a centre.
It preserves size and shape.
Its description needs a centre, angle and direction.
Mark the centre and use tracing paper if useful.
Turn every vertex through the same angle.
Measure from the centre, not from a shape’s corner unless that is the centre.
lessons.worked: (3,1) rotated 90° anticlockwise about (0,0) becomes (−1,3). The point stays the same distance from the origin. For a 180° turn, (x,y) becomes (−x,−y).
worked_steps: The point stays the same distance from the origin.
lessons.question: Rotate (2,5) 90° clockwise about the origin. Give the image and a full description.
lessons.mistake: Clockwise and anticlockwise give different images for a 90° turn.

cards.definition: A turn around a fixed centre.
The direction opposite to clock hands.

quiz.q: Rotate (4,−1) 180° about (0,0).
quiz.why: A half-turn reverses both coordinate signs.

misconception.q: Rotate (4,−1) 180° about (0,0). Sam answers: “(1,4).” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: A half-turn reverses both coordinate signs.

lessons.title: Translations and column vectors
notes: A translation slides every point by the same amount. It changes position but keeps size and orientation. A column vector records horizontal movement above vertical movement.
Use positive x for right and negative x for left. Use positive y for up and negative y for down. Add the same vector to each vertex.
note_points: A translation slides every point by the same amount.
It changes position but keeps size and orientation.
A column vector records horizontal movement above vertical movement.
Use positive x for right and negative x for left.
Use positive y for up and negative y for down.
Add the same vector to each vertex.
lessons.worked: The vector (3, −2) means 3 right and 2 down. It takes (−1,4) to (2,2). Every vertex moves in the same way.
worked_steps: The vector (3, −2) means 3 right and 2 down.
Every vertex moves in the same way.
lessons.question: Translate (−3,5) by the vector (4,−7). Find its image and describe the movement.
scheme: The image is (1,−2), moving 4 right and 7 down.
lessons.mistake: In a column vector, the horizontal movement is the top number.

cards.definition: A transformation moving every point by the same vector.
A quantity describing a directed movement.

quiz.q: Which movement is represented by (−2,3)?
quiz.why: The first component changes x and the second changes y.

misconception.q: Which movement is represented by (−2,3)? Sam answers: “2 up and 3 left.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The first component changes x and the second changes y.

lessons.title: Reflecting a whole shape
notes: Reflection flips a shape across a mirror line. Each point and its image are equally far from the line. The joining segment meets the mirror line at a right angle.
Reflect each vertex separately. Count perpendicular distances to the mirror line. Join the image vertices in the same order.
note_points: Reflection flips a shape across a mirror line.
Each point and its image are equally far from the line.
The joining segment meets the mirror line at a right angle.
Reflect each vertex separately.
Count perpendicular distances to the mirror line.
Join the image vertices in the same order.
lessons.worked: Reflect (2, 1) in the vertical line x = 4. The point is two units left of the line, so its image is two units right. The image is (6, 1).
worked_steps: Reflect (2, 1) in the vertical line x = 4.
The point is two units left of the line, so its image is two units right.
lessons.question: Reflect the triangle (1,1), (3,1), (1,2) in the y-axis. Give all three image vertices.
scheme: Keep y and reverse the sign of x.
lessons.mistake: Reflecting in y = x swaps coordinates; it does not just change a sign.

cards.definition: The line across which a shape is reflected.
The result of transforming a shape.

quiz.q: Reflect (2,5) in y = x. What is its image?
quiz.why: Reflection in y = x swaps x and y.

misconception.q: Reflect (2,5) in y = x. What is its image? Sam answers: “(−2,5).” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Reflection in y = x swaps x and y.

lessons.title: Combining transformations
notes: Several transformations can be applied in order. The second transformation acts on the first image. Reversing the order can change the final result.
Write the coordinates after each step. Use the stated centre or mirror line every time. Check the final image rather than assuming the operations can be swapped.
note_points: Several transformations can be applied in order.
The second transformation acts on the first image.
Reversing the order can change the final result.
Write the coordinates after each step.
Use the stated centre or mirror line every time.
Check the final image rather than assuming the operations can be swapped.
lessons.worked: Start at (1,2), translate 3 right to (4,2), then reflect in the y-axis to (−4,2). Reverse the order: reflect to (−1,2), then translate to (2,2). The final points differ.
worked_steps: Start at (1,2), translate 3 right to (4,2), then reflect in the y-axis to (−4,2).
Reverse the order: reflect to (−1,2), then translate to (2,2).
lessons.question: Start at (2,1). Translate 2 up, then rotate 180° about (0,0). Find the final point.
lessons.mistake: Apply transformations in the order given.

cards.definition: A sequence of transformations applied one after another.
A feature or point unchanged by a transformation.

quiz.q: Do a translation and a reflection always give the same result if their order is reversed?
quiz.why: The second step acts on a different intermediate image when the order changes.

misconception.q: Do a translation and a reflection always give the same result if their order is reversed? Sam answers: “Yes.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: The second step acts on a different intermediate image when the order changes.

lessons.title: Two equations at once
notes: A simultaneous solution makes two equations true at the same time. On a graph, it is a common intersection. Elimination removes one unknown by adding or subtracting equations.
Line up the matching terms. Add or subtract to remove one unknown. Find the other unknown, then substitute back.
note_points: A simultaneous solution makes two equations true at the same time.
On a graph, it is a common intersection.
Elimination removes one unknown by adding or subtracting equations.
Line up the matching terms.
Add or subtract to remove one unknown.
Find the other unknown, then substitute back.
lessons.worked: x + y = 9 and x − y = 3. Add the equations: 2x = 12, so x = 6. Then y = 9 − 6 = 3.
lessons.question: Solve x + y = 11 and x − y = 5. Check both equations.
lessons.mistake: A solution must satisfy both equations.

cards.definition: Equations solved using the same values of their unknowns.
Combining equations to remove one unknown.

quiz.q: Does (x,y) = (4,2) solve x + y = 6 and x − y = 2?
opts: No, only the first is true.
No, x and y must be equal.

misconception.q: Does (x,y) = (4,2) solve x + y = 6 and x − y = 2? Sam answers: “No, only the first is true.” Explain why this is wrong.

lessons.title: Adjusting equations before elimination
notes: Equivalent equations have the same solutions. Multiplying every term by a non-zero number keeps an equation equivalent. This can make coefficients match before elimination.
Choose the unknown to remove. Multiply a whole equation, including the constant. Add or subtract, then substitute back and check.
note_points: Equivalent equations have the same solutions.
Multiplying every term by a non-zero number keeps an equation equivalent.
This can make coefficients match before elimination.
Choose the unknown to remove.
Multiply a whole equation, including the constant.
Add or subtract, then substitute back and check.
lessons.worked: 2x + y = 11 and 3x + 2y = 19. Double the first: 4x + 2y = 22. Subtract the second: x = 3. Then y = 5, which works in both equations.
worked_steps: Double the first: 4x + 2y = 22. Subtract the second: x = 3.
Then y = 5, which works in both equations.
lessons.question: Solve 2x + y = 13 and 3x + 2y = 23.
scheme: Subtract the second to get x = 3.
Substitute into 2x + y = 13 to get y = 7.
lessons.mistake: Multiply every term on both sides of an equation.

cards.definition: Equations with the same solution set.
Replacing one unknown using an equivalent expression from another equation.

quiz.q: Double x + 3y = 8. What is the equivalent equation?
quiz.why: Every term on both sides is multiplied by 2.

misconception.q: Double x + 3y = 8. What is the equivalent equation? Sam answers: “2x + 3y = 8.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Every term on both sides is multiplied by 2.

lessons.title: Sine, cosine and tangent
notes: Trigonometry links sides and angles in right-angled triangles. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle. Opposite and adjacent are named from the angle you choose.
Sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse. Cosine = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, and tangent = opposite ÷ adjacent. Choose the ratio using the two sides you know or need, and use degree mode.
note_points: Trigonometry links sides and angles in right-angled triangles.
The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle.
Opposite and adjacent are named from the angle you choose.
Sine = opposite ÷ hypotenuse.
Cosine = adjacent ÷ hypotenuse, and tangent = opposite ÷ adjacent.
Choose the ratio using the two sides you know or need, and use degree mode.
lessons.worked: For a 30° angle with hypotenuse 10 cm, sin 30° = opposite ÷ 10. Multiply by 10: opposite = 10 × sin 30°. The opposite side is 5 cm.
worked_steps: For a 30° angle with hypotenuse 10 cm, sin 30° = opposite ÷ 10.
lessons.question: A right-angled triangle has a 30° angle and hypotenuse 14 cm. Find the opposite side.
lessons.mistake: Opposite and adjacent swap when you choose the other acute angle.

cards.definition: The side across from your chosen angle in a triangle.
The side next to your chosen angle, excluding the hypotenuse.

quiz.q: Which ratio is sine in a right triangle?
quiz.why: SOH reminds you: sine equals opposite over hypotenuse.

misconception.q: Which ratio is sine in a right triangle? Sam answers: “Adjacent ÷ hypotenuse.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: SOH reminds you: sine equals opposite over hypotenuse.

lessons.title: Finding angles with trigonometry
notes: Sine, cosine and tangent link sides and angles in right-angled triangles. An inverse trig function finds an angle from a ratio. Use degree mode for angles measured in degrees.
Label opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse from the chosen angle. Choose the ratio using the two known sides. Use sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹, then round as requested.
note_points: Sine, cosine and tangent link sides and angles in right-angled triangles.
An inverse trig function finds an angle from a ratio.
Use degree mode for angles measured in degrees.
Label opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse from the chosen angle.
Choose the ratio using the two known sides.
Use sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹ or tan⁻¹, then round as requested.
lessons.worked: Opposite = 3 cm and adjacent = 4 cm. tan θ = 3/4, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.75). θ is about 36.9°.
lessons.question: A right-angled triangle has opposite side 5 cm and hypotenuse 10 cm. Find the chosen acute angle.
lessons.mistake: sin⁻¹ is inverse sine here; it is not 1/sin.

cards.definition: The function used to find an angle from its sine ratio.
An angle greater than 0° and less than 90°.

quiz.q: cos θ = 0.5 for an acute angle. What is θ?
quiz.why: Use inverse cosine in degree mode: cos⁻¹(0.5) = 60°.

misconception.q: cos θ = 0.5 for an acute angle. What is θ? Sam answers: “30°.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Use inverse cosine in degree mode: cos⁻¹(0.5) = 60°.

lessons.title: Choosing Pythagoras or trigonometry
notes: Pythagoras links three sides of a right-angled triangle. Trigonometry links an angle with a side ratio. Choose from the information given.
Two known sides and one missing side: use Pythagoras. A known acute angle and one side: choose sine, cosine or tangent. For a 3-D problem, identify the right-angled triangle in a plane first.
note_points: Pythagoras links three sides of a right-angled triangle.
Trigonometry links an angle with a side ratio.
Choose from the information given.
Two known sides and one missing side: use Pythagoras.
A known acute angle and one side: choose sine, cosine or tangent.
For a 3-D problem, identify the right-angled triangle in a plane first.
lessons.worked: To find the hypotenuse from sides 5 and 12, use √(5² + 12²) = 13. With hypotenuse 10 and an angle of 30°, the opposite side is 10 sin 30° = 5. The methods answer different kinds of question.
worked_steps: To find the hypotenuse from sides 5 and 12, use √(5² + 12²) = 13.
With hypotenuse 10 and an angle of 30°, the opposite side is 10 sin 30° = 5.
The methods answer different kinds of question.
lessons.question: A ladder is 10 m long and makes a 60° angle with horizontal ground. Find its vertical height. Give a value to 2 decimal places.
scheme: The ladder is the hypotenuse and height is opposite.
lessons.mistake: The longest labelled side in a perspective sketch is not always the hypotenuse; locate the right angle.

cards.definition: A ratio of two sides of a right-angled triangle relative to a chosen angle.
A flat two-dimensional surface.

quiz.q: You know two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle and need its hypotenuse. Which method fits?
opts: Sine needs to be used first.
The angles must be measured first.
quiz.why: Pythagoras uses the two known sides directly.

misconception.q: You know two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle and need its hypotenuse. Which method fits? Sam answers: “Sine needs to be used first.” Explain why this is wrong.
ms: Pythagoras uses the two known sides directly.

lessons.title: Exact trig values and looking up or down
notes: An angle of elevation is measured upwards from a horizontal line. An angle of depression is measured downwards from a horizontal line. Some special angles have exact trig values.
sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = √2/2 and sin 60° = √3/2. Cosine gives these in reverse order for 30°, 45° and 60°. tan 30° = 1/√3, tan 45° = 1 and tan 60° = √3.
note_points: An angle of elevation is measured upwards from a horizontal line.
An angle of depression is measured downwards from a horizontal line.
Some special angles have exact trig values.
Cosine gives these in reverse order for 30°, 45° and 60°.
lessons.worked: A tower is 20 m horizontally away and its top is at 45° above eye level. Height above eye level = 20 × tan 45°. Since tan 45° = 1, the height above eye level is 20 m.
worked_steps: A tower is 20 m horizontally away and its top is at 45° above eye level.
Since tan 45° = 1, the height above eye level is 20 m.
lessons.question: Find the exact value of sin 60° × cos 30°.
lessons.mistake: Keep exact roots and fractions until the end if an exact answer is requested.

cards.definition: An angle measured upwards from a horizontal line.
An angle measured downwards from a horizontal line.

quiz.q: What is the exact value of sin 30°?
quiz.why: A 30°–60°–90° triangle gives sin 30° = 1/2.

misconception.q: What is the exact value of sin 30°? Sam answers: “√3/2.” Explain why this is wrong.
